# Kafka 2.8.2 wire protocol

This document is the grammar that the `main` branch implements. It describes **only** what Apache Kafka 2.8.2
speaks — the last release of the 2.x major, so it covers everything Kafka 2.0, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 2.6, 2.7 and
2.8 added and the bug-fix releases after them, which changed no wire format. Every line carries only its own
protocol document: the grammars of the lines below live on their own branches (`docs/protocol/1.1.md` on `1.x`,
`docs/protocol/0.11.0.md` on `0.11.x`, `docs/protocol/0.10.2.md` on `0.10.x`, `docs/protocol/0.9.0.md` on `0.9.x`,
`docs/protocol/0.8.2.md` on `0.8.x`), while their wire vectors travel upwards in [`vectors/`](vectors) and are
replayed against the classes of this line — the strongest regression test the repository has, because a 2.8.2 broker
still speaks every one of those older versions.

**The 2.x line is being built one Kafka minor at a time**, from 2.0 upwards, and this document grows with it: the
api-key table below is the full answer of a 2.8.2 broker from the first day, and every row says which of the
versions it names this branch already implements.

Sources, in decreasing order of authority:

1. The broker itself (Apache Kafka 2.8.2, `docker/kafka-2.8.2`, four listeners on 9092–9095).
2. The 2.8.2 sources. **The JSON message specifications are the schema authority**: from Kafka 2.4 the Java client
   generates its request and response classes from `clients/src/main/resources/common/message/<Api>{Request,Response}.json`,
   which carry `validVersions`, `flexibleVersions`, the `listeners` an api is served on and, per field, `versions`,
   `nullableVersions`, `taggedVersions`/`tag`, `default` and `entityType`, next to a `// Version N …` comment that
   names the KIP of every version. `Protocol.java` is long gone and the `schemaVersions()` of Kafka 1.x with it.
   Next to the specifications: `clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/protocol/{ApiKeys,Errors}.java` for
   the api table and the error codes, `common/protocol/types/*.java` and `common/protocol/ByteBufferAccessor.java`
   for the primitive types, `clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/record/*.java` for the message format,
   and `core/src/main/scala/kafka/server/{KafkaApis,AdminManager,DynamicBrokerConfig}.scala`,
   `core/src/main/scala/kafka/network/{SocketServer,RequestChannel}.scala`,
   `core/src/main/scala/kafka/coordinator/{group,transaction}/*.scala` and `core/src/main/scala/kafka/log/*.scala`
   for what the broker does with a request. The tags `2.0.1`, `2.1.1`, `2.2.2`, `2.3.1`, `2.4.1`, `2.5.1`, `2.6.3`,
   `2.7.2` and `2.8.2` all exist in the Apache repository; they are the last release of every 2.x minor, and "@
   2.4.1" in this repository means that tag, which is how a version is attributed to the minor release that added
   it.
3. The wiki page [A Guide To The Kafka Protocol](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/A+Guide+To+The+Kafka+Protocol)
   and the KIPs of the additions of this line, which the JSON comments name one by one: KIP-219 (a throttled broker
   answers first, which is what almost every api version of Kafka 2.0 is), KIP-320 (leader epochs), KIP-110 (zstd),
   KIP-290 (ACL pattern types), KIP-380 (broker epochs), KIP-368 (SASL re-authentication), KIP-207, KIP-394,
   KIP-430, KIP-339, KIP-392 (rack-aware fetching), KIP-345 (static membership), **KIP-482 (flexible versions:
   compact types and tagged fields)**, KIP-511 (the client software name of ApiVersions v3), KIP-455 (partition
   reassignment), KIP-460, KIP-464, KIP-467, KIP-496, KIP-525, KIP-360, KIP-447, KIP-559, KIP-546, KIP-554,
   KIP-569, KIP-497, KIP-584, KIP-588, KIP-599, KIP-516 (topic ids), KIP-518, KIP-664 and KIP-700, next to the KIPs
   of the grammar this document inherits: KIP-98, KIP-82, KIP-101, KIP-107, KIP-112/113, KIP-124, KIP-133, KIP-152,
   KIP-186, KIP-195, KIP-226, KIP-227, KIP-229 and KIP-48. The wiki was written for 0.10 and never caught up with
   anything after it; where it disagrees with the container, the container wins.

Notation follows the wiki: productions are camel case, primitive types lower case, `[foo]` is an array of `foo`,
and a sequence of productions means concatenation.

Like every line above `0.9.x`, this branch does not have to guess what its broker speaks: Kafka 0.10.0 added the
**ApiVersions** api (key 18), and the api-key table below is the literal answer of a real 2.8.2 broker to it.

## What 1.1.1 adds to the 0.11.0.3 protocol

Kafka 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 are a much smaller raise than the 0.11 line below: nine new api keys, seven new client-facing
api versions of apis that already existed (plus two broker-to-broker ones), sixteen new error codes — and **no new
primitive type, no new message format and no change to the request header**. Everything here is one more version of a schema that already exists, or one more
request class. The releases after 1.1.0 (1.0.1, 1.0.2, 1.1.1) are bug fixes and change nothing on the wire, which
is why this line speaks the last of them.

Every row below is implemented and verified against the container; the api section further down says what the
broker answered — the incremental fetch sessions of KIP-227 included, the Fetch v7 **frame** and the session state
machine of the consumer alike.

| Area | 0.11.0.3 | 1.1.1 | KIP | Since |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Api keys | 0-33 | 0-42: **AlterReplicaLogDirs 34, DescribeLogDirs 35, SaslAuthenticate 36, CreatePartitions 37, CreateDelegationToken 38, RenewDelegationToken 39, ExpireDelegationToken 40, DescribeDelegationToken 41, DeleteGroups 42** | 113, 152, 195, 48, 229 | 34-37 in 1.0, 38-42 in 1.1 |
| Message format | record batch v2 (magic 2) next to the message sets v0 and v1 | **unchanged** — magic 2, no new attribute bit; `log.message.format.version` of the container is `1.1-IV0` and a 1.1.1 broker still down-converts a batch for a Fetch below v4 | – | – |
| Produce (0) | v0-v3 | **v4**: the frame of v3, byte for byte — the version only says that the client understands the error code 56. **v5**: the response partition gains `log_start_offset` int64 after `log_append_time`, which is what lets a producer tell a spurious `OutOfOrderSequence` from a real one | – | 1.0 |
| Fetch (1) | v0-v5 | **v6**: the frame of v5, byte for byte (again the code 56). **v7**: incremental fetch sessions — the request gains `session_id` int32 and `epoch` int32 after `isolation_level`, and a trailing `forgotten_topics_data`, the response a top-level `error_code` int16 and `session_id` int32 after `throttle_time_ms`. `session_id = 0, epoch = -1` is the session-less full fetch of every older version, which the broker serves unchanged, and the incremental sessions are what `KafkaConsumer` speaks, one per broker | 227 | v6 1.0, v7 1.1 |
| Metadata (3) | v0-v4 | **v5**: every partition of the response gains `offline_replicas [int32]` after `isr`; the request is unchanged | 112, 113 | 1.0 |
| ControlledShutdown (7) | **v1 only** as far as ApiVersions is concerned, and every version answered | **v0 and v1**, and nothing above: the api moved to the schemas of the Java client, `RequestHeader` got a schema of its own for the client-id-less v0 frame, and a version above the table now costs the connection like everywhere else | – | 1.0 |
| SaslHandshake (17) | v0 | **v1**: the same frame; a client that sends v1 promises to continue with framed **SaslAuthenticate** requests instead of the raw, unframed token exchange, and gets an error code for a failed authentication where 0.11 closed the socket | 152 | 1.0 |
| DescribeConfigs (32) | v0 | **v1**: the request gains `include_synonyms` boolean after the resources; in the response entry the `is_default` boolean is **replaced** by `config_source` int8 and the entry gains `config_synonyms` | 226 | 1.1 |
| AlterConfigs (33) | v0 | **unchanged on the wire**, but a 1.1 broker accepts a **broker** resource for the dynamic configuration options of KIP-226, where 0.11 refused every broker resource with 42 — including the cluster-wide default resource, whose name is the empty string | 226 | 1.1 |
| Offsets (2), OffsetCommit (8), OffsetFetch (9), GroupCoordinator (10), JoinGroup (11), Heartbeat (12), LeaveGroup (13), SyncGroup (14), DescribeGroups (15), ListGroups (16), ApiVersions (18), CreateTopics (19), DeleteTopics (20), DeleteRecords (21), InitProducerId (22), OffsetForLeaderEpoch (23), the transaction apis (24-28), the ACL apis (29-31) | – | **unchanged** — same versions, same frames | – | – |
| LeaderAndIsr (4), UpdateMetadata (6) | v0 / v0-v3 | **v1** / **v4**, both broker-to-broker and not implemented here: the partition state gains `is_new` and `offline_replicas` respectively | 112, 113 | 1.0 |
| **AlterReplicaLogDirs (34)** | – | **new, v0**: `[log_dir [topic [partition]]]` → `throttle_time_ms [topic [partition error_code]]`; moves a replica to another log directory of the broker that hosts it, and answers 57 `LOG_DIR_NOT_FOUND` for a path the broker does not have — or for a relative one — and 9 `REPLICA_NOT_AVAILABLE` for a replica it does not host. The answer only says that the move was **accepted**; the copy runs in a `ReplicaAlterLogDirsThread` and is watched with DescribeLogDirs | 113 | 1.0 |
| **DescribeLogDirs (35)** | – | **new, v0**: `[topic [partition]]`, nullable for "every partition" → `throttle_time_ms [error_code log_dir [topic [partition size offset_lag is_future]]]`; broker-local, one entry per `log.dirs` entry — an **empty** topic array asks for no replica and answers the directories alone, a **null** one for every replica of the broker. A replica that is being moved is reported in both directories, `is_future` marking the destination | 113 | 1.0 |
| **SaslAuthenticate (36)** | – | **new, v0**: `sasl_auth_bytes` bytes → `error_code error_message sasl_auth_bytes`; carries the SASL token exchange as ordinary framed requests after a SaslHandshake **v1** | 152 | 1.0 |
| **CreatePartitions (37)** | – | **new, v0**: `[topic count assignment] timeout validate_only` → `throttle_time_ms [topic error_code error_message]`; controller-only like CreateTopics, and it can only grow a topic | 195 | 1.0 |
| **CreateDelegationToken (38), RenewDelegationToken (39), ExpireDelegationToken (40), DescribeDelegationToken (41)** | – | **new, v0**: tokens issued to a SASL principal; refused with 64 on a PLAINTEXT or one-way-SSL channel and disabled with 61 unless the broker has a `delegation.token.master.key`. A token can be issued, renewed, expired and described here; *authenticating* with one is a SASL/SCRAM login and is not implemented | 48 | 1.1 |
| **DeleteGroups (42)** | – | **new, v0**: `[group]` → `throttle_time_ms [group error_code]`, sent to the group coordinator; 68 `NON_EMPTY_GROUP` for a group that still has members, 69 `GROUP_ID_NOT_FOUND` for one the coordinator does not know | 229 | 1.1 |
| Group states | `PreparingRebalance`, **`AwaitingSync`**, `Stable`, `Empty`, `Dead` | the same five states, one of them **renamed**: `AwaitingSync` is called **`CompletingRebalance`** and that is the string DescribeGroups answers | – | 1.0 |
| Producer semantics | the broker remembers the **last batch** of a producer id per partition | the last **five** (`ProducerStateManager.NumBatchesToRetain = 5`), so a duplicate of any of them is answered as the original append and the "a duplicate of an older batch is 45" quirk of 0.11 is gone; **59** `UNKNOWN_PRODUCER_ID` says that the broker lost the state of a producer, and `log_start_offset` of a Produce v5 answer says why | 98 | 1.0 |
| Consumer semantics | `isolation.level = read_committed` | the same, plus the offline replicas of a Metadata v5 answer and the **incremental fetch sessions** of KIP-227, one of which `KafkaConsumer` holds with every broker it reads from | 227 | 1.1 |
| Error codes | -1 … 55 | -1 … **71**: 56-60 with Kafka 1.0 (storage, log directories, SASL authentication, the unknown producer id, a reassignment in progress), 61-71 with Kafka 1.1 (the delegation tokens, the empty/unknown group of DeleteGroups, the fetch sessions). Only **56, 70 and 71** are retriable | 113, 152, 48, 229, 227 | 56-60 1.0, 61-71 1.1 |
| An unparseable frame | the broker closes the connection | unchanged — and it is now the answer for **every** api of the table, ControlledShutdown included | – | 1.0 |

Everything else in this document is the 0.11.0.3 grammar, unchanged and re-verified against a 1.1.1 broker.

## Implementation model

Protocol classes do not hand-roll `pack()`/`unpack()` calls: every message and DTO declares its binary layout and the
engine reads and writes it. The design came up the cascade from `0.10.x`, which is why the shape of a class here is
the shape it has on the four lines below.

* `Protocol\Kafka\Protocol\BinarySchemaInterface::getScheme(): array` maps a property name to its type.
* `Protocol\Kafka\Protocol\BinarySchema` is the engine: `readObjectFromStream()`, `writeObjectToStream()`,
  `readSingleType()`, `writeSingleType()`, `getObjectTypeSize()`.
* A request extends its parent scheme: `parent::getScheme() + ['topics' => [BinarySchema::TYPE_STRING]]`.
* Arrays are `[ItemType]` for a plain list, `['keyField' => ItemClass::class]` for a list indexed by one of the item
  fields, and gain `BinarySchema::FLAG_NULLABLE => true` when `-1` is a valid count.

The type set of the apis is the one of 0.10, and **Kafka 1.1 adds no primitive type to it**: `TYPE_INT8`,
`TYPE_INT16`, `TYPE_INT32`, `TYPE_INT64`, `TYPE_BOOLEAN`, `TYPE_STRING`, `TYPE_NULLABLE_STRING`, `TYPE_BYTEARRAY`
(nullable) and int32-prefixed arrays. A *request* can carry a nullable array since 0.10 (the topics of Metadata v1
and of OffsetFetch v2, the log directories of DescribeLogDirs v0 and the owners of DescribeDelegationToken v0), so
`null` written as `ff ff ff ff` and `[]` written as `00 00 00 00` are two different requests here.

Kafka 0.11 added one family on top of it, and **only inside a record batch v2** — no request or response body of any
api uses it:

* `TYPE_VARINT_ZIGZAG` (11) — an int32 written zigzag-encoded, 7 bits per byte;
* `TYPE_VARLONG_ZIGZAG` (12) — the same for an int64;
* `TYPE_VARCHAR_ZIGZAG` (13) — a byte array whose length is such a varint, `-1` (`01`) meaning `null`;
* `FLAG_VARARRAY` (14) — an array whose element count is a varint instead of an int32.

`Common\Utils\ByteUtils` holds the zigzag and CRC-32C helpers of `org.apache.kafka.common.utils.ByteUtils`, and
`Stream::readVarint()`/`writeVarint()` the byte loop. **The numbers 5, 6 and 7 stay reserved**: they were
`TYPE_VARINT`, `TYPE_VARLONG` and `TYPE_VARCHAR` of the pre-schema `main`, which wrote *raw* (non-zigzag) varints,
and they are left free so that a reader of an old scheme cannot mistake one for the other.

An api that has more than one version and whose layout changes between them is described by one class per version:
a scheme is a static property of a class, so `OffsetCommitRequest` (the highest version) and `OffsetCommitRequestV0`
differ in their `VERSION` constant, which the version-aware `getScheme()` of the request and of its DTOs follows.
`XRequest` is always the highest version the broker of this line serves, and every `XRequestV<n>` below it only
lowers that constant.

Two defects of the engine of the pre-schema `main` are fixed here: `TYPE_INT8` is read as a **signed** value (the
attributes byte of a message and the error codes are signed), and `TYPE_BYTEARRAY` round-trips `null` as the int32
`-1` that the specification prescribes.

### Flexible versions in the engine (KIP-482)

**Kafka 2.4 gave the protocol a second encoding of the same types, and it is a mode rather than a set of types.**
From the `flexibleVersions` of an api on, *every* string, byte array and array of that version announces its length
as an unsigned varint of `length + 1` (`0` meaning `null`), and *every* structure of it — the body, every nested
structure and the request header — ends in a **tagged-field section**. There is no version in Kafka 2.8.2 that mixes
the two encodings, and the JSON specifications have no way of expressing one: a version is flexible or it is not.

The engine follows that shape exactly. **Flexibility is asked once per message and handed down**, so a DTO never
needs a version of its own and the same `FetchRequestTopic` scheme serves a Fetch v11 and a Fetch v12:

* `Protocol\Kafka\Protocol\FlexibleSchemaInterface::isFlexible()` is the question, and
  `AbstractProtocolMessage` answers it with `VERSION >= FLEXIBLE_VERSION`. A message class declares
  `public const int FLEXIBLE_VERSION = 12;` next to its `VERSION`; the default is `PHP_INT_MAX`, i.e. "never", which
  is what every api of the lines below this one is, and what SaslHandshake (17) and OffsetDelete (47) stay.
* Every method of `BinarySchema` takes the answer as its last parameter — `readSingleType($type, $stream, $path,
  $flexible)`, `writeSingleType($type, $value, $stream, $flexible)`, `getSingleTypeSize($type, $value, $flexible)` —
  and `readObjectFromStream()`, `writeObjectToStream()` and `getObjectTypeSize()` take it as `?bool`, where `null`
  means "ask the class itself". A top-level message is therefore read with `null` and every structure inside it with
  the `true` or `false` that came out of that question.
* `TYPE_STRING`, `TYPE_NULLABLE_STRING`, `TYPE_BYTEARRAY` and every array notation change their encoding with that
  flag and **nothing else changes**: the PHP value of a field is the same in both, which is what makes a scheme
  version-independent. `TYPE_STRING_NEVER_COMPACT` (9) is the one type that ignores the flag — the `client_id` of
  the request header v2, `"flexibleVersions": "none"` in `RequestHeader.json`.
* **Tagged fields are declared in the scheme** as ordinary `property => type` entries whose type is a
  `Protocol\Kafka\Protocol\TaggedField(tag, type, default)`, at the end of the structure:

  ```php
  public static function getScheme(): array
  {
      $body = parent::getScheme() + [
          'errorCode'      => BinarySchema::TYPE_INT16,
          'apiVersions'    => ['apiKey' => ApiVersionsResponseMetadata::class],
          'throttleTimeMs' => BinarySchema::TYPE_INT32,
      ];
      if (static::VERSION >= 3) {
          $body['supportedFeatures']      = new TaggedField(0, ['name' => ApiVersionsSupportedFeature::class], []);
          $body['finalizedFeaturesEpoch'] = new TaggedField(1, BinarySchema::TYPE_INT64, -1);
          $body['finalizedFeatures']      = new TaggedField(2, ['name' => ApiVersionsFinalizedFeature::class], []);
      }

      return $body;
  }
  ```

  The engine takes those entries out of the field sequence, writes them at the end of the structure in ascending
  order of their tag, and **leaves out every field whose value equals its declared default** — the rule of
  `Message.write()` in the Java client, and the reason a captured frame survives a decode and encode round trip. A
  structure of a flexible version that declares no tagged field at all still gets the empty section (`00`), and one
  that is not flexible ignores the declaration altogether.
* A tag that the scheme does not declare is **skipped by its announced size** and kept as raw bytes by every class
  that uses `Protocol\Kafka\Protocol\PreservesUnknownTaggedFields` — every request and response does — so that a
  frame of a later Kafka release survives the round trip instead of losing bytes.
* **A structure of the specification ends in a tagged-field section; a group of fields does not.** The difference is
  invisible in the plain encoding - neither is counted or delimited on the wire - but a flexible version gives every
  real structure a `00` the broker expects and a field group none. Where this package wraps two or more *flat* fields
  of a specification in an object of its own, the field is declared `new InlineStruct(TheClass::class)` instead of
  `TheClass::class`: the scheme of that class is inlined into the enclosing structure and gets no section. The marker
  belongs to the **field**, not to the class - `Common\Security\KafkaPrincipal` is an `InlineStruct` as the `owner`
  of a CreateDelegationToken or DescribeDelegationToken answer, where `PrincipalType` and `PrincipalName` are two
  ordinary fields of the response, and a *real* structure as an entry of the `[]CreatableRenewers` of the request.
  An entry of a `[]Something` array of the specification is never an `InlineStruct`.
* The **headers** are part of the same mechanism: `AbstractRequest::getHeaderVersion()` and
  `AbstractResponse::getHeaderVersion()` are the `ApiKeys.requestHeaderVersion()`/`responseHeaderVersion()` of the
  Java client, and they decide whether the scheme of the header carries a `TYPE_TAG_BUFFER` entry
  (`headerTaggedFields`). The two exceptions of the protocol are two overrides: `ControlledShutdownRequest` answers
  the header v0 for its version 0, and `ApiVersionsResponse` answers the header **v0 for every version**, flexible
  body or not.

A version bump therefore adds a class, a `VERSION` and - when the version is flexible - a `FLEXIBLE_VERSION`, and
never a second scheme for the same structure.

## Protocol primitive types

| Type    | Encoding                                                                         |
|---------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `int8`  | 1 byte, signed                                                                    |
| `int16` | 2 bytes, signed, big endian                                                       |
| `int32` | 4 bytes, signed, big endian                                                       |
| `int64` | 8 bytes, signed, big endian (two's complement)                                    |
| `boolean` | 1 byte: `00` is false, **any** non-zero byte is true; this client writes `01`   |
| `float64` | **Kafka 2.6 (KIP-546).** 8 bytes of an IEEE 754 double in **network order**, `Type.FLOAT64` of the Java client (`ByteBuffer.putDouble`); the quota values of the keys 48 and 49 are the only fields of 2.8.2 that use it. `TYPE_FLOAT64`, `pack('E')` |
| `string`| `int16` length `N` followed by `N` bytes of UTF-8; `N = -1` (`ff ff`) means `null` |
| `bytes` | `int32` length `N` followed by `N` bytes; `N = -1` (`ff ff ff ff`) means `null`    |
| `[foo]` | `int32` element count `N` followed by `N` repetitions of `foo`                     |
| `varint` | **Kafka 0.11, record batch v2 only.** An int32 zigzag-encoded (`0 → 0, -1 → 1, 1 → 2, -2 → 3 …`) and written 7 bits per byte, least significant group first, the high bit set on every byte but the last: 1 to 5 bytes (`ByteUtils.writeVarint` @ 0.11.0.3). `TYPE_VARINT_ZIGZAG` of the engine, `Common\Utils\ByteUtils` for the zigzag step |
| `varlong` | The same encoding of an int64, 1 to 10 bytes. `TYPE_VARLONG_ZIGZAG` |
| varint `bytes` | `varint` length `N` followed by `N` bytes; `N = -1` (`01`) means `null` - the key, value and headers of a record. `TYPE_VARCHAR_ZIGZAG` |
| varint `[foo]` | `varint` element count `N` followed by `N` repetitions of `foo` - the headers of a record. `FLAG_VARARRAY` (the count is zigzag-encoded too) |
| `uuid` | **Kafka 2.8 (KIP-516).** 16 raw bytes, no length prefix; `00…00` is "no id". `TYPE_UUID` |
| `unsigned_varint` | **Kafka 2.4 (KIP-482).** The value itself, 7 bits per byte, least significant group first, the high bit set on every byte but the last: 1 to 5 bytes, **no zigzag step** (`ByteUtils.writeUnsignedVarint` @ 2.8.2). `Stream::readUnsignedVarint()`/`writeUnsignedVarint()`; it carries every length of the flexible encoding |
| `compact_string` | **Flexible versions only.** `unsigned_varint` `N + 1` followed by `N` bytes of UTF-8; `0` means `null` (`compact_nullable_string`), and a non-nullable field that is sent as `0` is a protocol error |
| `compact_bytes` | **Flexible versions only.** The same encoding for a byte array |
| `compact_[foo]` | **Flexible versions only.** `unsigned_varint` `N + 1` element count followed by `N` repetitions of `foo`; `0` means `null` |
| `TAG_BUFFER` | **Flexible versions only.** The tagged-field section that closes every structure: `unsigned_varint` number of fields, then per field an `unsigned_varint` tag, an `unsigned_varint` size and `size` bytes of value, the tags ascending. An empty section is the single byte `00`, and a reader skips a tag it does not know by its size |

**The compact types are not new types but the same ones in a flexible version**, which is why the table above lists
them once: from the `flexibleVersions` of an api on, every `string`, `bytes` and `[foo]` of that version *is* the
compact one and every structure of it ends in a `TAG_BUFFER`. The one field of Kafka 2.8.2 that stays behind is the
`client_id` of the request header v2 (`"flexibleVersions": "none"`).

Byte-exact examples, as implemented by `Protocol\Kafka\IO\Stream`:

| Value                     | Bytes                     |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| `int16` `-1`              | `ff ff`                   |
| `int16` `-32768`          | `80 00`                   |
| `int32` `-1`              | `ff ff ff ff`             |
| `int64` `-1`              | `ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff` |
| `string` `null`           | `ff ff`                   |
| `string` `""`             | `00 00`                   |
| `string` `"test"`         | `00 04 74 65 73 74`       |
| `bytes` `null`            | `ff ff ff ff`             |
| `bytes` `""`              | `00 00 00 00`             |
| `boolean` `false` / `true`| `00` / `01`               |
| empty array               | `00 00 00 00`             |
| null array                | `ff ff ff ff`             |
| `varint` `0` / `-1` / `1` | `00` / `01` / `02`        |
| `varint` `64` / `-65`     | `80 01` / `81 01`         |
| `varint` `300`            | `d8 04`                   |
| `varint` `2147483647`     | `fe ff ff ff 0f`          |
| `varint` `-2147483648`    | `ff ff ff ff 0f`          |
| `varlong` `2^31`          | `80 80 80 80 10`          |
| `varlong` `PHP_INT_MAX`   | `fe ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff 01` |
| varint `bytes` `null` / `""` / `de ad be ef` | `01` / `00` / `08 de ad be ef` |
| `unsigned_varint` `0` / `1` / `127` | `00` / `01` / `7f` |
| `unsigned_varint` `128` / `16383` / `16384` | `80 01` / `ff 7f` / `80 80 01` |
| `unsigned_varint` `2^28-1` / `2^28` / `2^32-1` | `ff ff ff 7f` / `80 80 80 80 01` / `ff ff ff ff 0f` |
| `compact_string` `null` / `""` / `"test"` | `00` / `01` / `05 74 65 73 74` |
| `compact_bytes` `null` / `""` / `de ad` | `00` / `01` / `03 de ad` |
| empty `compact_[foo]` / null `compact_[foo]` | `01` / `00` |
| `compact_[foo]` of two items | `03` … |
| empty `TAG_BUFFER` | `00` |
| `TAG_BUFFER` with the int64 tag 1 = 0 | `01 01 08 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` |

An empty string and a null string are different values on the wire; the client id of a request, for example, is always
an empty string and never null. The same holds for the compact types, where the distinction is `01` against `00` — and
a compact length is never `-1`: the `0` that the `+ 1` frees up is what `null` is written as.

## Common request and response structure

Every request and every response is framed by its size:

```
RequestOrResponse => Size (RequestMessage | ResponseMessage)
  Size => int32
```

`Size` is the length in bytes of everything that follows it. A client reads a response by first reading these four
bytes as an integer `N` and then reading exactly `N` more bytes.

### Requests

There are **three** request headers in Kafka 2.8.2, and `RequestHeader.json` declares all three:

```
RequestHeader (Version: 0) => ApiKey ApiVersion CorrelationId
RequestHeader (Version: 1) => ApiKey ApiVersion CorrelationId ClientId
RequestHeader (Version: 2) => ApiKey ApiVersion CorrelationId ClientId TAG_BUFFER
  ApiKey        => int16
  ApiVersion    => int16
  CorrelationId => int32
  ClientId      => string     (int16 length, never compact)
```

* `ApiKey` — numeric id of the API being invoked (see the table below).
* `ApiVersion` — version of that API; the broker answers in exactly the format that matches the requested version.
* `CorrelationId` — user-supplied value that the broker passes back unmodified.
* `ClientId` — user-supplied identifier of the client application.

**Which header a frame carries follows from its api version and nothing else**, and the broker decides it the same
way the client does: `ApiKeys.requestHeaderVersion(apiVersion)` @ 2.8.2 answers the header **v2** from the first
flexible version of that api on, the header **v0** for the single frame that has no client id — ControlledShutdown
v0 — and the header **v1** everywhere else. The client side of it is
`AbstractRequest::getHeaderVersion()`.

Two consequences a client has to know:

* The `ClientId` keeps its `int16` length prefix **even in the header v2**, where every other string of the frame is
  compact. `RequestHeader.json` marks the field `"flexibleVersions": "none"` with the comment *"older brokers must be
  able to read the request header for any ApiVersionsRequest, even if it is from a newer version"*.
* `RequestHeader.parse` reads the api key and the api version **before** anything validates them, so a frame of a
  version the broker does not serve is read with the header that version *would* have. Asking an unknown version of
  ApiVersions with the old header is therefore a parse failure and costs the connection, while the same frame with
  an empty tag buffer is answered — see "An api the broker does not serve closes the connection".

A Metadata request v0 with client id `test`, correlation id `1` and an empty topic list is therefore:

```
00 00 00 12   Size = 18
00 03         ApiKey = 3 (Metadata)
00 00         ApiVersion = 0
00 00 00 01   CorrelationId = 1
00 04 74 65 73 74   ClientId = "test"
00 00 00 00   [TopicName] = empty
```

and the ApiVersions v3 request of the same client — the first flexible frame this branch sends — is:

```
00 00 00 2c   Size = 44
00 12         ApiKey = 18 (ApiVersions)
00 03         ApiVersion = 3
00 00 00 01   CorrelationId = 1
00 04 74 65 73 74   ClientId = "test"      (int16 length: the one string that stays plain)
00            TAG_BUFFER of the request header v2: no tagged field
18 6c 69 73 61 63 68 65 6e 6b 6f 2d 6b 61 66 6b 61 2d 63 6c 69 65 6e 74
              ClientSoftwareName = "lisachenko-kafka-client"   (compact: 23 + 1 = 0x18)
04 32 2e 38   ClientSoftwareVersion = "2.8"                    (compact: 3 + 1)
00            TAG_BUFFER of the body
```

### Responses

There are **two** response headers, and a response carries the one its api version prescribes
(`ApiKeys.responseHeaderVersion(apiVersion)`, `AbstractResponse::getHeaderVersion()`):

```
ResponseHeader (Version: 0) => CorrelationId
ResponseHeader (Version: 1) => CorrelationId TAG_BUFFER
  Size          => int32
  CorrelationId => int32
```

The broker guarantees that responses on a single connection come back in the order the requests were sent, and every
response repeats the correlation id of its request.

**The header v1 belongs to every flexible version — except one.** The answer of **ApiVersions** (key 18) always
carries the header v0, flexible body or not; the generator writes that exception out by hand, with the comment
*"ApiVersionsResponse always includes a v0 header. See KIP-511 for details."* The reason is the same as for the
plain `client_id` above: a client that guessed the version too high has to be able to read the correlation id and
the error code of the answer without knowing which header the broker used. The v3 answer of the container therefore
opens with the correlation id and the error code directly, and its compact api array follows:

```
00 00 01 9e   Size = 414
00 00 00 6a   CorrelationId = 106          (and no TAG_BUFFER: the response header v0 of this api)
00 00         ErrorCode = 0
39            [ApiKeys] = 56 entries       (compact: 56 + 1 = 0x39)
00 00 00 00 00 09 00                       Produce, v0-v9, and the TAG_BUFFER of the entry
…
00 00 00 00   ThrottleTimeMs = 0
01            TAG_BUFFER of the body: one tagged field
01 08 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00              tag 1 = FinalizedFeaturesEpoch, 8 bytes, 0
```

There is exactly one exception to the request/response symmetry: a Produce request with `RequiredAcks = 0` gets no
response at all.

## API keys

From `clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/protocol/ApiKeys.java` @ 2.8.2, which ends at key **64**, and
from the JSON message specifications next to it, which say for every api which versions are valid, which of them are
**flexible** (KIP-482) and on which **listener** it is served. Identifiers follow the classes of the `1.x` line
wherever the concept exists on both, and the Java client's names for what Kafka 2.x adds. Api key 10 is therefore
still called **GroupCoordinator** here, although the sources renamed it to `FindCoordinator` in 0.11; the 0.8.2
sources called it `ConsumerMetadataRequest`.

The table below is not a guess but the literal answer of the container to an **ApiVersions** request (key 18),
decoded by [`tests/Integration/ApiVersionProbeTest.php`](../../tests/Integration/ApiVersionProbeTest.php) and stored
as the wire vectors `apiversions.response.v0`, `.v1` and `.v2`. The same test sends a real frame of every key at the
**maximum version** of the table — with the request header v2 and a compact body wherever that version is flexible —
and checks that the broker really answers it, and one frame above every one of them to check that it really does not.

**A 2.8.2 broker answers with 56 keys**: 0 to 51, 56, 57, 60 and 61. The set is the one of the **listener** the
request arrived on: Kafka 2.8 (KIP-500) built `ApiVersionManager` around the three listener types `zkBroker`,
`broker` and `controller` that every JSON specification names, and the container is a ZooKeeper-backed broker, so
the KRaft apis of the controller — the raft apis 52 to 55 (KIP-595), `Envelope` (58), `FetchSnapshot` (59) and the
broker registration apis 62 to 64 — are missing from its answer and cost the connection when they are sent anyway.
As before, an api whose `minRequiredInterBrokerMagic` is above the message format of the broker is dropped from the
answer as well; the container runs `2.8-IV1`, which is magic 2 and drops nothing.

The columns:

* **Versions served** is the `validVersions` of the JSON specification and the range the container reports. Every
  minimum is 0 since Kafka 1.0.
* **Flexible from** is the first version whose frame is written with the compact types and the tagged fields of
  KIP-482 (`flexibleVersions` of the *request*); `–` means the api never became flexible. Only **SaslHandshake**
  (17) and **OffsetDelete** (47) never did.
* **What Kafka 2.x added** names every version above the ceiling of the `1.x` line and the minor release that added
  it, verified against the tags `2.0.1`, `2.1.1`, `2.2.2`, `2.3.1`, `2.4.1`, `2.5.1`, `2.6.3`, `2.7.2` and `2.8.2`.
* **Implemented here** lists the versions this branch has a class for; the one in **bold** is the version the client
  sends. **The 2.x line is built one Kafka minor at a time**, so a version the broker serves and this branch has not
  reached yet is named as *not yet implemented*; when the line is complete that qualifier is gone from every row.

The keys **4, 5, 6, 27 and 56** are answered by a 2.8.2 broker like any other request, and the probe sends one frame
of each without changing anything: 4, 5 and 6 with the controller epoch `-1` and the broker epoch `-1`, which are
stale, so the broker answers the error code **11** (`StaleControllerEpoch`) and changes nothing; 27 with an empty
marker array, which it answers with an empty array of its own; and 56 (`AlterIsr`, the broker-to-controller api of
KIP-497) with the broker epoch `-1`, which is answered with the code **77** (`StaleBrokerEpoch`).

**Every row starts at the minimum version 0.** That has been true since Kafka 1.0, which gave the client-id-less
frame of ControlledShutdown v0 a request header schema of its own; a 0.9 to 0.11 broker reported `MinVersion = 1`
for key 7.

**The set of keys is not a constant of the release**, and a client must read the table it gets instead of the one
printed here: the listener decides it (above), and so does the `inter.broker.protocol.version` of the broker.

**The ACL apis 29, 30 and 31 are not implemented on this line** (decision 3 of the epic, inherited from the two
lines below): they only do anything on a broker configured with an `authorizer.class.name`, and this repository
captures every wire vector from a real broker. Without an authorizer a 2.8.2 broker answers a DescribeAcls with the
error code **54** (`SecurityDisabled`) and the message `No Authorizer is configured on the broker` — it does answer
them, which is what the probe checks.

**The four delegation-token apis 38 to 41 are served and answer 64 on the PLAINTEXT listener.** A token is only
issued over a channel that authenticated a real principal, so `KafkaApis` @ 2.8.2 refuses the request with
`DELEGATION_TOKEN_REQUEST_NOT_ALLOWED` before it reads the body. The container does carry a
`delegation.token.secret.key` — the 2.x name of the `delegation.token.master.key` of the 1.x image — so the answer
is not the 61 (`DELEGATION_TOKEN_AUTH_DISABLED`) of a broker without one, and the apis are exercised over the SASL
listeners 9094 and 9095, where the principal of the connection is the SASL/PLAIN user. *Using* a token afterwards
needs SASL/SCRAM, which this client does not implement.

### An api the broker does not serve closes the connection

**This is the behaviour that changed in Kafka 0.10 and that every release since keeps, and it is the one a client of
the two lowest lines gets wrong.** A 0.9.0.1 broker silently *dropped* a frame it could not parse and kept the
connection open; every broker from 0.10.2.2 to 2.8.2 **closes the connection**.

What changed with the generated message classes of Kafka 2.4 is only the *reason* the broker logs.
`RequestContext.parseRequest()` @ 2.8.2 parses every incoming frame with the `<Api>RequestData` class of the version
in its header, and that class refuses a version it does not know with an `UnsupportedVersionException`;
`Processor.parseRequestHeader` refuses an api key that is not enabled on the listener and one that `ApiKeys.forId()`
cannot name at all; and a body that does not match the schema of its version still ends in a
`BufferUnderflowException` or a `SchemaException`. `SocketServer.processCompletedReceives` wraps all of them in an
`InvalidRequestException` and closes the channel. All five frames below were sent to the container of this line:

```
ERROR Closing socket for 172.18.0.2:9092-172.18.0.1:49438-545 because of error (kafka.network.Processor)
org.apache.kafka.common.errors.InvalidRequestException: Error getting request for apiKey: OFFSET_COMMIT,
apiVersion: 9, connectionId: …, listenerName: ListenerName(PLAINTEXT), principal: User:ANONYMOUS
Caused by: org.apache.kafka.common.errors.UnsupportedVersionException: The OFFSET_COMMIT protocol does not
support version 9
```

```
ERROR Closing socket for … because of error (kafka.network.Processor)
org.apache.kafka.common.errors.InvalidRequestException: Received request api key VOTE which is not enabled
```

```
ERROR Closing socket for … because of error (kafka.network.Processor)
org.apache.kafka.common.errors.InvalidRequestException: Error parsing request header. Our best guess of the
apiKey is: 65
Caused by: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Unexpected api key: 65
```

```
ERROR Closing socket for … because of error (kafka.network.Processor)
org.apache.kafka.common.errors.InvalidRequestException: Error getting request for apiKey: JOIN_GROUP,
apiVersion: 1, connectionId: …, listenerName: ListenerName(PLAINTEXT), principal: User:ANONYMOUS
Caused by: org.apache.kafka.common.protocol.types.SchemaException: Error reading field 'member_id': Error reading
string of length 25455, only 10 bytes available
```

```
ERROR Closing socket for … because of error (kafka.network.Processor)
org.apache.kafka.common.errors.InvalidRequestException: Error getting request for apiKey: DESCRIBE_GROUPS,
apiVersion: 5, connectionId: …, listenerName: ListenerName(PLAINTEXT), principal: User:ANONYMOUS
Caused by: java.nio.BufferUnderflowException
	at org.apache.kafka.common.utils.ByteUtils.readUnsignedVarint(ByteUtils.java:146)
```

The last two are bodies, not versions: a JoinGroup **v1** frame carrying a **v0** body — the key and the version are
served, the bytes behind them are not — and a DescribeGroups **v5** frame whose compact array announces three groups
and carries none, or which forgets the tagged-field section at the end of its body. **A flexible frame is refused
exactly like any other malformed one**: there is no error code for a length the broker cannot follow, the
`readUnsignedVarint` in the stack trace is the only hint, and the connection is gone.

Note the first example: the version of the *error* moves with the release. On 1.1.1 the connection died for
OffsetCommit **v4**, which a 2.8.2 broker serves; the frame that dies here is v9. The same holds for every api this
line raises, which is exactly why the test that pins this behaviour derives its frames from the served api table
instead of hard-coding version numbers.

For a client this means:

* The answer to "why did my request never come back" is "the broker hung up", not "the broker dropped it". A
  read on that connection ends in the end of the stream, which this client reports as `NetworkException` (code 13),
  not in a request timeout.
* Only that one connection is lost. The broker itself is unaffected, and the next connection is answered normally.
* A client must never send a version it has not seen in an ApiVersions answer, and never a **flexible** frame to a
  version that is not flexible, or the other way round.

There is exactly **one** exception, and it is verified by the probe:

**ApiVersions answers an unknown version instead of closing.** `RequestContext.parseRequest()` @ 2.8.2 special-cases
key 18 before it parses anything: `isUnsupportedApiVersionsRequest()` rebuilds the request as an
`ApiVersionsRequest(new ApiVersionsRequestData(), (short) 0, header.apiVersion())` and never touches the body, so
that `KafkaApis.handleApiVersionsRequest` sees `hasUnsupportedRequestVersion` and answers
`getErrorResponse(Errors.UNSUPPORTED_VERSION)` — the error code **35**, written in the layout of **version 0** no
matter which version was asked for. The connection survives it, which is what makes the answer usable: a client that
guessed too high reads the 35 and retries with a version it knows. Two details of that answer changed in Kafka 2.4:

* the array is **not empty any more**. KIP-511 fills it with the one row of the ApiVersions api itself
  (`18 0 3` on this container), so that the client learns *which* version to ask for instead of only that it asked
  wrongly. A 1.1.1 broker answered `00 00 00 00` here.
* the **request header still has to be the one the requested version prescribes**. `RequestHeader.parse` @ 2.8.2
  reads the api key and the api version and asks `ApiKeys.forId(apiKey).requestHeaderVersion(apiVersion)` how to
  read the rest of the header, *before* anything validates the version — and for ApiVersions that answer is the
  header **v2** for every version above 2, served or not. A v4 frame with the plain header of the versions 0 to 2 is
  therefore a parse failure like any other:

```
ERROR Closing socket for … because of error (kafka.network.Processor)
org.apache.kafka.common.errors.InvalidRequestException: Error parsing request header. Our best guess of the
apiKey is: 18
Caused by: java.nio.BufferUnderflowException
	at org.apache.kafka.common.utils.ByteUtils.readUnsignedVarint(ByteUtils.java:146)
```

  while the same frame with an empty tag buffer behind the client id is answered with the 35. "Raise the version
  until the broker complains" is therefore not a strategy a client can use above Kafka 2.3 without also raising the
  header.

### Every api of the table validates its version

*Up to Kafka 0.11 this section described the opposite, and its heading was "The last Scala api does not check its
version".* Kafka 0.10 moved every api but one to the schemas of the Java client, which validate the version, and
0.11 did not finish the job either: the exception was **ControlledShutdown (key 7)**, whose frame `RequestChannel`
still handed to the Scala `ControlledShutdownRequest.readFrom(buffer)` before the request header was parsed at all,
and that parser only asked whether the version was above 0, to decide whether a client id followed. A 0.9 to 0.11
broker therefore answered key 7 with **any** version, although its ApiVersions answer reported the single version 1
for it.

**Kafka 1.0 removed the exception** — `ControlledShutdownRequest` became an ordinary request class, and the one
thing that really is special about its v0, a request header without a client id, became a schema of its own — and
Kafka 2.4 made that schema a specification like every other: `RequestHeader.json` @ 2.8.2 declares three header
versions, `"validVersions": "0-2"`, with the comment *"Version 0 of the RequestHeader is only used by v0 of
ControlledShutdownRequest"* and the `ClientId` field marked `"versions": "1+"`.

So on this line key 7 carries the whole history of the request header in one api, and the probe sends all four of
its versions: **v0** with the header v0 (no client id), **v1** and **v2** with the common header v1, and **v3** —
the flexible version of Kafka 2.4 — with the header v2 and a compact body. All four are answered with the code 8
(`BrokerNotAvailable`) for a broker id the controller does not know, and **v4** closes the connection like every
other version above the table.

Every other key of the table validates its version the same way, including the fourteen that Kafka 2.x added: a
2.8.2 broker closes the connection for Produce v10, Fetch v13, Metadata v12, ElectLeaders v3, DescribeCluster v1 and
every other "one above the table" frame alike, and for the api key **65** (`DescribeTransactions`, Kafka 3.0) as
well.

### What is not in Kafka 2.8.2

Everything below is Kafka **3.0 or later**, or a deliberate omission of this line, and must not appear here:

* **The api keys above 64.** `ApiKeys.java` @ 2.8.2 ends at `UNREGISTER_BROKER` (64); `DescribeTransactions` (65),
  `ListTransactions` (66) and `AllocateProducerIds` (67) are Kafka 3.0, and everything after them is later still.
  `ApiKeys` of this branch stops at **64**, and the api key 65 is what the probe sends to see the connection close.
* **The error codes above 104**: `Errors.java` @ 2.8.2 ends at `INCONSISTENT_CLUSTER_ID` (104).
  `KafkaException::fromCode()` answers an unknown code with `UnknownErrorException`, which is what a client should
  do with a code it has never heard of.
* **The versions Kafka 3.x adds** — Produce v10, Fetch v13, Metadata v12, OffsetFetch v8, the `topic_id` of a Fetch
  request (KIP-516 in 3.1) — the api-key table above is the ceiling, and a frame above it costs the connection.
* **The KRaft apis and the KRaft mode**: the raft apis 52 to 55 (KIP-595), `Envelope` (58), `FetchSnapshot` (59) and
  the broker registration apis 62 to 64 (KIP-631) are part of `ApiKeys.java` @ 2.8.2 — their constants exist here so
  that any frame of the release can be named — but a ZooKeeper-backed broker does not serve them, and Kafka 2.8
  shipped KRaft as an early access feature that this line does not speak. `ApiVersionProbeTest` sends one frame of
  each to pin that the connection is closed with `Received request api key VOTE which is not enabled`.
* **The ACL apis `DescribeAcls` (29), `CreateAcls` (30) and `DeleteAcls` (31)**, which a 2.8.2 broker does serve but
  which this line leaves unimplemented by decision (as the two lines below did): they need a broker with an
  `authorizer.class.name`, and every wire vector of this repository comes from a real broker. The error codes 53 and
  65 belong to the same family and are implemented from the sources alone.
* **The replication apis `LeaderAndIsr` (4), `StopReplica` (5), `UpdateMetadata` (6) and `AlterIsr` (56)**, which a
  2.8.2 broker serves and which only the **controller** speaks. They are part of the protocol of this release, but
  no class of this package builds one; the probe sends them with a stale controller or broker epoch to check that
  the broker answers them (the error codes 11 and 77, and nothing changes). The two broker-to-broker apis this
  package *does* carry, `OffsetForLeaderEpoch` (23) and `WriteTxnMarkers` (27), have classes and wire vectors but no
  `Client` or `AdminClient` method either.
* **SASL/SCRAM, SASL/OAUTHBEARER and SASL/GSSAPI.** The transport of this line speaks PLAIN over SASL_PLAINTEXT and
  SASL_SSL, in the framed exchange of KIP-152; a delegation token can be *issued* by the apis 38 to 41 but not
  *used*, and a SCRAM credential can be created and described through the apis 50 and 51 but not logged in with,
  because both mean SASL/SCRAM.
* **Cooperative rebalancing** (KIP-429) and the subscription v1/v2 of the embedded consumer protocol: they are a
  client-library feature on top of the wire, and the assignors of this package stay the range and round-robin ones.

## ApiVersions API (key 18, v0 to v3)

Asks a broker which api keys and versions it serves. Kafka 0.10.0 added it, and it is the only request whose answer
tells a client what the peer on the other side speaks; on the two lowest lines of this repository there is no such
api, and the api-key table had to be probed frame by frame. Kafka 0.11 raised it to **version 1**, Kafka 2.0 to
**version 2** and Kafka 2.4 to **version 3** — the version this client sends, and the first flexible frame of the
whole protocol.

```
ApiVersionsRequest (Version: 0 … 2) =>

ApiVersionsRequest (Version: 3) => ClientSoftwareName ClientSoftwareVersion TAG_BUFFER
  ClientSoftwareName    => compact_string
  ClientSoftwareVersion => compact_string
```

The request has **no body at all** in the versions 0, 1 and 2 — *"Versions 0 through 2 of ApiVersionsRequest are the
same"*, `ApiVersionsRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 — so the whole frame is 4 bytes of `Size` plus 8 bytes of header plus the
client id, and the only difference between them is the `ApiVersion` field of the header.

**Version 3 carries the two fields of KIP-511**, and they are not the client id: the client id names the
*application* and may be anything, these two name the client *library* and its version, so that a broker can count
`kafka.server:type=ClientMetrics` per library instead of guessing. The broker matches both against
`[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9\-.]*[a-zA-Z0-9])?` (`ApiVersionsRequest.isValid()`) and answers the error code **42**
(`InvalidRequest`) when either fails — measured on the container with an empty name, an empty version, a name that
contains a `/` and a name that starts with a `-`, and captured as the vector
`apiversions.response.v3.invalid-software-name`. This client sends `lisachenko-kafka-client` and the Kafka line it
speaks, `2.8`, as `ApiVersionsRequest::CLIENT_SOFTWARE_NAME` and `::CLIENT_SOFTWARE_VERSION`.

```
ApiVersionsResponse (Version: 0) => ErrorCode [ApiKey MinVersion MaxVersion]
  ErrorCode  => int16
  ApiKey     => int16
  MinVersion => int16
  MaxVersion => int16

ApiVersionsResponse (Version: 1) => ErrorCode [ApiKey MinVersion MaxVersion] ThrottleTimeMs
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32

ApiVersionsResponse (Version: 2) => the frame of version 1, byte for byte

ApiVersionsResponse (Version: 3) => ErrorCode compact_[ApiKey MinVersion MaxVersion TAG_BUFFER] ThrottleTimeMs TAG_BUFFER
  TAG_BUFFER of the body =>
    tag 0 => SupportedFeatures  compact_[Name MinVersion MaxVersion TAG_BUFFER]
    tag 1 => FinalizedFeaturesEpoch  int64, default -1
    tag 2 => FinalizedFeatures  compact_[Name MaxVersionLevel MinVersionLevel TAG_BUFFER]
```

* `ErrorCode` belongs to the whole answer and is `0` or **35** (`UnsupportedVersion`).
* One entry per api the broker serves **on the listener the request arrived on**, in ascending order of `ApiKey`,
  including the broker-to-broker keys 4, 5, 6, 27 and 56 that no client ever sends. Both version bounds are
  **inclusive**, and the entry itself has no version of its own: the versions 0, 1 and 2 use the same three int16
  fields for it.
* A 2.8.2 broker answers with the **56** keys of the api-key table above. A client must not assume that set — the
  whole point of the api is that a later broker reports more and an older one reports fewer, and a KRaft controller
  or a broker with another `inter.broker.protocol.version` reports something else again.

**`ThrottleTimeMs` closes this answer instead of opening it.** KIP-124 gave fifteen apis of Kafka 0.11 a throttle
time and put it in front of the body in every one of them, and every api Kafka 1.x and 2.x add leads with it as
well, with exactly one exception, this api, where the field is appended. The reason is the paragraph below: the
answer to a version the broker cannot parse is written in the version 0 layout, so the `ErrorCode` has to sit at the
same offset in both versions or a client that guessed too high could not read it. Without a `request_percentage`
quota the field is 0, and an ApiVersions request is the last request a quota would ever throttle.

**What version 2 changes is not the frame but the moment it arrives.** KIP-219 (Kafka 2.0) bumped this api together
with almost every other one: a broker that has to throttle a request of the bumped version answers **first** and
mutes the channel for the throttle window afterwards, where a broker that has to throttle an older version mutes the
channel first and answers at the end of it. A client that sends a bumped version therefore promises to honour
`throttle_time_ms` itself. `ApiVersionsResponse.json` @ 2.8.2 writes it down as *"Starting in version 2, on quota
violation, brokers send out responses before throttling"*, and the schema of v2 is the schema of v1.

**What version 3 changes is the encoding, and one thing about it is unique in the protocol.** The body is flexible —
the api array counts `56 + 1` in a single byte, every entry ends in a tag buffer of its own, and the body ends in
one that carries the three features of KIP-584 — but the **response header stays v0**: no tag buffer behind the
correlation id, so that the error code sits where a client of any version can read it. `ApiVersionsResponse.json`
says so in as many words (*"Tagged fields are only supported in the body but not in the header. The length of the
header must not change in order to guarantee the backward compatibility"*), and it is the only api of Kafka 2.8.2
whose two headers disagree that way: the *request* v3 uses the header v2.

The three tagged fields are the feature mechanism of **KIP-584**, which was meant to replace
`inter.broker.protocol.version` in a KRaft cluster: `supported_features` (tag 0) is what the broker can do,
`finalized_features` (tag 2) what the cluster agreed on, and `finalized_features_epoch` (tag 1) the version of that
agreement. **A ZooKeeper-backed 2.8.2 broker answers exactly one of them**, tag 1 with the value `0`: it supports no
feature, has finalized none, and the epoch is on the wire only because its default is `-1` — a tagged field whose
value is the default is left out, so the `0` of the feature ZooKeeper node has to be written. That is the whole
tagged-field section of the answer, `01 01 08 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00`, and it is the shortest demonstration of the
rule that governs every tagged field of the protocol.

`Protocol\Kafka\Protocol\Request\ApiVersionsResponse` indexes the array by `ApiKey`, so a caller asks for one api
directly (`supports(ApiKeys::FETCH, 12)`, `maxVersionOf(ApiKeys::METADATA)`) and reads the features of KIP-584 from
`$supportedFeatures`, `$finalizedFeaturesEpoch` and `$finalizedFeatures`; `ApiVersionsResponseV2`,
`ApiVersionsResponseV1` and `ApiVersionsResponseV0` are the same class with the version constant lowered, and
`ApiVersionsRequestV2`, `ApiVersionsRequestV1` and `ApiVersionsRequestV0` the same request with the lower version in
its header and without the body of v3.
`Client::apiVersions(Node $node)` returns the whole response and `Admin\AdminClient::getApiVersions(Node $node)`
the indexed array; every broker answers for itself, so a rolling upgrade shows up as brokers with different ranges.

**This client does not negotiate with the answer.** Like the lines below it, it sends the fixed versions a broker of
its own Kafka release serves — the "Implemented here" column of the api-key table — and the api is there to report
what the peer is, not to choose a version at runtime.

Three properties make the request usable as the *first* frame on a connection, and all three are verified against
the container:

1. **An unknown version is answered, not punished.** Every other key or version a 2.8.2 broker cannot parse costs
   the connection; ApiVersions is special-cased in `RequestContext.parseRequest()`, so a version it does not serve
   comes back as the error code 35 in the layout of **version 0**, and the connection stays open. Since Kafka 2.4
   (KIP-511) the array of that answer carries the single row of ApiVersions itself instead of being empty, and since
   the same release the frame has to carry the **request header v2** as soon as the version asked for is above 2 —
   both are described under "An api the broker does not serve closes the connection" above, and both are what the
   vector `apiversions.response.v0.unsupported-version` shows.
2. **It is answered before authentication.** On a SASL listener the broker answers ApiVersions while the connection
   is still unauthenticated (`KafkaApis.handleApiVersionsRequest` says so in a comment), so a client can learn the
   surface of a broker before it knows whether it may talk to it at all. On an SSL listener the TLS handshake still
   comes first.
3. **It is cheap.** The request carries no state, changes nothing, and the answer of a 2.8.2 broker is 350 bytes in
   the versions 1 and 2 (346 in version 0) with a 23-character client id. The **v3** answer is 414 bytes: the
   compact array saves three bytes on its count and the 56 entries cost one tag buffer each, so the flexible
   encoding is *longer* here — it pays off where a frame carries strings, not fixed-width triples.

A broker of a lower line answers fewer keys, and one older than 0.10 has no key 18 at all: a **0.9.0.1** broker
drops the frame and never answers it, a **0.8.2.2** broker closes the socket. "No answer at all" is therefore how a
client recognises a pre-0.10 peer — there is no error code for it. A peer below Kafka 2.4 answers the
version 3 request of this line with the error code 35 in the version 0 layout, and has to be asked again with
`ApiVersionsRequestV2`, `ApiVersionsRequestV1` or `ApiVersionsRequestV0` — which is exactly the negotiation KIP-511
had in mind when it put the version range of this api into that error answer.

## MessageSet and Message

The message set format is shared by the Produce and Fetch APIs and by the on-disk log. Note that a `MessageSet` is
**not** preceded by an `int32` element count like a regular array — it is a raw byte region whose length is given by
the surrounding `MessageSetSize` field.

Kafka 0.10.0 added **message format v1** (KIP-31 and KIP-32) next to the format v0 of 0.8 and 0.9. A 0.10.2.2 broker
reads and writes both, and the `MagicByte` of a message says which one it is in — it is the discriminator that has to
be read before the rest of the message:

```
MessageSet => [Offset MessageSize Message]
  Offset      => int64
  MessageSize => int32

Message (MagicByte = 0) => Crc MagicByte Attributes Key Value
  Crc        => int32
  MagicByte  => int8
  Attributes => int8
  Key        => bytes
  Value      => bytes

Message (MagicByte = 1) => Crc MagicByte Attributes Timestamp Key Value
  Crc        => int32
  MagicByte  => int8
  Attributes => int8
  Timestamp  => int64
  Key        => bytes
  Value      => bytes
```

* `Crc` — CRC-32 (IEEE, the same polynomial as `crc32()` in PHP) of the message bytes that follow the CRC field,
  i.e. of `MagicByte Attributes [Timestamp] Key Value`. The `Timestamp` of a v1 message is part of the checksum.
* `Attributes`:

  | Bits | Meaning | Values |
  |------|---------|--------|
  | 0–2  | compression codec | 0 none, 1 gzip, 2 snappy, **3 lz4** |
  | 3    | timestamp type (v1 only) | 0 `CreateTime`, 1 `LogAppendTime` |
  | 4–7  | reserved, always 0 | |

  All four codecs are implemented by this client. In a message of format v0 bit 3 is reserved and stays 0.
* `Timestamp` — milliseconds since the epoch, or **-1** (`Message.NoTimestamp`) for a message that carries none. The
  broker accepts -1 and stores it as it is; `message.timestamp.difference.max.ms` (unlimited by default) is what
  bounds a `CreateTime` that is far away from the clock of the broker, and a violation is answered with
  **32 `InvalidTimestamp`**.
* The timestamp type is a property of the **topic** (`message.timestamp.type`, `CreateTime` by default): with
  `LogAppendTime` the broker overwrites the timestamp of every message it appends with its own clock and sets bit 3
  of the attributes.
* A compressed message is a regular message whose `Value` is a complete, compressed `MessageSet`.
* The server is allowed to return a **partial message at the end of a message set**; clients must silently drop a
  trailing message that is shorter than its announced size. The size of the smallest possible message —
  `MinMessageOverhead`, 14 bytes — is the one of a format v0 message without key and value, and a `MessageSize`
  below it means a corrupt set (a format v1 message without key and value is 22 bytes).

### Offsets inside a compressed message set

The `Offset` of the entries of a *produced* set is ignored: the broker assigns the real offsets when it appends the
set, so a producer numbers its messages 0, 1, 2 … Inside a **compressed** set the two message formats differ:

* **v0** — the broker rewrites the offset of every inner message with the absolute offset of the log.
* **v1** — the inner offsets stay **relative** (0, 1, 2 …) and only the offset of the **wrapper** message is
  rewritten, with the absolute offset of the *last* inner message. A reader has to decompress the whole set to see
  the last relative offset before it can translate the others:

      absolute = wrapperOffset - lastInnerOffset + innerOffset

  (`ByteBufferMessageSet.scala` and `RecordsIterator.DeepRecordsIterator` @ 0.10.2.2). The reason is streaming
  compression: the relative offset of an inner message is known while it is written, its absolute one is not.
  The vectors `messageformat.v1.createtime.gzip` and `messageformat.v0.lz4.broken-checksum` below are the same three
  records at the offsets 3, 4 and 5 in both formats: relative `0, 1, 2` under a wrapper at offset 5 in v1, absolute
  `3, 4, 5` under the very same wrapper offset in v0.

### Timestamps inside a compressed message set

The wrapper message of a v1 set carries the timestamp of the whole batch, and it is the only message whose
attributes are meaningful:

* the timestamp type of the wrapper applies to **every** message of the set;
* with `CreateTime` the wrapper carries the **largest** timestamp of its inner messages, and every inner message
  keeps its own;
* with `LogAppendTime` the wrapper carries the append time of the batch and the timestamps of the inner messages are
  **ignored** — the broker does not even rewrite them, as `messageformat.v1.logappendtime.gzip` below shows: the
  wrapper announces `0x09` (gzip + LogAppendTime) and the append time, while the compressed inner messages still
  hold the `CreateTime` values of the producer;
* a producer must write `CreateTime` in the attributes of every inner message, otherwise the broker rejects the set.

### The lz4 codec and the KAFKA-3160 checksum

The `Value` of an lz4 message is an **LZ4 frame** (the v1.5.1 frame format), as `KafkaLZ4BlockOutputStream` writes
it: the magic number `04 22 4d 18`, the `FLG` byte `0x60` (version 1, independent blocks, no checksums), the `BD`
byte `0x40` (64 KiB blocks), the header checksum `HC`, then `int32` little-endian block lengths with their blocks,
and a block length of `0` as the end mark. The highest bit of a block length marks a block that is stored
uncompressed because compressing it made it bigger.

`HC` is the second byte of the xxHash32 of the frame descriptor, `(xxh32(FLG BD) >> 8) & 0xff` = `0x82`. Until
Kafka 0.10.0 the clients hashed the magic number **together with** the descriptor, which gives `0x1a`
([KAFKA-3160](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-3160)). The fix could not be applied to the messages that
older clients still have to read, so the broken checksum became part of the format of **message format v0** and the
correct one is used from format v1 on (`MemoryRecordsBuilder.wrapForOutput()`:
`useBrokenFlagDescriptorChecksum = magic == 0`). A reader has to accept both, which is what this client does — the
0.10.2.2 broker itself writes `04 22 4d 18 60 40 1a` in every answer it down-converts to format v0.

### What the broker converts, and when

The message format of the **log** is the `message.format.version` of the topic (`log.message.format.version` of the
broker by default, **`2.8-IV1`** on the container of this line, which is still the magic byte 2), and the broker
converts whatever it is given on the way in and on the way out. Re-measured on the 2.8.2 container with three
topics — one on the default format, one with `message.format.version=0.10.0` and one with `0.9.0` — each written
once and then fetched with every version of the Fetch api this client has a class for:

| Topic format | Stored as | Fetch v0/v1 answers | Fetch v2/v3 answers | Fetch v4 and above answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `2.8-IV1` (the default) | magic **2**, record batch | magic **0**, no timestamps, **no headers**, absolute inner offsets | magic **1**, timestamps kept, **no headers** | magic **2**, as it lies in the log |
| `0.10.0` | magic **1**, timestamps kept | magic **0**, timestamps dropped | magic **1**, as stored | magic **1**, as stored |
| `0.9.0` | magic **0** | magic **0** | magic **0** | magic **0** |

The conversion is what `KafkaApis.handleFetchRequest` @ 2.8.2 decides on two things at once, the magic of the log
and the version of the request: `magic > V0 && versionId <= 1` asks for `MAGIC_VALUE_V0`, `magic > V1 && versionId
<= 3` for `MAGIC_VALUE_V1`, and everything else is answered with the region as it lies. A *higher* fetch version
than the log needs is never a conversion: a magic 1 log is answered as magic 1 to a Fetch v8.

**The record headers of the message format v2 are dropped by that conversion, silently.** The answer of a Fetch v2
or v3 for a batch whose records carry headers is the error code **0** and every record, without its headers —
"Ignore headers when down-converting to V0 and V1 since they are not supported",
`AbstractRecords.convertRecordBatch` @ 2.8.2. A **0.11.0.3** broker answered such a partition with the error code
-1 (`UnknownServerError`) and an empty record set instead, because the very same call threw
`IllegalArgumentException: Magic v1 does not support record headers`; that changed with Kafka 1.0 and is unchanged
on 2.8.2. The measurement is in "Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v12)" below.

A client of this line therefore sees timestamps only through a Fetch request of version 2 or above, which is what
`Client::fetch()` sends (v8); `Record::$timestamp` is `null` and `Record::$timestampType` is `NO_TIMESTAMP_TYPE`
for everything that arrives in format v0 — a topic of the older `message.format.version`, or any partition read
with an explicitly built `FetchRequestV1`/`FetchRequestV0`.

#### KIP-283 (Kafka 2.0): lazy down-conversion, and the switch that refuses it

Down-conversion is the most expensive thing a broker does for a client: before Kafka 2.0 the whole converted region
was built in the heap before the answer was written, which is how a single old consumer could drive a broker into
an out-of-memory death. **KIP-283** changed two things:

* the conversion became **lazy and chunked** — `LazyDownConversionRecords` converts a batch at a time while the
  answer is written to the socket, and guarantees only that at least one batch is converted, so the answer of a
  down-converting fetch may be **shorter** than `max_bytes` would allow;
* the conversion can be **switched off**, per topic with `message.downconversion.enable` and cluster-wide with the
  broker option `log.message.downconversion.enable` (`true` by default, which is what the container of this line
  answers for the broker resource 0).

With the option off, a fetch that would need a conversion is not served at all. Measured on a topic created with
`--config message.downconversion.enable=false`, written with one magic 2 batch:

| Request | Answer of the 2.8.2 container |
|---|---|
| Fetch **v3** (needs magic 1) | error code **35** `UNSUPPORTED_VERSION` for the partition, `high_watermark = -1`, an **empty** record set (`fetch.response.v3.downconversion-disabled`) |
| Fetch **v8** (needs nothing) | error code 0 and the record batch as it lies |

**The code is 35, not 43.** `UNSUPPORTED_VERSION` is what `KafkaApis` puts into the partition entry — "if
down-conversion is disabled for the particular partition … sending unsupported version response" — and **43**
`UNSUPPORTED_FOR_MESSAGE_FORMAT`, which is the code of a *timestamp lookup* on a log below magic 1, never appears
here. The error is per partition, not per request: the other partitions of the same fetch are served normally, and
the connection stays open.

A follower is exempt (`!fetchRequest.isFromFollower`), so replication is never refused by this option — it only
ever stops a *client* from paying for the conversion.

## RecordBatch (message format v2)

Kafka 0.11 replaced the message set with the **record batch** (KIP-98 for the format, KIP-82 for the headers). It
is the third message format of the protocol, the `MagicByte` 2, and it is what the log of a topic with the default
`message.format.version=0.11.0` holds and what a Produce v3 and a Fetch v4/v5 carry. A byte region of a partition is
still not a protocol array — it has no element count, only the `MessageSetSize`/`RecordSetSize` of the field around
it — but the entries of that region are now batches instead of messages:

```
RecordBatch =>
  BaseOffset           => int64
  BatchLength          => int32
  PartitionLeaderEpoch => int32
  Magic                => int8 (2)
  Crc                  => int32 (CRC-32C, unsigned)
  Attributes           => int16
  LastOffsetDelta      => int32
  FirstTimestamp       => int64
  MaxTimestamp         => int64
  ProducerId           => int64
  ProducerEpoch        => int16
  BaseSequence         => int32
  RecordCount          => int32
  Records              => the RecordCount records, compressed as one block when a codec is announced

Record =>
  Length         => varint
  Attributes     => int8
  TimestampDelta => varlong
  OffsetDelta    => varint
  Key            => varint-prefixed bytes
  Value          => varint-prefixed bytes
  Headers        => varint-counted [Header]

Header =>
  HeaderKeyLength   => varint
  HeaderKey         => string
  HeaderValueLength => varint
  HeaderValue       => bytes
```

Every length and both deltas are **zigzag varints** (`TYPE_VARINT_ZIGZAG`, `TYPE_VARLONG_ZIGZAG`,
`TYPE_VARCHAR_ZIGZAG` of the engine, see "Protocol primitive types"), a length of -1 (`01`) is `null` and a length
of 0 (`00`) is the empty byte array. The `Attributes` of a *record* are unused in 0.11 and always 0; the count of the
headers is a varint too, and a header key is a UTF-8 string that is never null, while a header value may be.

The fixed part of a batch is exactly **61 bytes** (`RECORD_BATCH_OVERHEAD`), from `BaseOffset` through
`RecordCount`; `BatchLength` counts everything after itself, so a batch occupies `12 + BatchLength` bytes, the same
`Offset`/`MessageSize` shape a message set entry has. That is not an accident: the `MagicByte` sits at **offset 16**
of an entry in all three formats — after the 8-byte offset, the 4-byte length and either the CRC of a message or the
`PartitionLeaderEpoch` of a batch — which is what lets a reader look at the format of a region before it decides how
to parse it. `MemoryRecords` of this client does exactly that, entry by entry, and hands each entry to `MessageSet`
or to `RecordBatch`.

### Attributes

| Bits | Meaning | Values |
|------|---------|--------|
| 0–2  | compression codec | 0 none, 1 gzip, 2 snappy, 3 lz4, **4 zstd** (Kafka 2.1, KIP-110) |
| 3    | timestamp type | 0 `CreateTime`, 1 `LogAppendTime` |
| 4    | transactional | 1 when the batch belongs to a transaction (KIP-98) |
| 5    | control batch | 1 when the records are markers of the transaction protocol |
| 6–15 | reserved, always 0 | |

The field is an `int16` now, and only its low byte is used — `DefaultRecordBatch.attributes()` reads the `int16` and
casts it to a `byte`. A batch of the format v2 always announces a timestamp type: unlike a message of the format v0,
it has no "no timestamp type" state.

### The checksum is a CRC-32C, and it does not cover the whole batch

`Crc` is the **CRC-32C** (Castagnoli, RFC 3720 section B.4 — `hash('crc32c')` of PHP, `Crc32C.java` of the broker),
not the CRC-32 (IEEE) of a message, and it covers the batch from the `Attributes` field to its end, i.e. everything
that follows the checksum itself. Three fields are therefore *outside* of it:

* `BaseOffset` — the broker assigns the real offsets when it appends the batch;
* `BatchLength` — it does not change;
* `PartitionLeaderEpoch` — assigned by the leader on append (KIP-101), and the whole point of leaving it out of the
  checksum is that a broker must not have to recompute the checksum of every batch it receives.

The checksum is also *behind* the magic byte, which is what makes reading the magic first mandatory: in the message
formats v0 and v1 the CRC comes first and the magic second.

### Offsets, timestamps and sequence numbers are deltas

A record stores none of its three numbers in full, only the difference to the header of its batch:

    offset    = BaseOffset     + OffsetDelta
    timestamp = FirstTimestamp + TimestampDelta
    sequence  = BaseSequence   + OffsetDelta

`LastOffsetDelta` is the delta of the last record, so `BaseOffset + LastOffsetDelta` is the last offset of the batch
and `BaseSequence + LastOffsetDelta` its last sequence number (wrapping at the largest int32, as
`DefaultRecordBatch.incrementSequence()` does). Both survive log compaction even when the records they describe are
removed, because the broker rebuilds the state of a producer from them; that is why a batch may hold **zero**
records and still exist, and why `RecordCount` is a plain `int32` outside the compressed block.

`FirstTimestamp` is always the `CreateTime` of the first record, *even in a `LogAppendTime` batch*: with
`LogAppendTime` the broker only overwrites `MaxTimestamp` with the time of the append and sets bit 3, and every
record of the batch reads that `MaxTimestamp` as its timestamp while the deltas of the producer stay in the log
untouched. The vector `messageformat.v2.none.logappendtime` shows it: `FirstTimestamp` and `MaxTimestamp` are 19
milliseconds apart, the records still carry the deltas 0, 8 and 8, and `DumpLogSegments` prints the same
`LogAppendTime` for all three of them. With `CreateTime` `MaxTimestamp` is simply the largest timestamp of the
batch. An empty batch has `FirstTimestamp` -1 (`NO_TIMESTAMP`).

### Compression compresses the records, not a wrapper

There is no wrapper message any more. The 61 header bytes are always plain and the bytes after them are the
compressed block of the `RecordCount` records, so a reader knows how many records a batch holds, what their offsets
and timestamps are and whether the batch is transactional without decompressing anything. The codecs and their
framings are the ones of the message set — gzip, xerial-framed snappy, an LZ4 frame — with one difference:

* an **lz4** batch of the magic 2 always carries the *correct* frame descriptor checksum `0x82`. The KAFKA-3160
  breakage is bound to the message format v0 (`useBrokenFlagDescriptorChecksum = magic == 0`), so it can never
  appear in a record batch; `messageformat.v2.lz4.createtime` starts with `04 22 4d 18 60 40 82`.

Re-compressing a block with another implementation gives different — equally valid — bytes, which is why
`RecordBatch` keeps the records part exactly as it read it and `toBuffer()` reproduces a captured batch byte for
byte.

### The zstd codec (Kafka 2.1, KIP-110)

**Kafka 2.1 added a fourth codec, the compression type `4`, zstd**, and it belongs to the message format v2 alone.
`CompressionType.ZSTD` @ 2.8.2 is `new CompressionType(4, "zstd", …)`, a produce of a zstd batch needs **Produce
v7** and a fetch of a zstd *topic* needs **Fetch v10**; both of the lower versions are refused with the error code
**76** `UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE`, see "Version 10 and the zstd codec (KIP-110)" under the Fetch api for the
two measurements. Nothing else about the batch changes: the three attribute bits hold the codec as they always
did, the 61 header bytes stay plain, and the records block is a zstd stream instead of a gzip, snappy or lz4 one.

**This client compresses and decompresses zstd through `ext-zstd`** (`zstd_compress()` and `zstd_uncompress()`), a
**suggested** dependency of `composer.json` and the only codec of the four that needs an extension which is not in
a default PHP build — gzip is `ext-zlib`, snappy and lz4 are implemented in PHP in this package. Writing a
pure-PHP zstd codec is not the business of a protocol client, so the extension is where the line is drawn, and the
absence of it is handled instead of hidden:

* `CompressionCodec::isSupported(CompressionCodec::ZSTD)` is `false` without the extension, and
  `CompressionCodec::isZstdAvailable()` says so directly;
* `ProducerConfig` refuses `compression.type = zstd` at construction time with the list of the codecs that are
  really available, so a producer fails where the mistake is, not inside a broker answer;
* a zstd batch that a **fetch** brings in raises `UnsupportedCompressionTypeException` — the client-side half of
  the code 76 — instead of handing half-decoded bytes to the application. It is raised where the answer is
  *decoded*, not where the records are used: `MemoryRecords::fromBuffer()` decodes every batch of a fetched
  region, so a partition of a zstd topic is an exception for the whole answer it arrived in. The header of a
  batch is readable either way — `RecordBatch::fromBuffer()` reads the 61 plain bytes, and with them the codec,
  the record count and the offsets, without touching the compressed block.

With the extension installed all four codecs round trip, and a batch this client compressed is read back by the
Java client and the other way round: zstd has one frame format (RFC 8478) and no Kafka-specific framing, unlike
the xerial framing of snappy or the KAFKA-3160 lz4 checksum.

### Control batches

A batch whose attributes have bit 5 set carries **markers of the transaction protocol** instead of data. A client
never hands its records to an application: `MemoryRecords::getRecords()` drops them, and a `read_committed` consumer
uses them to decide which of the batches around them belong to a committed transaction. The only markers of Kafka
0.11 are the two ends of a transaction, written by the transaction coordinator itself:

```
Key => Version Type
  Version => int16 (0)
  Type    => int16 (0 ABORT, 1 COMMIT)

Value => Version CoordinatorEpoch
```
