| 17   | InvalidTopic                | `The topic is being deleted`                                              |
| 80   | PreferredLeaderNotAvailable | A `StateChangeFailedException` of a preferred election: the preferred replica is not in the ISR (an unclean election answers 83 `EligibleLeadersNotAvailable` instead, which needs version 1) |
| 84   | ElectionNotNeeded           | `Leader election not needed for topic partition.` — measured on the container for a partition whose leader is already its preferred replica |

The **84** is worth a second look: the error code was added in Kafka 2.4, but a 2.8.2 broker answers it to a
**version 0** client as well — the per-partition codes are not translated for the older version, only the
top-level one is left out. A client of this api therefore has to know the codes 80, 83 and 84 whatever version it
sends. Their neighbours in `Errors.java` @ 2.8.2 belong elsewhere: **81** `GroupMaxSizeReached`
("The consumer group has reached its max size.", `group.max.size` of KIP-389) and **82** `FencedInstanceId` (the
static membership of KIP-345) are answers of the group membership apis and never appear here.

`TimeoutMs` is how long the controller waits for the elections to finish before it answers (60 seconds in the Java
client, and the default of `ElectLeadersRequest`).

**The two election types of KIP-460** (`ElectionType` of the Java client, `Admin\ElectionType` here) are the whole
content of the byte:

| Byte | Type | What the controller does |
|------|------|--------------------------|
| 0 | `PREFERRED` | Moves the leadership to the **preferred replica** - the first broker of the assignment - when that replica is in the ISR. The election of `auto.leader.rebalance.enable` and of KIP-183 |
| 1 | `UNCLEAN` | Makes the first **live** replica the leader of a partition that has no leader at all, accepting the loss of every record the old leader had and the new one has not. The emergency button of `kafka-leader-election.sh --election-type unclean` |

`KafkaController.processReplicaLeaderElection` @ 2.8.2 decides per partition which ones are *electable* at all,
and the two types ask different questions:

```scala
case ElectionType.PREFERRED => currentLeader != preferredReplica
case ElectionType.UNCLEAN   => currentLeader == LeaderAndIsr.NoLeader || !liveBrokerIds.contains(currentLeader)
```

everything else lands in `alreadyValidLeader` and is answered **84** `ElectionNotNeeded`. **Measured on the
container**: an unclean election of a partition that still has a live leader is therefore the very same 84 as a
preferred one - the type does not make the controller elect where nothing has failed - and an unknown topic is the
same 3 in both. The **83** `EligibleLeadersNotAvailable` is what an unclean election gets when the controller does
try and the `StateChangeFailedException` comes back ("Eligible topic partition leaders are not available."), i.e.
when the partition has no live replica either; a one-broker container cannot produce it, because the one broker
that would have to be dead is the one answering the request. It is documented from
`KafkaController.processReplicaLeaderElection` @ 2.8.2, which picks the code from the election type:

```scala
val error = if (electionType == ElectionType.PREFERRED) Errors.PREFERRED_LEADER_NOT_AVAILABLE
            else Errors.ELIGIBLE_LEADERS_NOT_AVAILABLE
```

**The top-level error code of version 1 is 0 for everything that reaches the controller.**
`handleElectReplicaLeader` @ 2.8.2 builds the answer with `sendResponseCallback(ApiError.NONE)` on the normal path
and with the 31 `ClusterAuthorizationFailed` only when the authorizer refuses the client `Alter` on the cluster -
the one case in which the controller is never asked. Every measured answer of this document carries the 0, and
`Client::electLeaders()` throws for anything else, because such an answer names no partition to attach an error to.

`AdminClient::electLeaders()` takes an `Admin\ElectionType` for the kind of election and refuses a value that is
neither of the two with an `UnsupportedVersionException`.

## IncrementalAlterConfigs API (key 44, v0 and v1)

Changes **single options** of a topic or a broker. New in Kafka **2.3** (KIP-339), and the api that repairs the one
real defect of the AlterConfigs above it: that request carries the whole configuration a resource should have
afterwards, so a client that wants to change one option has to read the current configuration first, send it all
back, and lose whatever another client changed in between. This one names an operation per option and leaves every
option it does not mention exactly as it is.

**Kafka 2.4 added the version 1** (KIP-482): the same fields of KIP-339 in the flexible encoding, and nothing
else. It is the version this client sends; `IncrementalAlterConfigsRequestV0` / `…ResponseV0` are the frame Kafka
2.3 introduced.

```
IncrementalAlterConfigsRequest => [resources] validate_only
  resources => resource_type resource_name [configs]
    resource_type => INT8
    resource_name => STRING
    configs       => name config_operation value
      name             => STRING
      config_operation => INT8
      value            => NULLABLE_STRING
  validate_only => BOOLEAN
```

```
IncrementalAlterConfigsResponse => throttle_time_ms [responses]
  throttle_time_ms => INT32
  responses        => error_code error_message resource_type resource_name
    error_code    => INT16
    error_message => NULLABLE_STRING
    resource_type => INT8
    resource_name => STRING
```

The answer is byte for byte the one of AlterConfigs, under another name (`responses` instead of `resources`); the
request differs in the entry of an option alone, which gained the `config_operation` byte between the name and the
value.

**The four operations** are `AlterConfigOp.OpType` @ 2.8.2, and `ZkAdminManager.prepareIncrementalConfigs`
applies them to the `Properties` of the resource before it validates the result as a whole:

| Byte | Operation | What it does |
|------|-----------|--------------|
| 0 | `SET` | `properties.setProperty(name, value)` |
| 1 | `DELETE` | `properties.remove(name)` — the option falls back to the value it **inherits** (the broker setting behind it, which is not always the documented default), and it is the **only** operation whose value may be null |
| 2 | `APPEND` | Adds the comma separated values to a **list** option, starting from its current value or, when it has none, from its default |
| 3 | `SUBTRACT` | Removes them from that list. Removing a value the list does not have changes nothing, and removing every value leaves the **empty** list instead of restoring the default |

Everything else is unchanged from the AlterConfigs section: any broker serves a topic resource, a `broker:<id>`
resource is served by that broker alone, `broker:` (the empty name) is the cluster-wide default of KIP-226, and
`validate_only` runs the whole validation without writing anything.

**What the broker answers.** `ZkAdminManager.incrementalAlterConfigs` @ 2.8.2 validates the whole resource before
it writes anything, and reports one error code per resource with the message of the exception it caught. Measured
on the container, on a topic of one partition:

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| `SET retention.ms=3600000`, `APPEND cleanup.policy=compact`, `DELETE segment.bytes` | **0**, no message; `cleanup.policy` reads back `delete,compact` (the APPEND started from the default `delete`) and `retention.ms` `3600000`, both with the source `DYNAMIC_TOPIC_CONFIG` |
| `SUBTRACT cleanup.policy=compact` | **0**; the option reads back `delete` again |
| `APPEND retention.ms=1000` — an option that is not a list | **42** `InvalidRequest`, `Config value append is not allowed for config key: retention.ms` |
| The same option twice in one resource | **42**, `Error due to duplicate config keys : retention.ms` |
| `SET` with a **null** value | **42**, `Null value not supported for : SET:retention.ms` |
| `SET not.an.option=1` | **40** `InvalidConfig`, `Unknown topic config name: not.an.option` |
| `APPEND not.an.option=1` | **-1** `Unknown`, and **no message at all** — see below |
| `SET retention.ms=999000` with `validate_only` | **0**, and the option keeps the value it had |
| The default broker resource, the static option `log.dirs`, `validate_only` | **42**, `Invalid config value for resource ConfigResource(type=BROKER, name=''): Cannot update these configs dynamically: Set(log.dirs)` |
| The default broker resource, the dynamic option `log.retention.ms`, `validate_only` | **0** |

**The -1 of an APPEND to an option that does not exist** is a defect of `prepareIncrementalConfigs` @ 2.8.2 worth
knowing about, because a client cannot tell it from a broker that broke. Its `listType()` reads

```scala
val configKey = configKeys(configName)
if (configKey == null)
  throw new InvalidConfigurationException(s"Unknown topic config name: $configName")
```

— and `configKeys` is an immutable Scala `Map`, whose `apply` throws `NoSuchElementException` for a key it does
not hold, so the null check below it is dead code. That exception is neither a `ConfigException` nor an
`IllegalArgumentException`, so the catch block hands it to `ApiError.fromThrowable` unchanged and the resource is
answered with the unknown server error and a null message. A `SET` of the same name reaches the validation of the
whole `Properties` instead and is the proper **40** with `Unknown topic config name: not.an.option`.

**Which broker serves it** is what the AlterConfigs section says: a topic resource goes to any broker, a
`broker:<id>` resource only to that broker, and `broker:` (the empty name) is the cluster-wide default of KIP-226.
Only the options of `DynamicBrokerConfig.AllDynamicConfigs` can be changed at runtime, and a resource that names
one that cannot is refused **as a whole**. This repository never really alters the broker of the container - it is
shared with the other suites of this line - so both broker frames above were sent with `validate_only`.

`IncrementalAlterConfigs` also accepts a **`BROKER_LOGGER`** resource (type id 8, KIP-412), whose "options" are
log4j logger names and whose values are log levels. It is a per-broker, in-memory change that ZooKeeper never sees,
`SET` and `DELETE` are the only operations it allows, and this client does not model the resource type - the
`ConfigResource` of this package knows the types a config api of Kafka 0.11 to 2.8 stores.

## DescribeLogDirs API (key 35, v0 to v2)

Reports what each **log directory** of one broker holds. The api arrived with Kafka **1.0** (KIP-113) as
version 0.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`DESCRIBE_LOG_DIRS_REQUEST_V1 = DESCRIBE_LOG_DIRS_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and it is the version this client sends; a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version
below it. The pair `describelogdirs.request.v1` / `describelogdirs.response.v1` at the end of this document was
captured on the 2.8.2 container.

**Kafka 2.6 added the version 2**, the first **flexible** version of the api (`"flexibleVersions": "2+"` of
`DescribeLogDirsRequest.json` and `DescribeLogDirsResponse.json` @ 2.8.2), and it adds no field: the same two
structures in the compact encoding, with the request header v2 and a tagged-field section at the end of the
header, of every topic entry, of every partition entry, of every log directory and of the body. The nullable
`Topic` array of the request is the compact nullable one, so the `ff ff ff ff` that asks for **every** replica of
every directory becomes the single byte `00` and the whole request is 15 bytes. It is the version this client
sends; `DescribeLogDirsRequestV1`/`DescribeLogDirsResponseV1` keep the frame of the versions 0 and 1, whose
vectors are replayed through them.

```
DescribeLogDirsRequest => [Topic]
  Topic => TopicName [PartitionId]        -- the Topic array is NULLABLE
    TopicName   => string
    PartitionId => int32
```

```
DescribeLogDirsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [LogDir]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  LogDir => ErrorCode LogDirPath [Topic]
    ErrorCode   => int16
    LogDirPath  => string
    Topic => TopicName [Partition]
      TopicName => string
      Partition => PartitionId Size OffsetLag IsFuture
        PartitionId => int32
        Size        => int64
        OffsetLag   => int64
        IsFuture    => boolean
```

A Kafka broker may be given more than one data directory - `log.dirs` is a list - and every replica lives in exactly
one of them. Before KIP-113 that was invisible from outside: a client could not tell which disk a partition was on,
and could not ask for it to be moved. This api answers the first question and
"AlterReplicaLogDirs API (key 34, v0 to v2)" the second. The container of this repository runs with **two** of them,
`log.dirs=/tmp/kafka-logs,/tmp/kafka-logs-2`, which is what every observation below was measured on.

**The api is broker-local.** `KafkaApis.handleDescribeLogDirsRequest` @ 1.1.1 hands the partitions to the local
`ReplicaManager.describeLogDirs`, so a broker only ever answers for its own disks; an administrator asks each broker
of the cluster separately, which is why `Admin\AdminClient::describeLogDirs()` takes a **list of broker ids** and
returns a map keyed by them. Sending the request to another broker is not an error - it answers about *itself*.

**The request array is nullable, and its two empty shapes are opposites.** `null`
(`DescribeLogDirsRequest.isAllTopicPartitions`) asks for **every** replica of every directory, which is what the
Java admin client and `kafka-log-dirs.sh --describe` always send; an **empty array** asks for no replica at all. On
the container the difference is dramatic and both answers are documented as vectors: the empty array answers 64
bytes - the two directories with an empty topic array each - while the null array answered **235 207 bytes** for
the several thousand replicas the shared container held when the vectors were captured. Name the partitions when
they are known.

**A 2.8.2 broker ignores the selection altogether**, and that is what the version 2 frames of this document
measured: `KafkaApis.handleDescribeLogDirsRequest` @ 2.8.2 builds the answer from
`replicaManager.describeLogDirs(partitions)` only to group *every* log of the directory around it, so a request
that names one partition, a request with an empty array and a request with the null one are answered with the
same frame - 16 391 bytes and 581 replicas when the version 2 pair was captured, against the 64 bytes a 1.1.1
broker answered an empty array with. That is why `describelogdirs.response.v1` and `describelogdirs.response.v2`
are the two **constructed** vectors of this api: the captured answers with the topics of the other suites removed.
An empty array is therefore no longer the cheap "which disks does this broker have" of the 1.x line; the frame it
saves is in the request alone (23 bytes against 15 for the null one).

The answer always lists **every** directory of `log.dirs`, whether or not it holds anything of the request, and
only the replicas that really live in it. On the container the entries arrive in the order of `log.dirs` -
`ReplicaManager.describeLogDirs` maps over `config.logDirs.toSet`, and a Scala set of two elements iterates in
insertion order - but `kafka-log-dirs.sh` prints them in the order of a Java `HashMap`, which is another one
entirely, so a client keys the answer by the path and never by position. Its three per-replica fields come from
`ReplicaManager.describeLogDirs` as `new ReplicaInfo(log.size, getLogEndOffsetLag(…), log.isFuture)`:

| Field       | What the broker puts in it                                                                     |
|-------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Size`      | `Log.size`, the bytes of the **log segments** of this replica in this directory; the indexes are not counted, so the number is much smaller than what `du` says about the directory |
| `OffsetLag` | For the **current** log `max(highWatermark - logEndOffset, 0)` - 0 on a healthy leader, and 0 for every replica of the one-broker container. For a **future** log `logEndOffset(current) - logEndOffset(future)`, i.e. the records the mover still has to copy. `-1` (`DescribeLogDirsResponse.INVALID_OFFSET_LAG`) when the broker has no replica object for the partition at all |
| `IsFuture`  | `true` for the log an AlterReplicaLogDirs created and that `ReplicaAlterLogDirsThread` is filling |

Error codes observed and documented on the 1.1.1 container:

| Code | Name              | Where it appears                                                                  |
|------|-------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None              | Per directory: the disk is online and `Topic` is what it holds of the request       |
| 56   | KafkaStorageError | Per directory: the directory is configured but **offline**, and its topic array is empty |
| -1   | Unknown           | Per directory: any other failure while it was read                                  |

There is **no top-level error code**: a failure is always a property of one directory. The one whole-answer case is
authorization - a client that may not `Describe` the cluster resource gets an empty `LogDir` array, which the Java
admin client turns back into 31 (ClusterAuthorizationFailed).

**Quirk: an unknown topic or partition is neither an error nor an entry.** The broker intersects the requested set
with the logs it has (`logsByDir` filtered by `partitions.contains`), so a topic the cluster does not have simply
produces nothing - the answer is the two directories with empty topic arrays, exactly as for an empty request array.
There is no code 3 anywhere in this api, and the request does not create the topic it names.

**Quirk: a partition that is being moved is reported twice.** While `ReplicaAlterLogDirsThread` runs, the source
directory reports the replica with `IsFuture = false` and the real `Size`, and the destination reports the *same*
partition with `IsFuture = true`, a `Size` that starts at 0 and grows, and an `OffsetLag` that starts at the whole
log and falls to 0. `describelogdirs.response.v0.future` is that answer: the same partition in both directories, the
future one 1000 records behind. When the mover swaps the logs, the future entry becomes the current one and the
source directory loses its entry - it is then reported with an empty topic array again.

`kafka-log-dirs.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe` of the image sends exactly this api with a null
topic array and prints the answer as JSON, which is the cross-check for everything above.

**What a 2.8.2 broker answers, and what it ignores.** The partition filter of the request is applied to the
*partitions* alone: `ReplicaManager.describeLogDirs` @ 2.8.2 groups **every** log of a directory by topic and only
then keeps the partitions the request named, so the answer carries one entry per topic of the broker - the ones
nobody asked for with an empty partition array - where a 1.1.1 broker answered the requested topics alone. A
request for one partition of one topic on the shared container of this line therefore comes back with a hundred
topic names and 12 kB of frame, and `AdminClient::describeLogDirs()` hands that map on as the broker sent it.
A caller that wants the replicas it asked for reads them out of the answer by name; it may not assume that the
answer holds nothing else. The stored `describelogdirs.response.v1` is the captured answer with those foreign
topics removed - the only constructed vector of this line.

## AlterReplicaLogDirs API (key 34, v0 to v2)

Moves a replica to **another log directory of the same broker**. The api arrived with Kafka **1.0**
(KIP-113) as version 0.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`ALTER_REPLICA_LOG_DIRS_REQUEST_V1 = ALTER_REPLICA_LOG_DIRS_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and it is the version this client sends; a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version
below it. The pair `alterreplicalogdirs.request.v1` / `alterreplicalogdirs.response.v1` at the end of this document was
captured on the 2.8.2 container.

```
AlterReplicaLogDirsRequest => [LogDir]
  LogDir => LogDirPath [Topic]
    LogDirPath => string
    Topic => TopicName [PartitionId]
      TopicName   => string
      PartitionId => int32
```

```
AlterReplicaLogDirsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [Topic]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Topic => TopicName [Partition]
    TopicName => string
    Partition => PartitionId ErrorCode
      PartitionId => int32
      ErrorCode   => int16
```

The counterpart of "DescribeLogDirs API (key 35, v0 to v2)": it says where a replica **should** live, so that the disks of
a broker can be evened out without moving the partition to another broker. The request is grouped by destination
directory because that is the *value* of the map the Java client keeps
(`Map<TopicPartition, String>`, inverted by `AlterReplicaLogDirsRequest.toStruct`); the answer is grouped by topic
and does not repeat the destination. Like DescribeLogDirs the api is **broker-local**, so the request goes to the
broker that hosts the replica - `Admin\AdminClient::alterReplicaLogDirs()` is keyed by an
`Admin\TopicPartitionReplica`, which names the broker, and splits the call per broker id.

**The answer only says that the request was accepted.** `ReplicaManager.alterReplicaLogDirs` runs inside the request
handler: it validates the directory, creates the **future log** (`Partition.maybeCreateFutureReplica`) and starts a
`ReplicaAlterLogDirsThread` for the partition, and then answers 0. The copy itself runs in the background and is
watched with DescribeLogDirs, whose `IsFuture` entry disappears when the mover swaps the logs in. On the container a
partition of 8 MB is moved in about a quarter of a second - unless the mover is bounded with the dynamic broker
option `replica.alter.log.dirs.io.max.bytes.per.second` (KIP-113), which AlterConfigs of the broker resource accepts
and the broker applies at once; the integration suite sets it to 1 MB/s to watch a move in flight on any disk.

Error codes measured on the 1.1.1 container:

| Code | Name                | Request that produces it                                                         |
|------|---------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                | The move was accepted and started - or the replica already sits in that directory   |
| 9    | ReplicaNotAvailable | This broker has no replica of that partition, including a topic the cluster does not have |
| 56   | KafkaStorageError   | The named directory is one of `log.dirs` but is offline                             |
| 57   | LogDirNotFound      | The path is not one of `log.dirs`, or it is relative                                |
| 31   | ClusterAuthorizationFailed | The client may not `Alter` the cluster resource                             |

**Quirk: an unknown replica is 9, not 3.** The topic apis answer an unknown topic-partition with 3
(UnknownTopicOrPartition); this one does not have that code at all.
`ReplicaManager.alterReplicaLogDirs` calls `getReplicaOrException`, which throws a `ReplicaNotAvailableException`,
and `Errors.forException` maps that to **9** - for a partition the topic does not have *and* for a topic the cluster
has never heard of. The topic is not created either, whatever `auto.create.topics.enable` says: nothing in the path
touches the metadata cache.

**Quirk: 57 for a relative path, even when it names a real directory.** `LogManager.isLogDirOnline` compares the
value against `logDirs.map(_.getAbsolutePath)` and throws a `LogDirNotFoundException` when it is not in the list, so
`kafka-logs` is refused with **57** although `/tmp/kafka-logs` is accepted. "The absolute log directory path" of the
schema is a requirement, not a description.

**Quirk: the directory the replica is already in answers 0 and does nothing.** `maybeCreateFutureReplica` only
creates a future log when the destination differs from the current directory, so the request is a no-op with the
error code 0 - which makes the api idempotent: sending the same assignment twice is harmless, and the second call
does not restart a move that is already finished.

**Quirk: naming another directory while a move runs cancels or redirects it.** A request for a partition that
already has a future log in a *different* directory makes `alterReplicaLogDirs` remove the fetcher, drop the future
replica (`removeFutureLocalReplica` and `logManager.asyncDelete(isFuture = true)`) and start again towards the new
destination - the bytes copied so far are thrown away. Naming the directory the replica is **currently** in is the
same branch, and it is how a running move is **cancelled**: measured on the container, a move of an 8 MB partition
that had copied 820 397 of its bytes was answered 0 and the partition stayed in its original directory. The deletion
of the abandoned log is `logManager.asyncDelete`, i.e. a scheduler task, so a DescribeLogDirs that arrives right
behind the answer can still see the future entry for a moment - `tests/Integration/LogDirsApiTest.php` therefore
polls for the settled state rather than asserting on the next frame.

**Quirk: an empty `LogDir` array is answered with an empty topic array**, not with an error: the broker maps over
an empty map. The same is true of a directory entry whose topic array is empty.

`kafka-log-dirs.sh` of the image only knows `--describe`, `--broker-list` and `--topic-list`; the tool that sends
*this* api from the command line is `kafka-reassign-partitions.sh` with a `log_dirs` field in its assignment JSON.

**Quirk: a resource type that is neither a topic nor a broker fails the WHOLE request.** The message comes from the
authorization split of `KafkaApis.handleAlterConfigsRequest`, which throws out of the `partition` before
`AdminManager` sees anything, so every resource of that request is answered with 42 and `Unexpected resource type
GROUP` - the resources that would have been fine are not applied. DescribeConfigs throws in the same place, with a
message that names the resource.

**Quirk: removing a dynamic broker config does not always put the old value back.** After
`log.cleaner.backoff.ms` had been set to 16000 and the entry was removed again, the container answered the option
with the value **17000** of a *cluster default* that had been removed in the same breath, at the source
`DEFAULT_CONFIG`, whose synonym said 15000 - the config store was empty, the live `KafkaConfig` was not. Setting the
option back to its documented default explicitly and removing it afterwards leaves the broker consistent, which is
what `ConfigsApiTest` does; a test that changes a dynamic broker option should restore it that way and never rely
on the removal alone.

**A partition the broker does not know is 3 on a 2.8.2 broker, not 9.** The catch block of
`ReplicaManager.alterReplicaLogDirs` still turns a `NotLeaderOrFollowerException` into the error code **9**
(`ReplicaNotAvailable`) - the comment there says "retaining REPLICA_NOT_AVAILABLE exception for
ALTER_REPLICA_LOG_DIRS for compatibility" - but that exception is only raised when the metadata cache knows the
partition. `getPartitionOrError` @ 2.8.2 answers `UnknownTopicOrPartitionException` for a topic the broker does
not know and for a partition index the topic does not have, so both are the error code **3** where a 1.1.1 broker
answered 9. The move of a replica the broker really hosts is unchanged, and neither case creates a topic.

### What Kafka 2.8 changed here (KIP-482)

**Kafka 2.8 added the version 2** and changed no field: the first flexible version of this api
(`"flexibleVersions": "2+"` in `AlterReplicaLogDirsRequest.json` @ 2.8.2). The log directory paths and the topic
names are compact, every array is a compact array, and the body, every directory, every topic and - in the answer -
every partition result end in a tagged-field section. The pair `alterreplicalogdirs.request.v2` /
`alterreplicalogdirs.response.v2` at the end of this document moves one replica of `t4-28-vectors` to the other
log directory of the container; `AlterReplicaLogDirsRequestV1` is the plain frame of Kafka 2.0.

## CreatePartitions API (key 37, v0 to v3)

Raises the number of partitions of topics that exist. New in Kafka **1.0** (KIP-195), **v0** in every release
of the 1.x line; it is the last piece of `kafka-topics.sh --alter` that needed ZooKeeper before.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`CREATE_PARTITIONS_REQUEST_V1 = CREATE_PARTITIONS_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and it is the version this client sends; a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version
below it. The pair `createpartitions.request.v1` / `createpartitions.response.v1` at the end of this document was
captured on the 2.8.2 container.

**Kafka 2.5 added the version 2**, the first **flexible** version of the api (`"flexibleVersions": "2+"` of
`CreatePartitionsRequest.json` @ 2.8.2): the same fields in the compact encoding, the request header v2, and a
tagged-field section at the end of the header, of every topic entry, of every assignment entry and of the body.
Nothing else moved - the `assignment` array is the compact nullable array, so the `ff ff ff ff` of a request that
leaves the placement to the controller is a single `00`.

**The tag buffer of an assignment entry is easy to lose.** `CreatePartitionsAssignment` of
`CreatePartitionsRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 is a **structure** with the single field `BrokerIds`, and in the plain
encoding of the versions 0 and 1 that is invisible: a structure is neither counted nor delimited, so a client that
writes the flat `[[0], [0]]` writes exactly the right bytes. From the version 2 on the structure ends in a
tagged-field section of its own, and a frame that is missing it is one byte short of what the broker expects: the
2.8.2 container **closes the connection without an answer** - no error code, no message, just a
`NetworkException` on the next read. `Protocol\Data\CreatePartitionsRequestAssignment` is that structure here, for
every version, which is why the v0 and v1 frames are unchanged to the byte. `CreatePartitionsRequest`/`CreatePartitionsResponse` are
the version 2 with `FLEXIBLE_VERSION = 2`, `CreatePartitionsRequestV1`/`CreatePartitionsResponseV1` keep the frame
of the versions 0 and 1, and the pair `createpartitions.request.v2` / `createpartitions.response.v2` at the end of
this document is the exchange that grew `t4-25-vectors` from one partition to two.

```
CreatePartitionsRequest => [TopicPartitions] Timeout ValidateOnly
  TopicPartitions => Topic Count Assignment
    Topic      => string
    Count      => int32
    Assignment => nullable array of BrokerIds   -- a STRUCT with one field
      BrokerIds => array of int32
  Timeout      => int32
  ValidateOnly => boolean
```

```
CreatePartitionsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [TopicErrors]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  TopicErrors => Topic ErrorCode ErrorMessage
    Topic        => string
    ErrorCode    => int16
    ErrorMessage => nullable string
```

`CreatePartitionsRequest.java` @ 1.1.1 declares `Count` and `Assignment` as a nested `new_partitions` STRUCT of the
topic entry; a struct is neither counted nor delimited on the wire, so the three fields travel one after the other
and `Data\CreatePartitionsRequestTopic` carries them flat.

**Only the active controller serves it**, like CreateTopics and DeleteTopics: every other broker answers each topic
of the request with 41 (NotController), and `Admin\AdminClient::createPartitions()` therefore looks the controller
up and repeats the request once on that code. `Timeout` is how long the controller waits for the new partitions to
exist before it answers - a timeout of 0 answers immediately with the error code **7** and a null message for every
accepted topic, while the partitions are created anyway - and `ValidateOnly` runs the whole validation and creates
nothing.

**The api can only ever GROW a topic.** `Count` is the number of partitions the topic should have *afterwards*, not
the number to add, and `AdminManager.createPartitions` refuses anything that is not above the current count:
`Topic already has 3 partitions.` for the same number and `Topic currently has 3 partitions, which is higher than the
requested 2.` for fewer, both with the error code 37. Kafka cannot merge the log of two partitions, and shrinking a
compacted topic would move keys to another partition.

`Assignment` is `null` (`ff ff ff ff`) for "let the controller place the new partitions", or one entry per **added**
partition - `Count` minus the current count - each of them one broker id per replica, the leader first. Its length
and its width are both checked: `Increasing the number of partitions by 2 but 1 assignments provided.` and
`Unknown broker(s) in replica assignment: 7.`, both the error code 39.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Name                     | Request that produces it                                | ErrorMessage                                               |
|------|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                     | The topic has the requested number of partitions now    | `null`                                                      |
| 3    | UnknownTopicOrPartition  | A topic the cluster does not have                       | `The topic 't4-configs-absent' does not exist.`             |
| 7    | RequestTimedOut          | `Timeout = 0`; the partitions are created anyway        | `null`                                                      |
| 37   | InvalidPartitions        | A count at or below the current partition count         | `Topic already has 3 partitions.`                           |
| 39   | InvalidReplicaAssignment | An assignment of the wrong length                       | `Increasing the number of partitions by 2 but 1 assignments provided.` |
| 39   | InvalidReplicaAssignment | An assignment that names a broker the cluster does not have | `Unknown broker(s) in replica assignment: 7.`           |
| 41   | NotController            | A broker that is not the active controller              | *(not producible on a one-broker container)*                |
| 42   | InvalidRequest           | The same topic twice in one request                     | `Duplicate topic in request.`                               |
| 44   | PolicyViolation          | A `create.topic.policy.class.name` refused the count    | *(the container runs without a policy)*                     |

**A one-broker container cannot produce the 41.** The only broker of the cluster is the controller, so the
`NotController` path of `Admin\AdminClient::createPartitions()` - look the controller up again and send the request
once more - is covered by the unit tests with a scripted broker (`tests/Unit/Admin/AdminClientTest.php`) and not
against the container, exactly like the same path of CreateTopics.

**Quirk: the answer arrives before the other brokers know.** A successful answer means that the CONTROLLER has the
new partitions; a Metadata request that overtakes the update of the metadata cache can still report the old
partition count or answer 5 (LeaderNotAvailable) for the new partitions for a moment, exactly as after
CreateTopics. `TopicAdminApiTest` polls the metadata until the count is there.

**Quirk: an unknown topic is 3 here, and the defaults in DescribeConfigs.** This api reads the current partition
count out of ZooKeeper and knows the difference; `DescribeConfigs` merges an empty entity config with the broker
defaults and answers 0 for a topic that does not exist. Neither of them creates the topic.

### What Kafka 2.7 changed here (KIP-599)

**Kafka 2.7 added the version 3**, "identical to version 2 but may return a THROTTLING_QUOTA_EXCEEDED error"
(`CreatePartitionsRequest.json` @ 2.7.2): no field moves, and the version is the promise of the client that it
understands the error code **89** and repeats the topics the controller mutation quota refused - see "KIP-599: the
version that is answered instead of being held back" in the CreateTopics section.
`CreatePartitionsRequestV2`/`CreatePartitionsResponseV2` keep the frame of the version 2.

## DeleteGroups API (key 42, v0 to v2)

Makes a coordinator forget consumer groups and the offsets they committed. New in Kafka **1.1** (KIP-229), **v0**;
before it, `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --delete` had to write to ZooKeeper.

```
DeleteGroupsRequest => [GroupId]
  GroupId => string
```

```
DeleteGroupsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [GroupErrorCodes]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  GroupErrorCodes => GroupId ErrorCode
    GroupId   => string
    ErrorCode => int16
```

**Version 1 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219)** is that same frame with a higher version field — `DeleteGroupsRequest.json`
@ 2.8.2 has the single field `GroupsNames` at `0+`; `DeleteGroupsRequestV0` keeps the version a 1.1.1 broker
serves.

**Version 2 (Kafka 2.4, KIP-482) is the first flexible version of the api**, and it is the version this client
sends: the group names become a **compact array of compact strings**, the request header is the header **v2**
whose tag buffer follows the client id, the answer is read with the response header **v1**, and a tagged-field
section closes the body as well as every group result of it. Not a field was added on either side, so
`DeleteGroupsRequestV1`/`DeleteGroupsResponseV1` are the very same content as the plain frame of Kafka 2.0 - see
the vectors `deletegroups.request/response.v2` against `…v1` - and `DeleteGroupsRequestV0`/`DeleteGroupsResponseV0`
are the frame below them, whose answer has no `throttle_time_ms`.

The request is the frame of DescribeGroups and takes the same route: a group is deleted by **its own coordinator**
({@see GroupCoordinator}, key 10), and any other broker answers it with 16 (NotCoordinatorForGroup).
`Admin\AdminClient::deleteConsumerGroups()` looks a coordinator up for every group and sends one request per
coordinator; on the one-broker container every group is coordinated by the same node, so a call is always one frame.
There is no `error_message` anywhere in this api and no top-level error code: one entry per group, and the code is
everything the coordinator says.

`GroupCoordinator.handleDeleteGroups` @ 1.1.1 removes the group from its cache and writes a **tombstone** for every
offset the group committed into `__consumer_offsets`. Measured on the container: after the answer the group is gone
from ListGroups, an OffsetFetch of it answers `-1` for every partition, and DescribeGroups answers the state `Dead`
with the error code 0 - the same answer it gives for a group that never existed.

**A group is only deletable when it has no member left.** A group in the state `Empty` - every member gone or timed
out, offsets still there - and one in `Dead` are deleted; a group with a live member is answered with **68**
(NonEmptyGroup) and keeps everything, so the offsets of running consumers can not be thrown away by accident. A
group the coordinator has never heard of is **69** (GroupIdNotFound), which is the one way to tell "there was
nothing to delete" from "it is still in use", and an **empty** group id is 24 (InvalidGroupId).

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Name                         | Request that produces it                                  |
|------|------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                         | An `Empty` group: it and its committed offsets are gone   |
| 24   | InvalidGroupId               | An empty group id in the array                            |
| 68   | NonEmptyGroup                | A group that still has a member                           |
| 69   | GroupIdNotFound              | A group the coordinator does not know, and a group that was deleted a moment ago |
| 14   | GroupLoadInProgress          | The coordinator is still reading `__consumer_offsets`     |
| 15   | GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable | The coordinator is shutting down                          |
| 16   | NotCoordinatorForGroup       | The broker does not coordinate that group *(one broker: not producible)* |
| 30   | GroupAuthorizationFailed     | *(needs an authorizer, not producible on the container)*  |

**Quirk: an `Empty` group without offsets does not stay deletable.** `GroupMetadataManager.cleanupGroupMetadata()`
runs every `offsets.retention.check.interval.ms` (600 s by default, the value of the container) and transitions
**every** group that is `Empty` and holds no offset at all to `Dead`, removing it from the cache - the group is then
answered with 69 instead of being deleted, although nothing ever deleted it. A group that committed an offset
survives until `offsets.retention.minutes`. A test that deletes a group it created has to give it an offset, or it
fails whenever the cleanup happens to run in between; `AdminGroupApiTest` does exactly that.

**Quirk: a duplicate group in the request collapses.** `DeleteGroupsRequest.java` reads the array into a
`Set<String>`, so a request that names the same group twice is answered with **one** entry for it. The request
itself is a plain array on the wire, and this client sends `array_unique()` of what it was given.

**Quirk: an empty group array is legal.** It is answered with the throttle time and an empty result array, without
a coordinator lookup on this side - `Admin\AdminClient::deleteConsumerGroups([])` sends nothing at all.

**Quirk: the entries are not in the order of the request.** The coordinator walks a Scala `Map`, so
`deletegroups.response.v0` reports the group it never knew before the one it deleted, although the request named
them the other way round.

## OffsetDelete API (key 47, v0)

Makes a coordinator forget the committed offsets of **single partitions** of a group, without touching the group
itself. New in Kafka **2.4** (KIP-496), **v0**, and it is still the v0 in 2.8.2 — the api was never bumped and,
unlike everything else Kafka 2.4 added, it is **not flexible**: `OffsetDeleteRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 declares no
`flexibleVersions`, so every string is int16-prefixed and every array is counted by an int32. Together with
SaslHandshake (17) it is one of the two client apis of this line that the compact encoding never reaches.

```
OffsetDeleteRequest => GroupId [Topics]
  GroupId => string
  Topics  => Name [Partitions]
    Name       => string
    Partitions => PartitionIndex
      PartitionIndex => int32
```

```
OffsetDeleteResponse => ErrorCode ThrottleTimeMs [Topics]
  ErrorCode      => int16
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Topics         => Name [Partitions]
    Name       => string
    Partitions => PartitionIndex ErrorCode
      PartitionIndex => int32
      ErrorCode      => int16
```

**The top-level error code comes before the throttle time**, which no other api of this protocol does — every other
answer that carries a throttle time opens with it (KIP-124) or closes with it (the token apis). It is not a mistake
of this document: `OffsetDeleteResponse.json` @ 2.8.2 declares `ErrorCode` first and `ThrottleTimeMs` second, the
generated `OffsetDeleteResponseData` writes them in that order, and `offsetdelete.response.v0` shows the two fields
exactly there.

The request goes to **the coordinator of the group** (GroupCoordinator, key 10); any other broker answers 16
(NotCoordinatorForGroup). `Admin\AdminClient::deleteConsumerGroupOffsets()` looks the coordinator up and sends one
frame.

**What the coordinator allows depends on the state of the group**, and only part of it is reported per partition.
`GroupCoordinator.handleDeleteOffsets` @ 2.8.2 decides in this order:

| State of the group                                | What happens                                                    |
|---------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Empty` — no member left                          | Every partition of the request is deleted                        |
| `PreparingRebalance`, `CompletingRebalance`, `Stable` **and** `protocol_type = consumer` | The partitions of the topics its members are subscribed to are refused with **86**, the rest are deleted |
| any other live state, i.e. another protocol type  | The whole request is refused with the top-level **68**            |
| `Dead`, or a group the coordinator does not know  | The top-level **69**                                              |

**A top-level error carries no topic at all.** `KafkaApis.handleOffsetDeleteRequest` @ 2.8.2 builds the answer with
`getErrorResponse()` as soon as the coordinator reports a group error, so the 18-byte frames of
`offsetdelete.response.v0.non-empty-group` and `offsetdelete.response.v0.group-id-not-found` say nothing about the
partitions that were asked for. Everything else is per partition, and one refused partition does not spoil the
others.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Where            | Request that produces it                                                        |
|------|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | top level        | Every partition carries its own code                                             |
| 0    | per partition    | The committed offset is gone — **and also** a partition that never had one       |
| 3    | per partition    | A topic or a partition this broker's metadata cache does not have                |
| 86   | per partition    | A live `consumer` group is subscribed to that topic                              |
| 68   | top level        | A live group whose members joined with another protocol type                     |
| 69   | top level        | A group the coordinator does not know, a `Dead` one, and one that just lost its last offset |
| 14   | top level        | The coordinator is still reading `__consumer_offsets`                            |
| 15   | top level        | The coordinator is shutting down                                                 |
| 16   | top level        | The broker does not coordinate that group *(one broker: not producible)*         |
| 24   | top level        | An empty group id                                                                |
| 29   | per partition    | *(needs an authorizer, not producible on the container)* the client may not read the topic |
| 30   | top level        | *(needs an authorizer, not producible on the container)* the client may not delete the group |

**Quirk: a partition that never had a committed offset is answered with 0.** The coordinator collects the partitions
it considers eligible, hands them to `cleanupGroupMetadata` and then writes `NONE` for **all** of them without
asking how many offsets were really removed. A caller therefore can not tell "there was an offset and it is gone"
from "there was nothing" — measured with a partition of a topic the group had never committed for.

**Quirk: deleting the last committed offset of an `Empty` group deletes the group.** `cleanupGroupMetadata` ends with
`if (group.is(Empty) && !group.hasOffsets) group.transitionTo(Dead)` and drops the group from the cache, so the very
next OffsetDelete — or DeleteGroups, or DescribeGroups — for it answers 69 and `Dead`. Measured: a group with two
committed offsets is still `Empty` after the first partition is deleted and `Dead` after the second one.

**Quirk: a live group can lose the offsets of the topics it is not consuming.** The subscription of a `consumer`
group is only known per topic, so a `Stable` group is refused with 86 for the topics its members subscribed to and
**deleted** for every other topic of the same request. Measured on a group that is subscribed to one topic and had
committed an offset for another.

**Quirk: an unparseable subscription protects every topic.** `GroupMetadata.isSubscribedToTopic` answers `true` when
the coordinator could not compute the subscription of the group — the protocol type is not `consumer`, no protocol
was chosen yet, or the `Subscription` bytes of a member do not parse — because it would rather refuse a deletion
than lose an offset. A group whose members joined the `consumer` protocol with arbitrary metadata therefore answers
86 for **every** topic it is asked about.

**Quirk: an empty topic array is legal.** It is answered with the error code of the *group* and an empty topic
array, i.e. 0 for a group that exists and 69 for one that does not — so the empty request is a cheap existence
probe. `Admin\AdminClient::deleteConsumerGroupOffsets()` with an empty partition list sends nothing at all and
answers the empty array.

## AlterPartitionReassignments API (key 45, v0)

Moves the replicas of partitions to other brokers, or cancels a move that is still running. New in Kafka **2.4**
(KIP-455), **v0**, and **flexible from that version on** — the api was added by the release that introduced KIP-482,
so it has no plain-encoded version at all.

```
AlterPartitionReassignments Request (Version: 0) => TimeoutMs Topics TAG_BUFFER
  TimeoutMs  => int32
  Topics     => compact_[ Name Partitions TAG_BUFFER ]
    Name       => compact_string
    Partitions => compact_[ PartitionIndex Replicas TAG_BUFFER ]
      PartitionIndex => int32
      Replicas       => compact_nullable_[int32]
```

```
AlterPartitionReassignments Response (Version: 0) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ErrorMessage Responses TAG_BUFFER
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
  ErrorMessage   => compact_nullable_string
  Responses      => compact_[ Name Partitions TAG_BUFFER ]
    Name       => compact_string
    Partitions => compact_[ PartitionIndex ErrorCode ErrorMessage TAG_BUFFER ]
```

**What KIP-455 replaced.** Until Kafka 2.4 a reassignment was a JSON document written into the ZooKeeper znode
`/admin/reassign_partitions` by `kafka-reassign-partitions.sh`: **one** reassignment could be in flight for the whole
cluster, it could not be cancelled, and the only way to watch it was to read the znode again. The api submits
reassignments **per partition**, cancels them one by one, and `ListPartitionReassignments` (key 46) reports what is
still running.

* **Only the active controller serves it**, like CreateTopics and CreatePartitions: another broker answers the
  **top-level** error code 41 (`NotController`). `AdminClient::alterPartitionReassignments()` looks the controller
  up, and repeats the request once after a fresh metadata fetch if it moved in between.
* `Replicas` is the **whole replica set the partition should end up with**, in order — the first broker id is the
  preferred leader — and not the set to add; the controller works out what to add and what to remove. `null` is the
  second meaning of the field: it **cancels** a reassignment that is in progress and restores the original set.
* `TimeoutMs` is how long the controller waits to *register* the reassignment, not for the data to move. The answer
  says that the target assignment was written; the replicas are copied afterwards by the replica fetchers, at the
  rate that `leader.replication.throttled.rate` and `follower.replication.throttled.rate` allow, and the work is
  watched with key 46.

**The error of this api is per partition, and the top level says nothing about them.** Measured on the container,
with a one-partition topic on a one-broker cluster:

| What was asked | Partition error | Message |
|---|---|---|
| the replica set the partition already has | **0** | `null` |
| a replica set that names a broker which is not alive (`[0, 7]`) | **39** `InvalidReplicaAssignment` | `Replica assignment has brokers that are not alive. Replica list: ArrayBuffer(7), live broker list: Set(0)` |
| an empty replica list | **39** | `Empty replica list specified in partition reassignment.` |
| a cancellation (`null`) with nothing in progress | **85** `NoReassignmentInProgress` | `No partition reassignment is in progress.` |
| a topic or a partition that does not exist | **3** `UnknownTopicOrPartition` | `The partition does not exist.` |

**Quirk: a reassignment to the current replica set is accepted, not refused.** The controller registers it, sees
that there is nothing to add and nothing to remove, and completes it before it answers — which is the only
successful reassignment a one-broker cluster can produce, and what `alterpartitionreassignments.response.v0` is.

**Quirk: the cancellation of a partition that does not exist is 85, not 3.** `KafkaController` looks a cancellation
up in the reassignments it has in flight before it asks whether the partition exists at all, so "there is nothing to
cancel" wins over "there is no such partition".

**Quirk: the top-level error message of a successful answer is the EMPTY string, not null.** The partitions of the
same answer carry a **null** message when they have no error, so both values of a compact nullable string are on the
wire of one frame: `01` for the empty string of the top level and `00` for the null of a partition.

**Quirk: an empty replica list is refused here, and this client refuses it earlier.**
`Admin\NewPartitionReassignment` throws an `InvalidArgumentException` for `[]`, because the only way to say "stop
what you are doing" is `null`, and an empty list is a request the broker will answer with 39.

## ListPartitionReassignments API (key 46, v0)

Says which partitions the cluster is reassigning right now. New in Kafka **2.4** (KIP-455), **v0**, flexible from
that version on, and the replacement of `kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --verify`.

```
ListPartitionReassignments Request (Version: 0) => TimeoutMs Topics TAG_BUFFER
  TimeoutMs => int32
  Topics    => compact_nullable_[ Name PartitionIndexes TAG_BUFFER ]
    Name             => compact_string
    PartitionIndexes => compact_[int32]
```

```
ListPartitionReassignments Response (Version: 0) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ErrorMessage Topics TAG_BUFFER
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
  ErrorMessage   => compact_nullable_string
  Topics         => compact_[ Name Partitions TAG_BUFFER ]
    Name       => compact_string
    Partitions => compact_[ PartitionIndex Replicas AddingReplicas RemovingReplicas TAG_BUFFER ]
```

* **`null` asks for every reassignment of the cluster, an empty array for none of them.** The two are one byte apart
  (`00` against `01`) and they are not the same question; on a shared cluster a client names its own partitions.
* There is **one** error code, for the request as a whole — 41 (`NotController`) or 31
  (`ClusterAuthorizationFailed`) — and it is what `Client::listPartitionReassignments()` throws. A topic or a
  partition that does not exist is **not** an error: it is simply absent from the answer, because the answer is what
  is going on and not what was asked for.
* `Replicas` is the replica set of the partition **at this moment**, which during a reassignment is the union of the
  old and the new one: the controller adds every target replica first, waits for it to catch up, and removes the
  ones that are leaving afterwards. The target set is therefore `Replicas` minus `RemovingReplicas` and the original
  one `Replicas` minus `AddingReplicas`, which is what `Admin\PartitionReassignment::getTargetReplicas()` and
  `::getOriginalReplicas()` compute.

**A one-broker cluster can never answer anything but the empty list**, and that is not a limitation of the test but
of the cluster: every replica of every partition is already on the only broker, so a reassignment is complete before
the controller answers the request that submitted it. `listpartitionreassignments.response.v0` is therefore the
empty answer — 14 bytes, the shortest complete frame of any api of this document — and the shape of a partition in
flight is documented above from `ControllerContext` @ 2.8.2 and replayed as a constructed vector in the unit tests.

## DescribeClientQuotas API (key 48, v0 and v1)

Reads the **client quotas** of the cluster. New in Kafka **2.6** (KIP-546), **v0**; **v1** (Kafka **2.8**) is the
same frame in the flexible encoding and adds no field.

**The version 0 is a plain frame**, which is worth saying because Kafka 2.6 is well past KIP-482:
`DescribeClientQuotasRequest.json` @ **2.6.3** and @ **2.7.2** both declare `"flexibleVersions": "none"`, and only
@ **2.8.2** does it say `"validVersions": "0-1"`, `"flexibleVersions": "1+"`. This api and its altering half are
therefore the last two of the 2.x line to become compact, two releases after the encoding arrived.

```
DescribeClientQuotasRequest (Version: 0 and 1) => [Components] Strict
  Components => EntityType MatchType Match
    EntityType => string
    MatchType  => int8          (0 exact name, 1 the <default> entity, 2 any name of this type)
    Match      => nullable string
  Strict => boolean
```

```
DescribeClientQuotasResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ErrorMessage [Entries]     (the array is nullable)
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
  ErrorMessage   => nullable string
  Entries => [Entity] [Values]
    Entity => EntityType EntityName
      EntityType => string
      EntityName => nullable string        (null is the <default> entity of that type)
    Values => Key Value
      Key   => string
      Value => float64
```

**This is where `float64` enters the protocol.** Eight bytes of an IEEE 754 double in network order, and the only
two apis of Kafka 2.8.2 that carry one are this and AlterClientQuotas — a quota is a rate, and
`request_percentage` of `12.5` is not expressible any other way. `TYPE_FLOAT64` of the engine writes it with
`pack('E')`.

Until Kafka 2.6 a client quota could only be read out of **ZooKeeper**, which is why every quota test of the lines
below this one shells `kafka-configs.sh --zookeeper` into the container. The api is declared
`"listeners": ["zkBroker"]`, and it is answered **from the quota cache of whatever broker receives it** — there is
no coordinator and no controller in this path, so `AdminClient::describeClientQuotas()` sends it to the first
broker that answers.

**The filter is a conjunction of components**, one per entity type, and a request with no component at all
describes every quota of the cluster. A quota entity is an **array** of `(entity type, name)` pairs, because Kafka
attaches a quota to a combination as readily as to one name: `client-id` alone, `user` alone, `user` *and*
`client-id` together, or `ip` (KIP-612). A `null` entity name is the `<default>` entity of that type — what
`kafka-configs.sh` prints as `<default>` — and `MATCH_TYPE_DEFAULT` is how a filter asks for it.

**`strict` is about the types the filter does *not* name.** Measured on the container with one quota on
`client-id=X` and one on the pair `(user=Y, client-id=X)`:

| Filter                                              | `strict` | Answered                                  |
|-----------------------------------------------------|----------|---------------------------------------------|
| any name of type `client-id`                        | false    | both entities                              |
| any name of type `client-id`                        | **true** | only the entity that is *only* a `client-id` |
| the exact name `client-id=X`                        | false    | both entities                              |
| no component at all                                 | false    | every quota entity of the cluster          |

**An entry carries every quota of its entity**, not only the ones the caller was interested in — the filter selects
entities, never keys.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Name                | Request that produces it                                                    |
|------|---------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                | The filter was understood; `entries` is the (possibly empty) list of matches  |
| 35   | UnsupportedVersion  | An entity type the broker does not know — *"Custom entity type 'x' not supported"* |
| -1   | UnknownServerError  | A **match type** the broker does not know, see the quirk below                |
| 41   | NotController       | *(not producible on the container: the api is answered by any ZooKeeper-backed broker)* |

**Quirk: the entry array is `null` for an error and empty for "nothing matched".**
`DescribeClientQuotasResponse.fromException()` @ 2.8.2 builds every error answer with a null array, while a filter
that simply found nothing answers the empty one — so a caller that only looks at the count cannot tell a refusal
from an empty cluster, and has to read the error code.

**Quirk: an unknown match type is the error code -1 and not 42.** `DescribeClientQuotasRequest.filter()` @ 2.8.2
turns the `int8` into a `ClientQuotaFilterComponent` with a `switch` whose `default` throws a plain
`IllegalArgumentException("Unexpected match type: 7")`, and that happens in `KafkaApis` *before* any error mapping.
The request therefore ends in the generic handler and is answered `UnknownServerError` with a **null** message,
which is a validation gap of the broker rather than a code it means to send. An unknown *entity type*, by contrast,
is refused properly — with 35, oddly, not with 42.

**Quirk: an entity whose quotas were all removed disappears.** `kafka-configs.sh --describe --entity-type clients`
still prints a line for it (`Configs for client-id 'x' are`, with nothing after the `are`), because the znode
survives; this api answers only entities that have at least one quota left.

## AlterClientQuotas API (key 49, v0 and v1)

Sets and removes client quotas. New in Kafka **2.6** (KIP-546), **v0**; like its describing half it is a **plain**
frame until Kafka **2.8** adds the flexible **v1**, which adds no field.

```
AlterClientQuotasRequest (Version: 0 and 1) => [Entries] ValidateOnly
  Entries => [Entity] [Ops]
    Entity => EntityType EntityName
      EntityType => string
      EntityName => nullable string
    Ops => Key Value Remove
      Key    => string
      Value  => float64
      Remove => boolean
  ValidateOnly => boolean
```

```
AlterClientQuotasResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [Entries]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Entries => ErrorCode ErrorMessage [Entity]
    ErrorCode    => int16
    ErrorMessage => nullable string
    Entity => EntityType EntityName
```

**There is no top-level error code**: one entry of the answer per entry of the request, in the order the request
named them, and the error stands **in front of** the entity it belongs to. One refused entity does not stop the
others, which is why `AdminClient::alterClientQuotas()` throws nothing and reports every entity instead.

**A change is a value plus a flag, never an absent field.** `Remove = false` sets the quota to `Value`,
`Remove = true` deletes it and the broker ignores `Value` — the frame has no optional fields, so a removal still
carries eight bytes of double. The Java client writes `Double.NaN` there; this client writes `0.0`, and the broker
reads and discards either. Removing a quota that was never set is **not** an error: it is answered with 0.

`ValidateOnly` asks the broker to check the request and write nothing, and answers the very same shape — measured:
a validate-only change of `producer_byte_rate` left the quota exactly as it was.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Name           | Request that produces it                                                      |
|------|----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None           | Every op of that entity was applied (or validated)                             |
| 42   | InvalidRequest | A quota name the broker does not know — *"Invalid configuration key x"* — and an entity type it does not know |
| 41   | NotController  | *(not producible on the container)* a broker that does not write the quota store |

**A `<default>` quota is a cluster-wide decision, so no test of this repository writes one.** The api can:
`ClientQuotaEntity::defaultOf('user')` is the `<default>` user entity, and a quota written there applies to every
principal that has none of its own — on the shared container of this line that would throttle every other suite.
The `<default>` entity is therefore only ever *read* here (`ClientQuotaFilterComponent::ofDefaultEntity()`), the
same restraint the reassignment apis show towards a null topic array.

**What this replaces.** `tests/Fixture/ClientQuota` still sets its quotas by shelling `kafka-configs.sh` into the
container, because the lines below this one had no protocol for it and the fixture is shared with the suites that
came from them. From this line on the same thing can be done with two requests, and
`tests/Integration/ClientQuotaApiTest.php` does exactly that — against quotas of its own client ids, which it
removes again when the class is done.

## DescribeUserScramCredentials API (key 50, v0)

Which SCRAM credentials a user has. New in Kafka **2.7** (KIP-554), **v0**, and **flexible from that version** —
2.7 is well past KIP-482, so every api it adds is compact from the start.

```
DescribeUserScramCredentialsRequest => [Users]           (the array is nullable)
  Users => Name
    Name => compact string
```

```
DescribeUserScramCredentialsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ErrorMessage [Results]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
  ErrorMessage   => compact nullable string
  Results => User ErrorCode ErrorMessage [CredentialInfos]
    User            => compact string
    ErrorCode       => int16
    ErrorMessage    => compact nullable string
    CredentialInfos => Mechanism Iterations
      Mechanism  => int8      (1 SCRAM-SHA-256, 2 SCRAM-SHA-512)
      Iterations => int32
```

Before Kafka 2.7 a SCRAM user existed only as a znode that `kafka-configs.sh --zookeeper --entity-type users`
wrote; KIP-554 gave it a protocol, and with it the `--bootstrap-server` form of that tool. Served by any
ZooKeeper-backed broker (`"listeners": ["zkBroker"]`) out of the credential cache it keeps for authentication.

**No answer ever carries a password, and there is no field for one.** A SCRAM credential *is* a salted password:
handing it out would hand out the ability to authenticate. What is describable is the mechanism and the iteration
count.

**`null` and the empty array mean the same thing here** — "every user that has a credential" — which is unique in
this protocol: everywhere else a nullable array distinguishes "all" from "none", and
`DescribeUserScramCredentialsRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 says *"or null/empty to describe all users"* in as many words.
Measured: both forms answer the same list.

**There is a top-level error code and a per-user one**, and they say different things. The top level is for what
the request as a whole ran into; the per-user code is about that user, and in practice it is **91**
(`ResourceNotFound`) — *"Attempt to describe a user credential that does not exist: X"* — for a user without a
single credential. A user is therefore never silently absent, which is what lets a caller tell "no credential"
from "not asked about". `AdminClient::describeUserScramCredentials()` turns that entry into an absent key of its
result, so the caller can simply look a user up.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Where         | Request that produces it                                       |
|------|---------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | top level     | The users could be looked up                                    |
| 0    | per user      | The user has at least one credential                            |
| 91   | per user      | The user has none                                               |
| 92   | per user      | *(the same user named twice in one request)*                    |
| 15   | top level     | *(the credential cache is not ready yet)*                       |
| 29/31| top level     | *(needs an authorizer, not producible on the container)*        |

## AlterUserScramCredentials API (key 51, v0)

Writes and removes SCRAM credentials. New in Kafka **2.7** (KIP-554), **v0**, flexible from that version.

```
AlterUserScramCredentialsRequest => [Deletions] [Upsertions]
  Deletions => Name Mechanism
    Name      => compact string
    Mechanism => int8
  Upsertions => Name Mechanism Iterations Salt SaltedPassword
    Name           => compact string
    Mechanism      => int8
    Iterations     => int32
    Salt           => compact bytes
    SaltedPassword => compact bytes
```

```
AlterUserScramCredentialsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [Results]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Results => User ErrorCode ErrorMessage
```

**The client derives the salted password; the broker never sees the password.** `SaltedPassword` is
`Hi(password, salt, iterations)` of RFC 5802 — PBKDF2-HMAC with the hash of the mechanism, 32 bytes for
SCRAM-SHA-256 and 64 for SCRAM-SHA-512 — which in PHP is
`hash_pbkdf2('sha256', $password, $salt, $iterations, 32, true)` and in Kafka is `ScramFormatter.hi()`.
`Admin\UserScramCredentialUpsertion` takes the password, generates a salt when it is given none, and does that
computation on the way to the wire; the password never leaves the process.

**The deletions come first on the wire and are applied first**, which is what makes "replace the credential of
this user" one request.

**There is no top-level error code, and the results are per *user*, not per change.** A request that deletes one
credential of a user and writes another is answered with a single entry for them — which is also why naming the
same user and mechanism twice is an error rather than a last-one-wins.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Name                   | Request that produces it                                                  |
|------|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                   | Every change of that user was applied                                      |
| 91   | ResourceNotFound       | Deleting a credential the user does not have — *"Attempt to delete a user credential that does not exist"* |
| 92   | DuplicateResource      | The same user and mechanism twice — *"A user credential cannot be altered twice in the same request"* |
| 93   | UnacceptableCredential | An iteration count below the minimum of the mechanism (4096 for both) — *"Too few iterations"*; also an unknown mechanism or a salt of the wrong length |
| 31   | ClusterAuthorizationFailed | *(needs an authorizer, not producible on the container)*                |

**Quirk: the changes of one user are applied all-or-nothing.** A request that writes the SHA-256 credential of a
user *and* deletes a SHA-512 one they do not have is answered with the single code 91 for that user, and **neither**
change is made - measured. The api has one result per user and, with it, one outcome per user: a caller that wants
the possible half of a change applied has to send it on its own. (This is also why the cleanup of
`UserScramCredentialsApiTest` describes the users first and deletes only the mechanisms they really have.)

**Using a SCRAM credential to log in is out of scope on this line.** A credential written here can be verified by
the broker, but this client speaks SASL/PLAIN only — the same limitation the delegation tokens of KIP-48 carry,
and for the same reason: a SCRAM login is a SASL/SCRAM exchange, not a protocol api. What the container shows is
that the credential really exists: `kafka-configs.sh --describe --entity-type users` prints
`SCRAM-SHA-256=salt=…,stored_key=…,server_key=…,iterations=8192` for the user this api wrote.

## UpdateFeatures API (key 57, v0)

Raises or deletes the finalized version level of a **feature** of the cluster. New in Kafka **2.7** (KIP-584),
**v0**, flexible from that version.

```
UpdateFeaturesRequest => TimeoutMs [FeatureUpdates]
  TimeoutMs => int32
  FeatureUpdates => Feature MaxVersionLevel AllowDowngrade
    Feature         => compact string
    MaxVersionLevel => int16
    AllowDowngrade  => boolean
```

```
UpdateFeaturesResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ErrorMessage [Results]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
  ErrorMessage   => compact nullable string
  Results => Feature ErrorCode ErrorMessage
```

**A feature is not an api version.** KIP-584 added a second, cluster-wide versioning axis: a named range that
*every* broker of the cluster supports (the `supported_features` of an ApiVersions answer) and a level the cluster
has *agreed* on (its `finalized_features`, with an epoch). This api is the write half of that; **the read half is
the ApiVersions v3 answer**, which is why `AdminClient::describeFeatures()` sends an ApiVersions and not a request
of its own — `Admin.describeFeatures()` of the Java client does the same.

**Controller-only**: `KafkaController.processFeatureUpdates` @ 2.8.2 answers the top-level **41** (`NotController`)
unless it is active, so `AdminClient::updateFeatures()` sends the request to the controller and repeats it once
against a freshly looked up one.

A `MaxVersionLevel` **below 1** is not a version but the request to **delete** the finalized feature, and every
lowering — a deletion included — needs `AllowDowngrade`.

**On a ZooKeeper-backed Kafka 2.8.2 cluster there is nothing to finalize.** Measured on the container: the
ApiVersions v3 answer carries **no** supported feature, an empty finalized set and the epoch **0**, and every
`FeatureUpdate` is answered with the per-feature code **42** (`InvalidRequest`) — *"Could not apply finalized
feature update because the provided feature is not supported."* for an addition and *"Can not delete non-existing
finalized feature."* for a deletion. The api is implemented here for the frame and for the day a cluster does
finalize something; there is no answer of `0` to be had from this container.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Where        | Request that produces it                                                    |
|------|--------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | top level    | The controller looked at the request; every feature carries its own code      |
| 42   | per feature  | A feature the cluster does not support, and the deletion of one it has not finalized |
| 41   | top level    | The request reached a broker that is not the active controller                 |
| 96   | per feature  | *(`FeatureUpdateFailed`: the write to ZooKeeper failed — not producible here)*  |

**Quirk: an empty update list is not refused.** The Java admin client rejects an empty map on the client side, and
`UpdateFeaturesRequest.json` has no minimum, but `processFeatureUpdatesWithActiveController` @ 2.8.2 simply
iterates an empty collection: the answer is the top-level **0** with no result at all. Measured.

## DescribeCluster API (key 60, v0)

The cluster id, the controller and the brokers, without naming a topic. New in Kafka **2.8** (KIP-700), **v0**,
flexible from that version.

```
DescribeClusterRequest => IncludeClusterAuthorizedOperations
  IncludeClusterAuthorizedOperations => boolean
```

```
DescribeClusterResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ErrorMessage ClusterId ControllerId [Brokers]
                           ClusterAuthorizedOperations
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
  ErrorMessage   => compact nullable string
  ClusterId      => compact string
  ControllerId   => int32                       (-1 while the cluster has no controller)
  Brokers => BrokerId Host Port Rack
    BrokerId => int32
    Host     => compact string
    Port     => int32
    Rack     => compact nullable string
  ClusterAuthorizedOperations => int32
```

**This is the smallest request of the protocol**: a single boolean. Until Kafka 2.8 the three facts it carries
could only be read out of a **Metadata** answer — a request about *topics* that happens to name the cluster id, the
controller and the brokers — so a client that wanted them alone sent an empty topic array and paid for the topic
machinery on the broker. KIP-700 gave them a request of their own, served by any broker
(`"listeners": ["zkBroker", "broker"]`).

**`cluster_authorized_operations` is `Integer.MIN_VALUE` (`-2147483648`) when the request did not ask for it**,
which is the default of the specification and not an error; `Admin\ClusterDescription::hasAuthorizedOperations()`
is that test. A request that *does* ask gets the bit field of KIP-430, one bit per `AclOperation` the caller may
perform on the cluster. Measured on the container, which runs **without** an authorizer and therefore allows
everything: **8096**, i.e. `0b1111110100000` — the bits 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12, which are `CREATE`, `ALTER`,
`DESCRIBE`, `CLUSTER_ACTION`, `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS`, `ALTER_CONFIGS` and `IDEMPOTENT_WRITE` of `AclOperation` @ 2.8.2
— the whole set `AclEntry.supportedOperations(CLUSTER)` names. (The same field appears in Metadata v8 and in
DescribeGroups v3 for their own resource types, with their own sets.)

`AdminClient::describeCluster()` sends this api; `AdminClient::describeClusterFromMetadata()` builds the same
`ClusterDescription` out of a Metadata answer, which is what a broker below Kafka 2.8 needs — the choice is the
caller's, because a 2.8.2 broker is the first that serves the key 60 at all.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Request that produces it                                                        |
|------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | Always, on a broker that serves the api                                          |
| 31   | *(needs an authorizer, not producible on the container)* `ClusterAuthorizationFailed` |

## DescribeProducers API (key 61, v0)

Which producers a partition still remembers. New in Kafka **2.8** (KIP-664), **v0**, flexible from that version.

```
DescribeProducersRequest => [Topics]
  Topics => Name [PartitionIndexes]
    Name             => compact string
    PartitionIndexes => compact array of int32
```

```
DescribeProducersResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [Topics]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Topics => Name [Partitions]
    Partitions => PartitionIndex ErrorCode ErrorMessage [ActiveProducers]
      PartitionIndex => int32
      ErrorCode      => int16
      ErrorMessage   => compact nullable string
      ActiveProducers => ProducerId ProducerEpoch LastSequence LastTimestamp CoordinatorEpoch
                         CurrentTxnStartOffset
        ProducerId            => int64
        ProducerEpoch         => int32
        LastSequence          => int32   (-1 when unknown)
        LastTimestamp         => int64   (-1 when unknown)
        CoordinatorEpoch      => int32
```
