  `transaction.state.log.min.isr=1`** on a one-broker cluster. Without them `__transaction_state` cannot be created
  and every transactional request ends in 15 (`GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable`), long after the api itself parsed
  fine. The container of this line sets both.
* **A 1.1.1 broker keeps reading and writing the older message formats.** A topic created with
  `--config message.format.version=0.10.0` or `0.9.0` stores the format that version implies, and a Fetch below the
  version that understands the newer format is answered **down-converted**. That is what keeps the wire vectors of
  the three lines below replayable against this broker, and it costs the broker a copy of the log region per
  answer. → "What the broker converts, and when".
* **(1.0) A record with headers is down-converted *without* them, and the fetch succeeds.**
  `AbstractRecords.downConvert()` @ 1.1.1 drops the headers for a magic below 2 ("Ignore headers when
  down-converting to V0 and V1 since they are not supported") and answers the partition with the error code **0**,
  where a 0.11.0.3 broker refused the whole conversion and answered **-1** with an empty record set. A client below
  Fetch v4 therefore reads such a partition happily and never learns that the records carried headers.
  → "Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v12)".
* **(0.11) A down-converted `LogAppendTime` batch stamps the timestamp type on every inner message.** A topic with
  `message.timestamp.type=LogAppendTime` and the default `message.format.version=0.11.0` stores a **record batch
  v2**, where the timestamp type is an attribute of the batch; converting it down to format v1 for a Fetch v2/v3
  rebuilds the set with `AbstractRecords.convertRecordBatch()`, and a magic 1 builder writes that timestamp type -
  and the append time - into **every** message it appends. The inner messages of the answer therefore carry the
  LogAppendTime bit and the append time, where a 0.10.2.2 broker, whose log held the client's own v1 set, left the
  inner attributes and `CreateTime` values untouched and set the bit on the wrapper alone. Either way a reader has
  to take the timestamp of the wrapper for the whole batch, which is what this client does.
  (`MessageFormatV1Test::testALogAppendTimeWrapperCarriesTheTimestampOfTheWholeCompressedBatch`.)

**The versions that KIP-124 raised (0.11)**

* **(0.11, superseded in 2.x) A 0.11 and a 1.1 broker never filled the `error_message` of GroupCoordinator v1.**
  The field is a `NULLABLE_STRING` that version 1 added right behind the error code, and every constructor of
  `FindCoordinatorResponse` that those brokers used set it to `null` — `this.errorMessage = null` in both public
  constructors — so it was `ff ff` for a successful lookup, for a lookup answered 15 while `__consumer_offsets` was
  being created and for a transactional id alike. **A 2.8.2 broker fills it**: every answer is built with
  `Errors.message()`, and the message of the error code 0 is the *name* `"NONE"`, see the group-membership block
  above. A client acts on `error_code` alone either way.
  (`ThrottleTimeApiTest::testTheErrorMessageOfACoordinatorAnswerIsTheNameOfItsErrorCode`.)
* **(0.11, superseded in 2.x) An unknown `coordinator_type` cost the connection instead of producing an error
  code.** On a 0.11 or 1.1 broker the type was parsed into an enum before the handler ever ran, and
  `FindCoordinatorRequest$CoordinatorType.forId` threw for anything but 0 and 1; `RequestChannel.Request` wrapped
  that in an `InvalidRequestException` and `SocketServer` closed the channel, exactly as for an unknown api key,
  with

  ```
  ERROR Closing socket for 172.18.0.2:9092-172.18.0.1:42964 because of error (kafka.network.Processor)
  org.apache.kafka.common.errors.InvalidRequestException: Error getting request for apiKey: 10 and apiVersion: 1
  Caused by: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Unknown coordinator type received: 7
  ```

  in the log. **A 2.8.2 broker answers the frame** with the error code 42 (`InvalidRequest`), the generic message
  of that code and the coordinator `-1:"":-1`, which is what the field always looked made for; the connection stays
  usable. `GroupCoordinatorRequest::COORDINATOR_TYPE_GROUP` and `…_TRANSACTION` are still the only two values a
  client may send. (`ThrottleTimeApiTest::testAnUnknownCoordinatorTypeIsAnsweredWithTheErrorCode42`.)
* **(0.11) The first lookup of a transactional id creates `__transaction_state`**, exactly as the first group
  lookup creates `__consumer_offsets`, and is answered with 15 (`GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable`) while that happens.
  On the container the topic appears with the 50 partitions of `transaction.state.log.num.partitions` and the
  replication factor 1 the image configures, and the next lookup answers 0 with broker 0. The id itself is neither
  created nor registered by the lookup — the broker only hashes the key onto a partition of that topic — so a
  lookup of an id that was never used is a normal question with a normal answer.
* **(0.11) Metadata v4 with `allow_auto_topic_creation = false` really creates nothing.** A request naming a topic
  the cluster does not have is answered with the topic error code **3** (`UnknownTopicOrPartition`) and an empty
  partition list, and `kafka-topics.sh --list` afterwards does not show the topic — where the same request with the
  flag `true`, or any version below 4, answers the code 5 (`LeaderNotAvailable`) and leaves a fresh topic behind.
  This is what lets `AdminClient::describeTopics()` be a question rather than a side effect.
  (`MetadataApiTest::testAVersionFourRequestWithoutAutoCreationDoesNotCreateTheTopic`.)
* **(0.11) Offsets v2 with `read_committed` answers the last stable offset, not the log end offset.** Without an
  open transaction the two are equal, which is why the vectors `offsets.response.v2.latest` and
  `offsets.response.v2.read-committed` carry the same offset; the difference only shows on a partition with an
  in-flight transaction, where the LSO stops at the first record of it. A consumer that fetches with
  `read_committed` has to list its end offsets with the same level, or it waits for records it will never be shown.
* **(0.11) The throttle time of every one of the fourteen apis is 0 on this container**, because it configures no
  quota at all. A non-zero one is only produced deliberately, by `QuotaThrottleTest`, which sets a
  `producer_byte_rate` for a client id of its own.

**(0.11) Transactions** — every bullet of this block was re-measured against the 1.1.1 container and answers as it
did on 0.11.0.3; the api block 24-28 is unchanged at version 0.

* **A fencing `InitProducerId` that has to roll a transaction back bumps the epoch by more than one.** The
  coordinator bumps the epoch once to fence the producer and abort the transaction it left open, and once more for
  the producer that is asking, and it answers **51** (`ConcurrentTransactions`) until the roll-back is through.
  Measured on the container: the epochs 0 and 1 for two lookups of an idle id, then a transaction opened with the
  epoch 1, and the next `InitProducerId` — after one 51 — answers the epoch **3**. A client may therefore not
  assume `epoch + 1`; the epoch of the answer is the only one that counts.
  → "InitProducerId API (key 22, v0 to v4)".
* **`EndTxn` is idempotent for a commit but not for an abort.** A transactional id in `CompleteCommit`
  that is asked to commit again is answered **0**; the same id asked to *abort* is answered **48**
  (`InvalidTxnState`). The state table of `TransactionCoordinator.handleEndTransaction` @ 0.11.0.3 accepts the
  result a completed transaction already has and refuses the other one, so a producer that lost the answer of its
  `EndTxn` may repeat it, and only that. `TransactionCoordinator.handleEndTransaction` @ 1.1.1 has the same table.
* **A `read_committed` fetch is not filtered by the broker.** It is bounded by the last stable offset and it
  carries an `aborted_transactions` array, but the aborted records and the ABORT control batch are in the answer:
  a partition with one aborted transaction of two records answers `hw = 3`, `lso = 3`, one aborted transaction,
  two batches and two records. The client drops them (see "Transactions"). A `read_uncommitted` fetch of the same
  partition answers `lso = -1` and `aborted_transactions = null`, and carries exactly the same bytes.
* **While a transaction is open, a `read_committed` fetch of its partition answers nothing at all.** The high
  watermark has moved past the records - a `read_uncommitted` reader sees them - but the last stable offset is
  still the first offset of the transaction, and the broker cuts the answer there: measured `hw = 2`, `lso = 0`,
  zero bytes of records.
* **The errors of AddPartitionsToTxn and TxnOffsetCommit are per partition, including the ones that are not about
  a partition.** Neither api has a top-level error code, so 47, 48, 49 and 51 - all statements about the
  transactional id - arrive repeated on every partition of the answer.
* **WriteTxnMarkers is the only answer of 0.11 without a `throttle_time_ms`**, and the unsecured container serves
  it to an ordinary client, which really appends the control batch it asks for.

**The admin, transaction and SASL apis of Kafka 2.0 (the KIP-219 bumps)**

* **(2.0) Fourteen apis of this group were raised by exactly one version, and not one byte of any frame changed.**
  CreateTopics v3, DeleteTopics v2, DeleteRecords v1, DescribeConfigs v2, AlterConfigs v1, AlterReplicaLogDirs v1,
  DescribeLogDirs v1, CreatePartitions v1, the four delegation-token apis v1, InitProducerId v1, AddPartitionsToTxn
  v1, AddOffsetsToTxn v1, EndTxn v1 and TxnOffsetCommit v1 are declared in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1 as
  `X_REQUEST_V<n> = X_REQUEST_V<n-1>`, answers included. The version is a **promise**, not a layout: a client that
  sends it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself. A 2.8.2 broker answers a throttled request of **every** version first
  and mutes the channel afterwards (`RequestHandlerHelper.sendResponseMaybeThrottle`: "Regardless of throttling,
  send the response immediately"), so the bump is visible on the wire only as the version field.
* **(2.8) A DescribeLogDirs answer names every topic of the log directory, whatever the request asked for.**
  `ReplicaManager.describeLogDirs` @ 2.8.2 groups **all** logs of a directory by topic and filters only the
  *partitions* inside those groups, so a request for one partition of one topic comes back with one entry per topic
  of the broker - the ones nobody asked for with an empty partition array. A 1.1.1 broker answered the requested
  topics alone. On the shared container of this line that is a 12 kB answer of a hundred foreign topics, which is
  why `describelogdirs.response.v1` is the one **constructed** vector of this line.
  → "DescribeLogDirs API (key 35, v0 to v2)".
* **(2.x) AlterReplicaLogDirs answers 3 for a partition the metadata cache does not know.** The catch block of
  `ReplicaManager.alterReplicaLogDirs` still maps a `NotLeaderOrFollowerException` to **9**
  (`ReplicaNotAvailable`) - "retaining REPLICA_NOT_AVAILABLE exception for ALTER_REPLICA_LOG_DIRS for
  compatibility" - but `getPartitionOrError` only raises that exception when `MetadataCache.contains(partition)`
  holds; for a topic the broker does not know, and for a partition index the topic does not have, it raises
  `UnknownTopicOrPartitionException` and the answer is **3**. A 1.1.1 broker answered 9 for all three cases.
  → "AlterReplicaLogDirs API (key 34, v0 to v2)".
* **(2.4) The `is_default` boolean of a DescribeConfigs v0 answer is always `false`.** From the release that
  generated the response from `DescribeConfigsResponseData`, `ConfigHelper.createTopicConfigEntry()` sets the
  config **source** and nothing ever calls `setIsDefault()`, so the field keeps the `false` of the generator - for
  an option the topic itself set and for an untouched default alike. A 1.1.1 broker wrote `is_default = (source ==
  DEFAULT_CONFIG)` into the same frame. The boolean has lost its meaning: a client that wants the source asks for
  version 1 or higher. → "DescribeConfigs API (key 32, v0 to v4)".
* **(2.x) `is_read_only` of a BROKER config entry no longer looks at the synonyms of the option.**
  `ConfigHelper.createBrokerConfigEntry()` @ 2.8.2 computes `readOnly = !AllDynamicConfigs.contains(name)`, where
  `AdminManager` @ 1.1.1 computed `!allNames.exists(AllDynamicConfigs.contains)` over the option **and its
  synonyms**. `log.retention.hours` is therefore read-only on a 2.8.2 broker and was writable on a 1.1.1 one,
  although `log.retention.ms` is dynamic in both. → "DescribeConfigs API (key 32, v0 to v4)".
* **(2.x) A topic that does not exist is the error code 3 for both config apis.** `ConfigHelper.describeConfigs()`
  asks the metadata cache before it reads anything (`if (metadataCache.contains(topic)) … else
  UNKNOWN_TOPIC_OR_PARTITION`) and `ZkAdminManager.alterTopicConfigs()` throws the same exception deliberately,
  where a 1.1.1 broker answered the **log defaults with the error code 0** for a describe and let the exception
  escape as the **-1** of an unexpected error for an alter. → "DescribeConfigs API (key 32, v0 to v4)" and
  "AlterConfigs API (key 33, v0 to v2)".
* **(2.4) The error code 59 (`UnknownProducerId`) is gone from the produce path.**
  `ProducerAppendInfo.checkSequence` @ 2.8.2 does not raise it at all: "If there is no current producer epoch
  (possibly because all producer records have been deleted due to retention or the DeleteRecords API) accept
  writes with any sequence number". A producer whose records were all deleted therefore keeps counting where it
  stood instead of numbering the partition from 0 again, and a first batch of a producer the broker knows nothing
  about is appended whatever sequence it carries. What is left of the idempotent guarantee is the **45**
  (`OutOfOrderSequence`) of a producer the broker does hold state of and the **47** of a fenced epoch.
  → "The idempotent producer".
* **(2.x) A successful SaslAuthenticate answer carries the EMPTY error message, not a null one.** The generated
  `SaslAuthenticateResponseData` initialises `ErrorMessage` with `""` and the authenticator never sets it on
  success, so the frame carries `00 00` where a 1.1.1 broker put the `ff ff` of a null string.
  → "SaslAuthenticate API (key 36, v0 to v2)".
* **(2.x) The 58 of a SASL/PLAIN token the mechanism cannot parse carries the message of the mechanism.**
  `Invalid SASL/PLAIN response: expected 3 tokens, got 1`, where a 1.1.1 broker answered the generic
  `Authentication failed due to invalid credentials with SASL mechanism PLAIN` for a malformed token as well as
  for a wrong password. → "SaslAuthenticate API (key 36, v0 to v2)".
* **(the image) `log.message.format.version=2.8-IV1` is in the `server.properties` of this container**, which the
  1.1.1 image did not write. Every topic therefore reports `message.format.version` with the source
  `STATIC_BROKER_CONFIG` next to `segment.bytes`, and neither of the two is a default although the topic itself
  sets nothing. → "DescribeConfigs API (key 32, v0 to v4)".
* **(2.1) The group coordinator stores a `committed_leader_epoch` without looking at it.** A TxnOffsetCommit v2 of
  a partition whose leader epoch is 0, sent with `committed_leader_epoch = 4242`, is answered with the error code
  **0** on the container: the epoch is data that travels with the offset, and the codes 74 `FencedLeaderEpoch` and
  75 `UnknownLeaderEpoch` are raised by the apis that read it back, not by the commit.
  → "TxnOffsetCommit API (key 28, v0 to v3)".
* **(2.1) The 73 `TopicDeletionDisabled` of DeleteTopics v3 cannot be produced on this container.**
  `delete.topic.enable` is `true` here and is not one of `DynamicBrokerConfig.AllDynamicConfigs`, so the branch
  `if (request.context.apiVersion < 3) Errors.INVALID_REQUEST else Errors.TOPIC_DELETION_DISABLED` of
  `KafkaApis.handleDeleteTopicsRequest` is documented from the sources; what the version buys is that code instead
  of the 42 a lower version keeps getting. → "DeleteTopics API (key 20, v0 to v6)".
* **(2.2) Every SaslAuthenticate v1 answer of this container carries the session lifetime 0.**
  `calcCompletionTimesAndReturnSessionLifetimeMs()` @ 2.8.2 sends 0 — "no expiration" — when neither
  `connections.max.reauth.ms` nor an expiring credential bounds the session, and the image sets no
  `connections.max.reauth.ms` on any listener while SASL/PLAIN has no expiry of its own. The option is
  **listener-wide**, so a suite that sets it would put every other suite of the shared container on a
  re-authentication clock; this line reads the field and implements no re-authentication.
  → "SaslAuthenticate API (key 36, v0 to v2)".
* **(2.2) A ControlledShutdown v2 with a broker epoch and an unknown broker id is -1, where v0 and v1 answer 8.**
  `doControlledShutdown` @ 2.8.2 checks the epoch **before** it checks that the broker is alive, and it reads the
  cached epoch out of `controllerContext.liveBrokerIdAndEpochs(id)`, a map with no entry for a broker id the
  cluster never had; the `NoSuchElementException` of that lookup comes back through `Try{}` as the unknown server
  error. Only `AbstractControlRequest.UNKNOWN_BROKER_EPOCH` (**-1**) skips the check and reaches the 8
  `BrokerNotAvailable` of the versions below, which is why -1 is the default of
  `AdminClient::controlledShutdown()` and the only epoch this repository sends.
  → "ControlledShutdown API (key 7, v0 to v3)".
* **(2.2) The per-partition error codes of ElectLeaders are not translated for a version 0 client.** The **84**
  `ElectionNotNeeded` and the **80** `PreferredLeaderNotAvailable` were added to `Errors.java` after the api, and a
  2.8.2 broker answers a version 0 request with them unchanged; only the **top-level** error code is left out of
  the v0 frame (`if (version >= 1)`), so the 31 of a client that may not `Alter` the cluster arrives per partition
  instead. A client of this api has to know the newer codes whatever version it sends.
  → "ElectLeaders API (key 43, v0 to v2)".
* **(2.2) An ElectLeaders with a null topic array answers with an empty result array on a healthy cluster.** The
  handler drops every `ELECTION_NOT_NEEDED` from the answer of an all-partitions election, and on a one-broker
  container every partition is already led by its only, preferred replica — so the whole cluster is 16 bytes of
  frame with zero topics in it. Measured once; no test of this repository sends that request, because it would
  elect for the partitions of every other suite of the shared container.
  → "ElectLeaders API (key 43, v0 to v2)".
* **(2.3) An APPEND or a SUBTRACT of an option name the broker does not know is the UNKNOWN SERVER ERROR, with no
  message at all.** `prepareIncrementalConfigs.listType()` @ 2.8.2 reads `val configKey = configKeys(configName)`
  and only then asks `if (configKey == null)`; `configKeys` is an immutable Scala `Map`, whose `apply` throws
  `NoSuchElementException` for a key it does not hold, so that null check is dead code and the exception falls
  through the catch block as **-1**. A `SET` of the very same name is the proper **40** `InvalidConfig` with
  `Unknown topic config name: not.an.option`, because it reaches the validation of the whole `Properties` instead.
  → "IncrementalAlterConfigs API (key 44, v0 and v1)".
* **(2.3) An APPEND or a SUBTRACT of an option that is not a list is 42, not 40.** `Config value append is not
  allowed for config key: retention.ms` is an `InvalidRequestException` of the handler, not a configuration error:
  the option exists and its value is fine, the operation is the thing the broker refuses. A client cannot tell from
  the code which of the two it got wrong, only from the message.
  → "IncrementalAlterConfigs API (key 44, v0 and v1)".
* **(2.3) The changes of one resource are applied all or nothing, and the broker checks the request itself first.**
  Two entries for the same option are **42** `Error due to duplicate config keys : retention.ms`, and a null value
  outside a DELETE is **42** `Null value not supported for : SET:retention.ms` - both before a single property is
  touched, so a resource that is refused keeps every value it had. The same holds for the broker resource: a
  request that names one option `DynamicBrokerConfig` cannot change at runtime refuses the whole resource with
  `Invalid config value for resource ConfigResource(type=BROKER, name=''): Cannot update these configs dynamically:
  Set(log.dirs)`. → "IncrementalAlterConfigs API (key 44, v0 and v1)".
* **(2.3) A DELETE gives an option back to the value it INHERITS, not to the documented default.** It removes the
  entry from the ZooKeeper node of the topic, and the next DescribeConfigs answers whatever the broker
  configuration says - which on this container is not the default for `message.format.version` and
  `segment.bytes`, see the observation about `log.message.format.version` above.
  → "IncrementalAlterConfigs API (key 44, v0 and v1)".
* **(2.4) A 2.8.2 broker creates a topic from the -1/-1 of KIP-464 whatever api version it was asked with.**
  `ZkAdminManager.createTopics` @ 2.8.2 resolves `NO_NUM_PARTITIONS` against `num.partitions` and
  `NO_REPLICATION_FACTOR` against `default.replication.factor` without looking at the version, so a **version 3**
  request of that shape is answered 0 on this container and creates the topic with 3 partitions and 1 replica. The
  version 4 of KIP-464 is therefore a **client-side** guard, not a broker check: the fallback is what the KIP
  added, so a broker of Kafka 2.3 or below answers the same bytes with 37 or 38.
  `CreateTopicsRequest.Builder.build(version)` @ 2.8.2 refuses the combination, and so does this client.
  → "CreateTopics API (key 19, v0 to v7)".
* **(2.4) An UNCLEAN election of a healthy partition is the same 84 as a preferred one.** The election type does
  not make the controller elect where nothing failed: `processReplicaLeaderElection` @ 2.8.2 asks
  `currentLeader == LeaderAndIsr.NoLeader || !liveBrokerIds.contains(currentLeader)` for an unclean election, and
  every partition that answers no to it lands in `alreadyValidLeader` with `ELECTION_NOT_NEEDED`. Measured on the
  container for both types, and for an unknown topic, which is the same 3 either way.
  → "ElectLeaders API (key 43, v0 to v2)".
* **(2.4) The top-level error code of an ElectLeaders v1 answer is 0 for everything that reaches the controller.**
  `handleElectReplicaLeader` @ 2.8.2 passes `ApiError.NONE` on the normal path and the 31
  `ClusterAuthorizationFailed` only when the authorizer refuses the client - the one case that never asks the
  controller and therefore names no partition. Measured 0 for a preferred election, an unclean one, an unknown
  topic and an all-partitions request. → "ElectLeaders API (key 43, v0 to v2)".
* **(2.6) The `config_type` of KIP-569 is filled whatever `include_documentation` says.**
  `ConfigHelper.createTopicConfigEntry` / `createBrokerConfigEntry` @ 2.8.2 end in
  `.setDocumentation(configDocumentation).setConfigType(dataType.id)`, where only the documentation is behind the
  flag - `if (includeDocumentation) … else null` - and the type is unconditional. Measured: a version 3 answer to a
  request without the flag carries the right type in every entry and the null string for the documentation.
  → "DescribeConfigs API (key 32, v0 to v4)".
* **(2.6) An unrestricted `include_documentation` answer is enormous.** The documentation strings are the prose of
  `ConfigDef.define(...)`: measured on the container, every option of a topic with documentation is 26 entries and
  **9 284 bytes**, and every option of the **broker** is 233 entries and **58 272 bytes** - against 74 bytes for the
  one option the vectors of this document ask for. A client that wants a type or a help text should name its
  `configuration_keys`. → "DescribeConfigs API (key 32, v0 to v4)".


## Error codes

The authority is `clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/protocol/Errors.java` @ 1.1.1, which ends at `71`.
The 0.10 line added the codes in three steps (**32-35** with 0.10.0, **36-42** with 0.10.1, **43-44** with 0.10.2),
Kafka 0.11 added **45-55** in one (45-47 the idempotent producer, 48-53 the transactions, 54-55 the ACL apis), and
this line adds **56-71** in two: **56-60** with Kafka 1.0 (a storage failure, a log directory, the SASL
authentication of KIP-152, the unknown producer id of the five-batch window, a reassignment in progress) and
**61-71** with Kafka 1.1 (the seven delegation-token codes of KIP-48, the two group codes of DeleteGroups and the
two fetch-session codes of KIP-227). Nothing above `71` exists on this branch — `LISTENER_NOT_FOUND` (72) is Kafka
2.0 — and `KafkaException::fromCode()` answers an unknown code with `UnknownErrorException`, which is what a client
should do with a code it has never heard of.

`R` marks the codes **this client** treats as retriable (`Common\Errors\RetriableException`), which is the set the
Java client marks with `RetriableException` and its subclass `InvalidMetadataException`, with the one documented
exception of the code 46 in the notes below. `Network\RetryPolicy` refreshes the metadata and sends the request
again for the codes 3, 5, 6 and 13.

Notes on the mapping:

* **Code 13 changed its meaning between the lines.** It was `StaleLeaderEpochCode` in `ErrorMapping.scala` @ 0.8.2.2
  and no broker ever sent it; from 0.9 it is `NETWORK_EXCEPTION`, whose Java class extends `InvalidMetadataException`
  and is therefore retriable. `NetworkException` on this branch carries that code and is also what the socket layer
  of this client raises for a connection that dies locally - **including the connection a 0.10 broker closes because
  it could not parse a frame**.
* **Code 4 is a leftover.** `Errors.java` skips it with a `// TODO: errorCode 4 for InvalidFetchSize`, but
  `ErrorMapping.scala` still maps `InvalidMessageSizeException` to it and the old Fetch path still produces it, so
  the class stays.
* **56, 70 and 71 are the only retriable codes of the sixteen this line adds**, as in `Errors.java` @ 1.1.1:
  `KafkaStorageException` extends `InvalidMetadataException` (the leader of the partition moved off the broker with
  the broken disk, so a metadata refresh finds a new one), and `FetchSessionIdNotFoundException` and
  `InvalidFetchSessionEpochException` extend `RetriableException` (the cure is one full fetch). The thirteen others
  are final. Note two identifiers that do **not** follow the Java client, and why: the code 58 is
  `SaslAuthenticationFailedException` here, because the Java name `SaslAuthenticationException` is already the
  client-side exception of this package, and the code 64 keeps the Java class name
  `UnsupportedByAuthenticationException` although its constant reads `DELEGATION_TOKEN_REQUEST_NOT_ALLOWED`.
* **59 `UnknownProducerId` extends `OutOfOrderSequenceException` here**, as `UnknownProducerIdException` does in
  `Errors.java` @ 1.1.1: it is the special case of an out-of-order sequence in which the broker knows why it lost
  track — the producer's records fell below the log start offset — and a producer answers it by resetting the
  sequence numbers of that partition instead of throwing the producer id away. See "The idempotent producer".
* **41 `NotController` is the only retriable code the 0.10 line adds.** `NotControllerException` extends
  `RetriableException` in `Errors.java` @ 0.10.2.2, because the cure is to look the controller up again and send the
  request to the new one; the other twelve are final. Note that code **40** is `InvalidConfigException` on this
  branch, not the `InvalidConfigurationException` of the Java client, whose name is already taken here by the
  client-side configuration error.
* **35 `UnsupportedVersion` never arrives from an api other than ApiVersions.** Every other key or version a 1.1.1
  broker cannot parse closes the connection instead of answering — ControlledShutdown included, which was the second
  exception up to 0.11 — see "An api the broker does not serve closes the connection".
* **46 `DuplicateSequenceNumber` is the only retriable code of the eleven Kafka 0.11 adds**, as in the Java client,
  where `DuplicateSequenceNumberException` extends `RetriableException` in `Errors.java` @ 0.11.0.3 (later releases
  renamed it `DuplicateSequenceException`). A duplicate sequence number means the batch is already in the log, so
  the idempotent producer treats the answer as a success rather than as something to send again; the flag records
  what the Java client says, not what this client does with it. `ConcurrentTransactions` (**51**) is not retriable
  in the hierarchy either, although the transactional producer retries it after a back-off.
* **A 1.1.1 broker never sends 46 to a client either.** Its duplicate check runs before the sequence validation and
  answers a duplicate with the code **0** and the offset of the original append — and on this line it does so for a
  duplicate of any of the **last five** batches of a producer id and partition
  (`ProducerStateManager.NumBatchesToRetain = 5`), where a 0.11 broker remembered one batch and answered **45** for
  anything older. The retriable flag of 46 therefore still describes a code this line implements from the
  specification, see "The idempotent producer".
* **47 is `INVALID_PRODUCER_EPOCH` in `Errors.java` but `ProducerFencedException` in `errors/`**, and this branch
  follows the exception name, as it does everywhere else — the class is what a caller catches.
* **42 `InvalidRequest` is what the broker log calls the frames it closes the socket for**, but it is not sent on
  the wire for them - the connection is already gone. It reaches a client only from an api that has a place to put
  it.
* The Scala sources speak of *consumers* where the Java ones speak of *groups* (`OffsetsLoadInProgressCode`,
  `ConsumerCoordinatorNotAvailableCode`, `NotCoordinatorForConsumerCode`, `UNKNOWN_CONSUMER_ID`,
  `IllegalConsumerGeneration`). The class names of this branch follow `main`, i.e. the group vocabulary.

**Which of them the container can produce.** The codes 29, 30, 31, 53 and 65 need an `authorizer.class.name` on the
broker and 44 a `create.topic.policy.class.name`; the container of `docker-compose.yml` runs without either, so
those six are implemented from the specification and not observed. **54 is observed**, though, and it is the code
that says so: an ACL api on a broker without an authorizer answers `SECURITY_DISABLED` with the message
`No Authorizer is configured on the broker`
(`ApiVersionProbeTest::testTheAclApisAreServedButDisabledWithoutAnAuthorizer`).

Of the sixteen codes this line adds, twelve are **observed today** — 58 and 59 by their own sections, 70 and 71 by
the fetch-session vectors of the Fetch section, and:

* **57** for an AlterReplicaLogDirs whose `log_dir` is not one of the two `log.dirs` of the image — and for a
  *relative* path that names one of them, because `LogManager.isLogDirOnline` compares absolute paths only. See
  "AlterReplicaLogDirs API (key 34, v0 to v2)", `tests/Integration/LogDirsApiTest.php` and the wire vector
  `alterreplicalogdirs.response.v0.unknown-log-dir`;
* **64** on every one of the four delegation-token apis over the PLAINTEXT listener
  (`ApiVersionProbeTest::testTheDelegationTokenApisRefuseAPlaintextConnection`, and again in
  `DelegationTokenApiTest`) — the container *has* a `delegation.token.master.key`, which is why the answer is not 61;
* **62, 63, 66 and 67** on the SASL listeners, all four of them measured against a token this client issued
  (`DelegationTokenApiTest`): 62 for an HMAC no token of the cluster has and for a token that was deleted, 63 for a
  principal that is neither the owner of a token nor one of its renewers, 66 for a token that is past its expiry or
  its maximum lifetime, and 67 for a renewer whose principal type is not `User`. The plan of this line expected
  none of them to be observable, because a token cannot be *used* without SASL/SCRAM — but every one of them is
  answered by the four apis of KIP-48 themselves, which need no SCRAM at all;
* **68** for a DeleteGroups of a group that still has a member and **69** for one the coordinator has never heard
  of, both as wire vectors of the DeleteGroups section (`deletegroups.response.v0.non-empty` and
  `deletegroups.response.v0`) and as integration tests of `AdminGroupApiTest`.

**58** is a wrong password over a SaslHandshake v1 exchange, see "SaslAuthenticate API (key 36, v0 to v2)"; **59** is a
producer whose records were deleted below the log start offset, see "The idempotent producer" and the vector
`produce.response.v5.unknown-producer-id`. **56** stays implemented from the sources although both apis that report
it are here: it needs a log directory that goes *offline*, and the two `log.dirs` of the container are the disks
every other test of the suite writes to. **70 and 71** are reachable only from a client that keeps a fetch
session (KIP-227): `FetchSessionApiTest` produces both by hand, and `FetchSessionConsumerTest` produces them under a
`KafkaConsumer`, which answers each of them with a full fetch of its own without the caller of `poll()` noticing.

The codes **60, 61 and 65** cannot be produced on this container at all — 60 needs a partition reassignment on a
multi-broker cluster, 61 a broker *without* a token master key (the image sets one, on purpose: without it the four
token apis would answer 61 instead of doing anything) and 65 an authorizer. Those three are implemented from
`Errors.java` alone.

The codes 72 and above (`LISTENER_NOT_FOUND` and everything after it) arrived with Kafka 2.0 and are not on this
branch.

The Java client calls the *client-side* exception of that code `SaslAuthenticationException`; in this package that
name belongs to the exception the socket layer raises to the application, which has existed since the 0.10 line and
is deliberately not a `KafkaException`, so the wire code is `SaslAuthenticationFailedException` and travels as its
cause.

## Wire vectors

Every frame below is a real frame of a real broker. A *request* vector is the frame this client sent and the broker
accepted, a *response* vector is the frame the broker sent back, byte for byte. There are exactly four exceptions,
all marked `source: constructed` in their vector file: `metadata.request.v0.all-topics`, which is built by the
client because a capture of the matching response would carry every topic of the test cluster,
`offsetfetch.response.v2.group-error`, whose group-level error code the single broker of the container cannot
produce (see the OffsetFetch section), and `describelogdirs.response.v1` and `describelogdirs.response.v2`, which
are the captured answers of the 2.8.2 container with the topics of the other suites removed - a 2.8.2 broker names
**every** topic of a log directory in that answer, whatever the request asked for (see the DescribeLogDirs
section).

**What this line captured on the `kafka-2-8-2` container.** The version bumps that KIP-219 gave the ten group apis
in Kafka 2.0 — OffsetCommit v4, OffsetFetch v4, FindCoordinator v2, JoinGroup v3, Heartbeat v2, LeaveGroup v2,
SyncGroup v2, DescribeGroups v2, ListGroups v2 and DeleteGroups v1 — are **20** frames, one request and one answer
each, and they are one life of one group: the client `kafka-client-t3-kip219` looks the coordinator of
`t3-kip219-group` up, joins it with a real `Subscription` for the topic `t3-kip219`, publishes the assignment of
the generation as its leader, heartbeats, commits and reads back an offset, describes the group and lists the
groups of the broker, leaves and finally deletes the group. Not one of those ten frames differs from the frame of
the version below it in anything but the api version field of its header.

**A vector is captured on the broker of the line that introduced the api version, and is not re-captured while the
frame does not change.** The api-key table above is what says whether it changed: a version that a 1.1.1 broker
still serves with the same schema still has the frame it had, which is why the vectors of the four lines below are
replayed against the classes of this line unchanged — a 1.1.1 broker still speaks every one of them. Concretely:

  **DeleteRecords, DescribeConfigs and AlterConfigs** (`delete-records.json`, `describe-configs.json`,
  `alter-configs.json`) are captured with the client id `t5-vectors` on one connection, against the topic
  `t5-vectors` (one partition, five records) and the broker resource `0` of the container. Every api contributes
  its happy path and two error cases: an offset above the high watermark and an unknown topic for DeleteRecords, a
  broker id the answering broker does not have for DescribeConfigs, and an unknown option name and a broker
  resource for AlterConfigs. The two `describeconfigs` requests name their options explicitly, because the answer
  for `config_names = null` is the ~40 entries of a whole topic or the ~180 of a broker.

  **InitProducerId and the idempotent producer** (`init-producer-id.json` and four more Produce v3 vectors) are
  captured with the client id `t7-vectors` over one connection: the request and the answer for a **null**
  transactional id, for the transactional id `t7-vectors-txn` - whose coordinator was looked up first, which is
  what creates `__transaction_state` - and for a `transaction_timeout_ms` of 999999999, which is the error code 50.
  The same connection produced the four Produce v3 frames of the idempotent producer against the topic
  `t7-vectors` (one partition): a batch of two records with the producer id of the first answer, the epoch 0 and
  the base sequence 0, the answer to *the very same frame sent again* - the error code 0 with the base offset of
  the original append - and the request and answer of a batch that starts at the sequence 9, which is the error
  code 45.

  **The transaction apis 24-28** (`add-partitions-to-txn.json`, `add-offsets-to-txn.json`, `end-txn.json`,
  `write-txn-markers.json`, `txn-offset-commit.json`) are captured with the client id `t8-vectors` over one
  connection, as one real transaction: the transactional id `t8-vectors-txn` writes two records into
  `t8-vectors`-0 (one partition of a three-partition topic), adds the offsets of the group `t8-vectors-group`,
  commits, and is then asked to abort the very transaction it committed, which is the error code 48. A second
  `InitProducerId` for the same id bumps its epoch, and the AddPartitionsToTxn that follows with the *old* epoch is
  the 47. `produce.request.v3.transactional` is the Produce v3 of that transaction, with the transactional id in
  the request and the attributes 0x10 on the batch. The transactional id `t8-vectors-abort-txn` writes two records
  into `t8-vectors-abort`-0 and **aborts** them, which is where `endtxn.request.v0.abort`, the `read_committed`
  answer `fetch.response.v5.aborted-transactions` with its non-empty `aborted_transactions` array, and the ABORT
  control batch `messageformat.v2.control.abort` come from. `writetxnmarkers.request.v0` is a real
  broker-to-broker frame that a client is allowed to send on an unsecured cluster: it writes a COMMIT marker for a
  plain producer id into `t8-vectors-marker`-0.

One group of vectors is not made of frames at all: the payloads of the consumer group protocol
(`consumer-protocol.json`, `kind: structure`) are the contents of a `member_metadata` or `member_assignment` byte
array, without a `Size` field and without a header, captured on the 0.9.0.1 container with the topic
`t6-consumer-protocol` (three partitions) from groups of Java `kafka-console-consumer.sh` members.

* What Kafka 1.x adds is captured on the **1.1.1** container that `docker-compose.yml` builds
  (`docker/kafka-1.1.1/`, four listeners, `log.message.format.version = 1.1-IV0`, two log directories and a
  delegation-token master key), one group of captures per api and with the same rule about the clock as the 0.11
  group. The two ApiVersions answers **`apiversions.response.v0` and `apiversions.response.v1`** were re-captured
  — the answer of this api *is* the api-key table, so it is re-captured on every line — and the **89** frames the
  line adds are the seven groups below: the two JBOD apis of KIP-113 (12 frames), SaslHandshake v1 and
  SaslAuthenticate (11), Produce v4/v5, Fetch v6/v7 and Metadata v5 (16), DescribeConfigs v1 with the dynamic
  broker configuration, CreatePartitions and DeleteGroups (28), the four delegation-token apis (14), the two
  Produce v5 pairs that Kafka 1.x changed for the idempotent producer (4) and the four Fetch v7 frames of the
  consumer side of a fetch session (4).
* What Kafka 2.x adds is captured on the **2.8.2** container that `docker-compose.yml` builds
  (`docker/kafka-2.8.2/`, four listeners, `inter.broker.protocol.version` and `log.message.format.version` at
  `2.8-IV1`, two log directories and a `delegation.token.secret.key`), one group of captures per api and with the
  same rule about the clock as the 0.11 group. The line is built one Kafka minor at a time, so this group grows
  with it. The three ApiVersions answers **`apiversions.response.v0`, `.v1` and `.v0.unsupported-version`** were
  re-captured first — the answer of this api *is* the api-key table, so it is re-captured on every line, and this
  broker answers 56 keys where the 1.1.1 one answered 43 — and the frames the line adds start with the **ApiVersions
  v2 pair** of KIP-219 (2), the version this client sends.

  **DescribeLogDirs and AlterReplicaLogDirs** (`describe-log-dirs.json`, `alter-replica-log-dirs.json`), the two
  JBOD apis of KIP-113: client id `t5-logdirs` on one connection, against the topic `t5-vectors-logdirs` (one
  partition, 1000 records of 8 KB, so that the mover needs long enough for its future log to be captured) and the
  two log directories `/tmp/kafka-logs` and `/tmp/kafka-logs-2` of the image. The group holds the two shapes of the
  nullable topic array - the **null** request, whose answer is *not* captured because it carries every partition of
  the container (235 207 bytes at the time of the capture), and the **empty** one with its 64-byte answer - the
  answer of one named partition, the answer taken **while a real move was running**, in which the partition is
  reported in both directories at once with `is_future = true` in the destination, and the three AlterReplicaLogDirs
  pairs: the accepted move, the 57 of a path that is not in `log.dirs`, and the 9 of a topic the cluster does not
  have.

  **SaslHandshake v1 and SaslAuthenticate v0** (`sasl-handshake.json`, `sasl-authenticate.json`): client id `t2` on
  the SASL_PLAINTEXT listener 9094, with the user `kafkatest` of the `jaas.conf` of the image, one connection per
  pair of frames - the accepted handshake and the token that authenticates on it, the same token with a wrong
  password (the error code **58** with the message of the broker), a handshake asking for `GSSAPI` (the 33), a
  second handshake (the 34 with an *empty* mechanism list) and a second `SaslAuthenticate` on the authenticated
  connection (the 34 that leaves it alive). The identical exchange was measured on the SASL_SSL listener 9095 and
  produces the same frames inside the TLS channel, so it contributes no vectors of its own. The **v0** vectors of
  the group are the ones captured on the 0.10.2.2 broker and are replayed unchanged, now through
  `SaslHandshakeRequestV0`: a 1.1.1 broker still serves the raw, unframed exchange, which was re-verified frame for
  frame on the same container.

  **Produce v4/v5, Fetch v6/v7 and Metadata v5** (`produce.json`, `fetch.json`, `metadata.json`): client id
  `t3-vectors` and the topic `t3-vectors` (three partitions, replication factor 1) over one connection. **Produce
  v4 and v5** write a record batch of two records into the partition 1 and into the partition 0, the second of
  them after a `DeleteRecords` had removed the first two records of that partition, which is where the
  `LogStartOffset = 2` of `produce.response.v5` comes from; the version 4 pair is the same body with the version 2
  answer, i.e. without that field. **Fetch v6** reads the partition 1 back, the version 5 frame with another api
  version in its header. **Fetch v7 and its sessions** (KIP-227) are six frames of one session: the full fetch
  with the epoch 0 that opens it over the partitions 1 and 2, the incremental fetch with an *empty* topics array
  that is answered with the one partition whose log grew, the incremental fetch that drops a partition in
  `forgotten_topics_data` and is answered without it although it had just been written to, and the two session
  errors - the epoch 99 of a live session (**71**) and the session id 2147483646, which the broker does not know
  (**70**). The session id of `fetch.response.v7` is the one the broker handed out on the day of the capture; it is
  a random non-zero int32 and means nothing beyond "a session was opened". **Metadata v5** is the metadata of
  `t3-vectors` with `allow_auto_topic_creation = false`, whose three partitions each end with the *empty*
  `offline_replicas` array of KIP-112/113 - the container has one broker, so no replica of anything can be offline.

  **DescribeConfigs v1, the dynamic broker configuration, CreatePartitions and DeleteGroups**
  (`describe-configs.json`, `alter-configs.json`, `create-partitions.json`, `delete-groups.json`): client id
  `t4-configs` over one PLAINTEXT connection, against the topics `t4-configs-own` (one partition, created with
  `segment.bytes=104857600` of its own, which is what gives its entry three synonyms of two different names) and
  `t4-configs-partitions` (one partition, raised to three), the broker resource `0` and the **default** broker
  resource, whose name is the empty string. The four DescribeConfigs v1 pairs are the topic with and without
  `include_synonyms`, the broker resource right after an AlterConfigs that set `log.cleaner.backoff.ms` on it - the
  source **2** with the static default behind it, and the sensitive `ssl.key.password` whose value is null in the
  entry and in its synonym - and the default resource with the source **3**. The three AlterConfigs pairs are that
  dynamic option (accepted), the same option on the default resource, and `log.retention.hours`, which is refused
  with 42 and `Cannot update these configs dynamically: Set(…)`; the two 0.11 vectors of a broker resource stay as
  history, because a 1.1.1 broker no longer refuses the frame at all. Every dynamic option was set back to its
  documented value and removed again right after the capture - the container is shared. CreatePartitions
  contributes the growth of a topic, an assignment with `validate_only`, a shrink (the 37) and an unknown topic (the
  3); DeleteGroups the group `t4-configs-group`, which committed an offset and was deleted while it was `Empty`
  (the 0, next to the 69 of a group that never existed in the same frame), and `t4-configs-member-group`, which a
  raw JoinGroup/SyncGroup member held while the delete was refused with **68** and released for the delete that
  followed.

  **The four delegation-token apis 38 to 41** (`delegation-tokens.json`, the one vector file of this repository
  that holds **several** apis - its `apiKey` is therefore null and every request vector carries the key of its own
  api): client id `t7-vectors` on the **SASL_PLAINTEXT** listener 9094 as the user `kafkatest` of the `jaas.conf`
  of the image, i.e. the principal `User:kafkatest`, plus two frames from the PLAINTEXT listener 9092 for the 64.
  The fourteen frames are one life of one token: it is created with the renewer `User:admin` and a maximum lifetime
  of one hour, described by its owner, renewed by ten minutes and finally deleted with a negative period, and the
  error cases are captured around it - the 67 of a renewer `Group:analytics`, the 63 of `User:admin` renewing a
  *second* token that names no renewer, the 62 of expiring the deleted token again, the 66 of a token created with
  `MaxLifeTime = 1`, and the 64 of a create and a describe over PLAINTEXT. Every token of the capture was expired
  again; the timestamps and the token ids are the ones of the day of the capture, and the hmac is the `HmacSHA512`
  of the token id under the master key of the image, which is public in `docker/kafka-1.1.1/`. The identical
  exchange was measured on the **SASL_SSL** listener 9095 and produces the same frames inside the TLS channel, so
  it contributes no vectors of its own.

  **The two frames a consumer adds to the fetch sessions** (`fetch.json`, four more Fetch v7 vectors): client id
  and topic `t8-vectors` (three partitions) over one raw connection, as the continuation of one session. The pair
  `fetch.request.v7.incremental-forgotten` is the request `FetchSessionHandler` builds after a rebalance - the
  topics array carries the positions of the two partitions that moved *and* `forgotten_topics_data` drops the third
  one, where T3's `fetch.request.v7.forgotten-topics` had an empty topics array - and its answer holds only the one
  partition whose log had grown. The pair `fetch.request.v7.close-existing` is the recovery from a session error:
  the session id of the client with the **epoch 0**, i.e. a full fetch that removes the old session and asks for a
  new one, answered with a **new** session id and with every partition of the request.

  **What Kafka 1.x changed for the idempotent producer** (`produce.json`, four more Produce v5 vectors): client id
  and topic `t6-idempotent` (one partition, replication factor 1) over one connection, with the producer id 574 of
  a `null` transactional id. Five batches of one record each are appended with the sequences 0 to 4; the first of
  them is then **sent again**, four batches back, and the answer is the error code 0 with the base offset 0 of the
  original append and the stored timestamp - the five-batch window of `ProducerStateEntry.NumBatchesToRetain` @
  1.1.1, where a 0.11.0.3 broker answered 45. A `DeleteRecords` to the offset 5 then removes every record of the
  partition, and the next batch of the same producer - base sequence 5 - is answered with the error code **59**
  `UNKNOWN_PRODUCER_ID` and the `LogStartOffset = 5` that Produce v5 exists for. The 0.11 group's four idempotent
  Produce **v3** frames (`t7-vectors`) are replayed unchanged next to them: the frame of a numbered batch, its
  duplicate and an out-of-order sequence did not change with the 1.x line, only what the broker answers to a
  duplicate that is no longer the last batch.

The same bytes live in machine-readable form in [`vectors/`](vectors), one file per api, together with the values
that each frame decodes into. `tests/Compliance` replays all of them through the request and response classes -
decode the frame, compare every field of the scheme, encode the message back and compare the bytes - and
`DocumentationSyncTest` checks that the dumps below and the vector files still hold the same bytes. Neither half can
therefore drift away from the code:

```bash
vendor/bin/phpunit --testsuite compliance
```

Each line of a dump is `<bytes>   # <path of the field> = <value>`; the path is the one of the scheme, e.g.
`topics[t10-vectors].partitions[0].leader`. A line without a comment continues the bytes of the line above it.

### `fetch.response.v1.throttled`

A fetch of a client that exceeded `consumer_byte_rate=1024`. The request started at the high watermark, so the
answer carries no record at all - and the broker still delayed it by 5943 ms, because the byte rate of the quota
window is what is over the bound, not this single answer.

<!-- vector: fetch.response.v1.throttled -->
```
00 00 00 2e                           # messageSize = 46
00 00 00 0c                           # correlationId = 12
00 00 17 37                           # throttleTimeMs = 5943
00 00 00 01                           # topics: 1 item(s)
00 0a 74 38 2d 76 65 63 74 6f 72 73   # topics[t8-vectors].topic = "t8-vectors"
```

that Kafka 0.11 added (KIP-124). It is the one api of the protocol that **appends** the field instead of prepending

### `apiversions.request.v2`

ApiVersions request v2, the version **this client sends**: the KIP-219 bump of Kafka 2.0, again the request header
and nothing else. Sending it is the promise that the client waits out a `throttle_time_ms` itself, because a broker
that throttles a v2 request answers first and mutes the channel afterwards.

<!-- vector: apiversions.request.v2 -->
```
00 00 00 21                                       # messageSize = 33
00 12                                             # apiKey = 18
00 02                                             # apiVersion = 2
```

### `apiversions.request.v3`

ApiVersions request v3, the version **this client sends** and the first flexible frame of the protocol: a request
header v2 whose `client_id` still carries an int16 length, an empty tag buffer behind it, the two compact strings of
KIP-511 and the empty tag buffer of the body.

<!-- vector: apiversions.request.v3 -->
```

00 12                                             # apiKey = 18
00 03                                             # apiVersion = 3
00 00 00 6a                                       # correlationId = 106
00 17 6b 61 66 6b 61 2d 63 6c 69 65 6e 74 2d 74   # clientId = "kafka-client-t1-vectors" (int16 length, never compact)
31 2d 76 65 63 74 6f 72 73
00                                                # TAG_BUFFER of the request header v2: no tagged field
18                                                # clientSoftwareName = "lisachenko-kafka-client" (compact: 23 + 1)
6c 69 73 61 63 68 65 6e 6b 6f 2d 6b 61 66 6b 61
2d 63 6c 69 65 6e 74
04                                                # clientSoftwareVersion = "2.8" (compact: 3 + 1)
32 2e 38
00                                                # TAG_BUFFER of the body: no tagged field
```

### `apiversions.response.v3`

The version 3 answer of the container: the same 56 keys, now as a **compact** array whose count is `56 + 1` in a
single byte and whose entries each end in a tag buffer of their own, and a body tag buffer that carries exactly one
of the three features of KIP-584 - the epoch `0`, which is on the wire because the default of the field is `-1`. The
answer opens with the correlation id and the error code directly: **this api keeps the response header v0** whatever
its version is, which is the one place in Kafka 2.8.2 where a flexible body travels behind a non-flexible header.

```
00 00                                             # errorCode = 0
```

### `apiversions.response.v3.invalid-software-name`

The answer to a v3 request whose `client_software_name` is `php/kafka`: the broker matches both KIP-511 strings
against `[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9\-.]*[a-zA-Z0-9])?` before it reads anything else and refuses the request with the
error code **42** (`InvalidRequest`) - not with the 35 of an unknown version, and not by closing the connection. The
api array is empty (the compact `01`), and the frame is the v3 layout, tag buffer included.

<!-- vector: apiversions.response.v3.invalid-software-name -->
```
00 00 00 0c                                       # messageSize = 12
00 00 00 6b                                       # correlationId = 107 (response header v0: this api never grew a tag buffer)
00 2a                                             # errorCode = 42 (InvalidRequest)
01                                                # apiVersions: 0 item(s) (compact count 0 + 1)
00 00 00 00                                       # throttleTimeMs = 0
00                                                # TAG_BUFFER of the body: 0 tagged field(s)
```

### `apiversions.response.v0.unsupported-version`

The answer to an ApiVersions request that carried the version **4**, which the broker does not serve: the error code
35 (`UnsupportedVersion`), written in the layout of version 0 - with no throttle time, although the same broker
serves the versions 1 and 2, because `RequestContext.parseRequest` @ 2.8.2 rebuilds such a request as a version 0
one. Two things about it are new in Kafka 2.4 and both are in these sixteen bytes: the array is **not empty**, it
carries the one row of the ApiVersions api itself so that the client learns which version to ask for (KIP-511), and
the request that produced it had to carry a **request header v2** - the broker reads the header of the version it
was asked for, and for this api that is the flexible header from version 3 on, so the same frame with the plain
header of the versions 0 to 2 is a parse failure and costs the connection. Every other key or version a 2.8.2 broker
cannot parse closes the connection as well; this one is answered, and the connection stays usable - the very next
ApiVersions v2 on the same socket was answered with the frame above.

<!-- vector: apiversions.response.v0.unsupported-version -->
```
00 00 00 10                                       # messageSize = 16
00 00 00 65                                       # correlationId = 101
00 23                                             # errorCode = 35 (UnsupportedVersion)
00 00 00 01                                       # apiVersions: 1 item(s)
00 12 00 00 00 03                                 # apiVersions[18] = ApiVersions, v0-v3
```

### `saslhandshake.request.v0`

SaslHandshake request v0 selecting the PLAIN mechanism. It is the very first frame of a connection to a SASL listener; only `ApiVersions` may precede it.

<!-- vector: saslhandshake.request.v0 -->
```
00 00 00 13               # messageSize = 19
00 11                     # apiKey = 17
00 00                     # apiVersion = 0
00 00 00 11               # correlationId = 17
00 02 74 38               # clientId = "t8"
00 05 50 4c 41 49 4e      # mechanism = "PLAIN"
```

### `saslhandshake.response.v0`

The answer of a broker that accepted the mechanism: error code 0 and its `sasl.enabled.mechanisms`.

<!-- vector: saslhandshake.response.v0 -->
```
00 00 00 11               # messageSize = 17
00 00 00 11               # correlationId = 17
00 00                     # errorCode = 0
00 00 00 01               # enabledMechanisms: 1 item(s)
00 05 50 4c 41 49 4e      # enabledMechanisms[0] = "PLAIN"
```

### `saslplain.token.client`

The initial response of the PLAIN mechanism for the user `kafkatest`, `authzid \0 authcid \0 passwd` (RFC 4616), as it travels after a **v0** handshake. The frame has no request header at all - the length prefix is the whole framing; `saslauthenticate.request.v0` is the very same payload with the header that Kafka 1.0 gave it.

<!-- vector: saslplain.token.client -->
```
00 00 00 1b                                       # token: 27 bytes
00                                                # authorization id = "" (empty)
6b 61 66 6b 61 74 65 73 74                        # user name = "kafkatest"
00
6b 61 66 6b 61 74 65 73 74 2d 73 65 63 72 65 74   # password = "kafkatest-secret"
```

### `saslplain.token.server`

The answer of a completed PLAIN exchange after a v0 handshake: the empty token of `PlainSaslServer.evaluateResponse()`, i.e. a frame that is nothing but a zero length. Ordinary requests follow it on the same connection. After a v1 handshake the same empty token is the `sasl_auth_bytes` of `saslauthenticate.response.v0`.

<!-- vector: saslplain.token.server -->
```
00 00 00 00   # token: 0 bytes
```

### `saslhandshake.request.v0.unsupported-mechanism`

SaslHandshake request v0 asking for GSSAPI on a broker whose `sasl.enabled.mechanisms` is `PLAIN`.

<!-- vector: saslhandshake.request.v0.unsupported-mechanism -->
```
00 00 00 14                  # messageSize = 20
00 11                        # apiKey = 17
00 00                        # apiVersion = 0
00 00 00 12                  # correlationId = 18
00 02 74 38                  # clientId = "t8"
00 06 47 53 53 41 50 49      # mechanism = "GSSAPI"
```

### `saslhandshake.response.v0.unsupported-mechanism`

Error code 33 (UnsupportedSaslMechanism) together with the mechanisms the broker does have. The broker closes the connection right after this frame, so there is no second chance on it.

<!-- vector: saslhandshake.response.v0.unsupported-mechanism -->
```
00 00 00 11               # messageSize = 17
00 00 00 12               # correlationId = 18
00 21                     # errorCode = 33 (UnsupportedSaslMechanism)
00 00 00 01               # enabledMechanisms: 1 item(s)
00 05 50 4c 41 49 4e      # enabledMechanisms[0] = "PLAIN"
```

### `saslhandshake.request.v1`

SaslHandshake request v1 selecting the PLAIN mechanism: the frame of v0 with another api version, and with it the promise that the tokens will follow inside `SaslAuthenticate` requests. It is the very first frame this client puts on a SASL connection.

<!-- vector: saslhandshake.request.v1 -->
```
00 00 00 13            # messageSize = 19
00 11                  # apiKey = 17
00 01                  # apiVersion = 1
00 00 00 15            # correlationId = 21
00 02 74 32            # clientId = "t2"
00 05 50 4c 41 49 4e   # mechanism = "PLAIN"
```

### `saslhandshake.response.v1`

The answer of a broker that accepted the mechanism - byte for byte the v0 answer, because the response schema of v1 *is* the one of v0.

<!-- vector: saslhandshake.response.v1 -->
```
00 00 00 11            # messageSize = 17
00 00 00 15            # correlationId = 21
00 00                  # errorCode = 0
00 00 00 01            # enabledMechanisms: 1 item(s)
00 05 50 4c 41 49 4e   # enabledMechanisms[0] = "PLAIN"
```

### `saslhandshake.request.v1.unsupported-mechanism`

SaslHandshake request v1 asking for GSSAPI on a broker whose `sasl.enabled.mechanisms` is `PLAIN`.

<!-- vector: saslhandshake.request.v1.unsupported-mechanism -->
```
00 00 00 14               # messageSize = 20
00 11                     # apiKey = 17
00 01                     # apiVersion = 1
00 00 00 19               # correlationId = 25
00 02 74 32               # clientId = "t2"
00 06 47 53 53 41 50 49   # mechanism = "GSSAPI"
```

### `saslhandshake.response.v1.unsupported-mechanism`

Error code 33 (UnsupportedSaslMechanism) with the mechanisms the broker does have; the version of the handshake changes nothing about that answer. The broker closes the connection right after this frame.

<!-- vector: saslhandshake.response.v1.unsupported-mechanism -->
```
00 00 00 11            # messageSize = 17
00 00 00 19            # correlationId = 25
00 21                  # errorCode = 33 (UnsupportedSaslMechanism)
00 00 00 01            # enabledMechanisms: 1 item(s)
00 05 50 4c 41 49 4e   # enabledMechanisms[0] = "PLAIN"
```

### `saslhandshake.request.v1.illegal-state`

A second SaslHandshake on a connection that already performed one: the handshake is answered exactly once.

<!-- vector: saslhandshake.request.v1.illegal-state -->
```
00 00 00 13            # messageSize = 19
00 11                  # apiKey = 17
00 01                  # apiVersion = 1
00 00 00 1e            # correlationId = 30
00 02 74 32            # clientId = "t2"
00 05 50 4c 41 49 4e   # mechanism = "PLAIN"
```

### `saslhandshake.response.v1.illegal-state`

The shortest SaslHandshake answer there is: error code 34 (IllegalSaslState) and an **empty** mechanism list, which is what a 1.1 broker puts into the error response (1.0.2 still filled it with `sasl.enabled.mechanisms`). The connection is closed after it. A v0 handshake never produces this frame - the second frame of such a connection is read as a token, and the socket goes away without an answer.

<!-- vector: saslhandshake.response.v1.illegal-state -->
```
00 00 00 0a   # messageSize = 10
00 00 00 1e   # correlationId = 30
00 22         # errorCode = 34 (IllegalSaslState)
00 00 00 00   # enabledMechanisms: 0 item(s)
```

### `saslauthenticate.request.v0`

SaslAuthenticate request v0 carrying the PLAIN token of the user `kafkatest`, sent right after the v1 handshake above. The `sasl_auth_bytes` are byte for byte the payload of `saslplain.token.client`, the frame a v0 exchange writes on the socket raw.

<!-- vector: saslauthenticate.request.v0 -->
```
00 00 00 2b                                       # messageSize = 43
00 24                                             # apiKey = 36
00 00                                             # apiVersion = 0
00 00 00 16                                       # correlationId = 22
00 02 74 32                                       # clientId = "t2"
00 00 00 1b                                       # saslAuthBytes: 27 bytes
00                                                # authorization id = "" (empty)
6b 61 66 6b 61 74 65 73 74                        # user name = "kafkatest"
00
6b 61 66 6b 61 74 65 73 74 2d 73 65 63 72 65 74   # password = "kafkatest-secret"
```

### `saslauthenticate.response.v0`

The answer of a completed PLAIN exchange: error code 0, no message at all (`ff ff`, the null of a NULLABLE_STRING) and the empty token of `PlainSaslServer.evaluateResponse()`. There is no `throttle_time_ms` - the api is one of the five KIP-124 left out. Ordinary requests follow it on the same connection.

<!-- vector: saslauthenticate.response.v0 -->
```
00 00 00 0c   # messageSize = 12
00 00 00 16   # correlationId = 22
00 00         # errorCode = 0
ff ff         # errorMessage = null
00 00 00 00   # saslAuthBytes: 0 bytes
```

### `saslauthenticate.request.v0.invalid-credentials`

The same request with a wrong password for an existing user.

<!-- vector: saslauthenticate.request.v0.invalid-credentials -->
```
00 00 00 27                           # messageSize = 39
00 24                                 # apiKey = 36
00 00                                 # apiVersion = 0
00 00 00 18                           # correlationId = 24
00 02 74 32                           # clientId = "t2"
00 00 00 17                           # saslAuthBytes: 23 bytes
00                                    # authorization id = "" (empty)
6b 61 66 6b 61 74 65 73 74            # user name = "kafkatest"
00
77 72 6f 6e 67 2d 73 65 63 72 65 74   # password = "wrong-secret"
```

### `saslauthenticate.response.v0.invalid-credentials`

What Kafka 1.0 added to the exchange: the error code 58 and the message of the broker, where a 0.11 broker closed the connection without a word. An unknown user is answered with exactly the same frame - the two are deliberately indistinguishable - and the connection is closed right after it.

<!-- vector: saslauthenticate.response.v0.invalid-credentials -->
```
00 00 00 3f                                                                     # messageSize = 63
00 00 00 18                                                                     # correlationId = 24
00 3a                                                                           # errorCode = 58 (SaslAuthenticationFailed)
00 33                                                                           # errorMessage: 51 bytes
41 75 74 68 65 6e 74 69 63 61 74 69 6f 6e 20 66 61 69 6c 65 64 3a 20 49 6e 76   # errorMessage = "Authentication failed: Invalid username or password"
61 6c 69 64 20 75 73 65 72 6e 61 6d 65 20 6f 72 20 70 61 73 73 77 6f 72 64
00 00 00 00                                                                     # saslAuthBytes: 0 bytes
```

A second SaslAuthenticate on an authenticated connection reaches `KafkaApis.handleSaslAuthenticateRequest` instead of the authenticator, which answers the error code 34 with this message - and, unlike every other refusal of the exchange, leaves the connection usable.

<!-- vector: saslauthenticate.response.v0.illegal-state -->
```

00 00 00 1c                                                                     # correlationId = 28
00 22                                                                           # errorCode = 34 (IllegalSaslState)
00 41                                                                           # errorMessage: 65 bytes
53 61 73 6c 41 75 74 68 65 6e 74 69 63 61 74 65 20 72 65 71 75 65 73 74 20 72   # errorMessage = "SaslAuthenticate request received after successful authentication"
65 63 65 69 76 65 64 20 61 66 74 65 72 20 73 75 63 63 65 73 73 66 75 6c 20 61
75 74 68 65 6e 74 69 63 61 74 69 6f 6e
00 00 00 00                                                                     # saslAuthBytes: 0 bytes
```

### `createtopics.request.v1`

CreateTopics request v1 that creates one topic with two partitions, one replica per partition, no explicit replica assignment and one topic level option, waiting up to 30 seconds for the controller.

<!-- vector: createtopics.request.v1 -->

### `messageformat.v2.none.control`

The control batch that the transaction coordinator appended when the transaction above was committed: the attributes are 0x30 (transactional and control), the batch holds one record whose key is the version 0 and the type 1 (COMMIT) and whose value is the version 0 and the coordinator epoch 0, and baseSequence is -1. A client never hands such a record to an application.

<!-- vector: messageformat.v2.none.control -->
```

00 00 00 42               # batches[0].batchLength = 66
00 00 00 00               # batches[0].partitionLeaderEpoch = 0
02                        # batches[0].magic = 2
b8 ef 36 37               # batches[0].crc = 3102684727 (CRC-32C of everything from attributes on)
00 30                     # batches[0].attributes = 0x0030 (codec none, CreateTime, transactional, control)
00 00 00 00               # batches[0].lastOffsetDelta = 0 (last offset 2)
00 00 01 a0 85 c3 dc 9c   # batches[0].firstTimestamp = 1788950600860
00 00 01 a0 85 c3 dc 9c   # batches[0].maxTimestamp = 1788950600860
00 00 00 00 00 00 00 02   # batches[0].producerId = 2
00 01                     # batches[0].producerEpoch = 1
ff ff ff ff               # batches[0].baseSequence = -1 (last sequence -1)
00 00 00 01               # batches[0].recordCount = 1
20                        # batches[0].records[0].length = 16
00                        # batches[0].records[0].attributes = 0
00                        # batches[0].records[0].timestampDelta = 0 (timestamp 1788950600860)
00                        # batches[0].records[0].offsetDelta = 0 (offset 2)
08                        # batches[0].records[0].key: 4 bytes
00 00                     # the control record key: version = 0
00 01                     # type = 1 (COMMIT)
0c                        # batches[0].records[0].value: 6 bytes
00 00                     # the end transaction marker: version = 0
00 00 00 00               # coordinatorEpoch = 0
00                        # batches[0].records[0].headers: 0 item(s)
```

### `fetch.response.v5.aborted`

A read_committed answer of a partition whose only transaction was aborted: one entry in AbortedTransactions with the
producer id of that transaction and the first offset it wrote. The record set still holds both batches - the
transactional data batch at the offset 0 and the control batch with the ABORT marker that the coordinator wrote at the
offset 1 - because the broker does not filter anything: dropping the records of an aborted producer is the job of the
consumer.

### `initproducerid.request.v0`

InitProducerId request v0 of an idempotent producer: a null transactional id, which any broker answers with a
producer id of its own block, and the `transaction.timeout.ms` default of 60000 ms, which it ignores for a null id.

<!-- vector: initproducerid.request.v0 -->
```
00 00 00 1a                           # messageSize = 26
00 16                                 # apiKey = 22
00 00                                 # apiVersion = 0
00 00 00 01                           # correlationId = 1
00 0a 74 37 2d 76 65 63 74 6f 72 73   # clientId = "t7-vectors"
ff ff                                 # transactionalId = null
00 00 ea 60                           # transactionTimeoutMs = 60000
```

### `initproducerid.response.v0`

The answer for a null transactional id: the next producer id of the block the broker reserved in ZooKeeper, always
with the epoch 0. Every request answers a new id.

<!-- vector: initproducerid.response.v0 -->
```
00 00 00 14               # messageSize = 20
00 00 00 01               # correlationId = 1
00 00 00 00               # throttleTimeMs = 0
00 00                     # errorCode = 0
00 00 00 00 00 00 00 0b   # producerId = 11
00 00                     # producerEpoch = 0
```

### `initproducerid.request.v0.transactional`

InitProducerId request v0 of a transactional producer: only the transaction coordinator of `t7-vectors-txn` may
answer it, and the transaction timeout is the one the coordinator holds against `transaction.max.timeout.ms`.

<!-- vector: initproducerid.request.v0.transactional -->
```
00 00 00 28                                       # messageSize = 40
00 16                                             # apiKey = 22
00 00                                             # apiVersion = 0
00 00 00 03                                       # correlationId = 3
00 0a 74 37 2d 76 65 63 74 6f 72 73               # clientId = "t7-vectors"
00 0e 74 37 2d 76 65 63 74 6f 72 73 2d 74 78 6e   # transactionalId = "t7-vectors-txn"
00 00 ea 60                                       # transactionTimeoutMs = 60000
```

### `initproducerid.response.v0.transactional`

The answer of the transaction coordinator: the producer id that `__transaction_state` holds for the id, with the
epoch 0 of its very first producer. Every later request for the same id answers the same producer id with a higher
epoch, which fences the producer before it - one higher for an id that has no transaction open, two higher for one
whose open transaction the coordinator has to roll back first.

<!-- vector: initproducerid.response.v0.transactional -->
```
00 00 00 14               # messageSize = 20
00 00 00 03               # correlationId = 3
00 00 00 00               # throttleTimeMs = 0
00 00                     # errorCode = 0
00 00 00 00 00 00 00 0c   # producerId = 12
00 00                     # producerEpoch = 0
```

```
3b 9a c9 ff                                       # transactionTimeoutMs = 999999999
```

### `produce.response.v3.duplicate`

The answer to the very same frame sent a second time, the retry of a batch whose acknowledgement got lost: the
broker recognises the triple (producer id, epoch, sequence range) of the batch it appended last and answers the
error code 0 with the offset of that **original** append, without writing anything. The `LogAppendTime` gives it
away - the topic keeps the `CreateTime` of the producer, so a real append answers -1 there, while a duplicate is
answered with the timestamp the log holds for the batch.

<!-- vector: produce.response.v3.duplicate -->
```

00 00 00 06                           # correlationId = 6
00 00 00 01                           # topics: 1 item(s)

00 00 00 00                           # topics[t7-vectors].partitions[0].partition = 0
00 00                                 # topics[t7-vectors].partitions[0].errorCode = 0
00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00               # topics[t7-vectors].partitions[0].baseOffset = 0
00 00 01 a0 86 49 bf dc               # topics[t7-vectors].partitions[0].logAppendTime = 1788959375324
00 00 00 00                           # throttleTime = 0
```

EndTxn v0 with `TransactionResult = 1`: commit the transaction of `t8-vectors-txn`. The single boolean
byte is the whole difference between a commit and an abort.

```
00 1a                                             # apiKey = 26
00 00                                             # apiVersion = 0
00 00 00 bd                                       # correlationId = 189

00 02                                             # producerEpoch = 2
01                                                # transactionResult = true
```

The answer to a commit: the error code 0 means that the coordinator wrote its decision into
`__transaction_state`, not that the control batches are in the partitions.

<!-- vector: endtxn.response.v0 -->
```
00 00 00 0a   # messageSize = 10
00 00 00 bd   # correlationId = 189
00 00 00 00   # throttleTimeMs = 0
00 00         # errorCode = 0
```

### `produce.response.v5.duplicate-in-window`

The answer of a **1.1.1** broker to that duplicate: the error code 0 and the base offset 0 of the original append, four batches back. A 0.11.0.3 broker, which kept a single batch per producer and partition, answered 45 (OutOfOrderSequence) for anything but the very last one; `ProducerStateEntry.NumBatchesToRetain = 5` @ 1.0.2 and 1.1.1 is what widened it to the last five. The `LogAppendTime` of 1789060611437 gives the duplicate away - the topic keeps the `CreateTime` of the producer, so a real append answers -1 there - and the `LogStartOffset` of version 5 is 0, the partition being untouched.

### `produce.response.v5.unknown-producer-id`

The error code **59** UNKNOWN_PRODUCER_ID (Kafka 1.0): `ProducerStateManager.truncateHead()` dropped the entry of every producer whose last record fell below the new log start offset, and a batch of a producer the broker has no entry for that does not start at the sequence 0 is answered with this code rather than with the 45 of a 0.11.0.3 broker. The `LogStartOffset` of 5 is what Produce v5 exists for here: it is above the offset 4 this producer last had acknowledged, so its records really were deleted, and the client numbers the partition from 0 again instead of throwing its producer id away.

<!-- vector: produce.response.v5.unknown-producer-id -->

```
00 00 00 01                                    # topics: 1 item(s)
```

### `produce.response.v6.throttled`

The answer of a Produce v6 request that a producer_byte_rate quota of 1024 bytes per second throttled: the batch was appended - the error code is 0 and the base offset is real - and the ThrottleTime behind the topics array is the 2381 ms the broker is about to mute the channel for. The answer itself arrived about 1 ms after the request was written: KIP-219 (Kafka 2.0) makes a broker answer a request of these versions first and delay afterwards, where a version 5 request would have waited the whole 2381 ms before its answer arrived.

<!-- vector: produce.response.v6.throttled -->
```
00 00 00 3a                           # messageSize = 58
00 00 00 2a                           # correlationId = 42
00 00 00 01                           # topics: 1 item(s)
00 0a 74 32 2d 76 65 63 74 6f 72 73   # topics[t2-vectors].topic = "t2-vectors"
00 00 00 01                           # topics[t2-vectors].partitions: 1 item(s)
00 00 00 00                           # topics[t2-vectors].partitions[0].partition = 0
00 00                                 # topics[t2-vectors].partitions[0].errorCode = 0
```

### `offsetdelete.response.v0.non-empty-group`

A group that has a live member and is **not** a `consumer` group - its members joined with another protocol type - falls into the `case _` of `GroupCoordinator.handleDeleteOffsets` and is refused as a whole with the top-level **68** (`NonEmptyGroup`). The answer is 18 bytes: the error code, the throttle time and an empty topic array, so nothing is said about the partitions of the request.

<!-- vector: offsetdelete.response.v0.non-empty-group -->
```

00 00 12 6a   # correlationId = 4714
00 44         # errorCode = 68
00 00 00 00   # throttleTimeMs = 0
00 00 00 00   # topics: 0 item(s)
```

### `offsetdelete.response.v0.group-id-not-found`

A group the coordinator has never heard of is the top-level **69** (`GroupIdNotFound`), in the same 18 bytes. A group that *had* offsets and lost the last of them answers this too, because deleting the last committed offset of an `Empty` group transitions it to `Dead` and removes it from the cache.
